detail.text: Her deck arrived after the talk (files/rousselot-whey-collagen-deck.pdf, 23 pages). Slides 17 to 23 come after the closing "Thank you" slide and are not in the recording (see the last bullet).

Whey launches: food and beverage supplement launches featuring whey grew 7.53% a year from 2023 to 2025 (she said seven and a half percent), from about 18,600 in 2023 to about 19,800 in 2024 and 21,600 in 2025, read from the chart [00:10] (slide 3).

The "8.7" she gave as the biggest growth yet is, on the slide, the 2024 to 2025 rise of +8.73% in the average price of those launches: US$3.17 per 100 g in 2023, US$3.32 in 2024, US$3.61 in 2025 and US$3.78 in 2026 to date [00:10] (slide 3).

WPC80 price: she said "in 2023 the price of a ton of whey protein concentrate of 80% was 5.7 k, whereas in 2026 it's almost 32 k. So really, in just three years' time, it's almost a sixfold" [00:10]. The slide gives US$5.7k a tonne in June 2023 and US$31.7k in June 2026; the slide's sources are Mintel and Vesper, and it does not say which market the price is for (slide 3).

Another speaker's view of the same price: Alan Johnstone (Nutrilution, unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of) used Vesper's EU price in euros a kilogram: WPC80 about €5.2 in June 2023 and €27.4 in June 2026, read from his chart, and €27.00 in the week of 25 August 2026. Hers is in US dollars a tonne (US$5.70 and US$31.70 a kilogram). The two differ in currency and unit; both show close to a sixfold rise.

Her drivers, which she said mean "those prices will be here to stay": demand from active lifestyle consumers, GLP-1 users advised to take extra protein, and China; whey is a by-product of cheese and cannot be scaled easily; gas, electricity, labour, filtration costs, tariffs, geopolitics and climate push the same way [00:10]. The slide groups them as supply and demand imbalance, rising production and operational costs, and global economic and environmental factors, citing The Guardian, Rabobank, ScienceInsights and New Hope Network (slide 4).

Whey and collagen launches by year, read from the chart: about 320 in 2023, 320 in 2024, 420 in 2025 and 520 in 2026 to date. The chart's sources are Mintel, Holland & Barrett, ON, David and Rousselot (slide 6).

Whey is a complete protein rich in BCAAs, for muscle building and repair. Peptan is hydrolysed collagen, rich in hydroxyproline (unique to animal-derived collagen and, she said, linked to holistic health benefits), glycine and proline [00:10]. The slide adds that whey lacks hydroxyproline and Peptan lacks tryptophan (slide 8).

The head-to-head (Robberechts et al., 2023, IJSNEM): randomised, double-blind, parallel; 22 healthy, active men; 45 g whey against 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan a day; three weeks of training; jump height and creatine kinase measured; no difference between groups at the end [00:10] (slide 9).

Soreness (Clifford et al., 2019): 24 men, 2 × 10 g Peptan or maltodextrin placebo with vitamin C from day -7 to day 2, with doses 40 minutes before and straight after 150 drop jumps on day 0; soreness and muscle power at 48 hours. She described it as seven days of 20 g [00:10] (slide 10).

Endotoxins (Taylor et al., 2022): randomised, double-blind, cross-over; 20 men; 10 g Peptan or flavoured water for seven days, the last dose 45 minutes before a 70-minute run; endotoxins were the same as without exercise, while on placebo they rose. Her hedge: "...it's really an indication that taking in peptan could lessen the amount of endotoxins in your blood and could reduce your digestive discomfort" [00:10]. The slide: "Peptan could lessen the increase of blood endotoxin levels, a known cause of inflammation" (slide 11).

Knees (Jiang et al., 2014): randomised, placebo-controlled; women with mild knee discomfort, 8 g a day for six months; joint discomfort (WOMAC) fell 10% at three months and 24% at six, and joint function (Lysholm) rose 4% and 7%, the chart marks each change p < 0.001 [00:10] (slide 12).

Sleep (Thomas et al., 2023): randomised, double-blind, cross-over; 13 men; 15 g an hour before bed for seven days; polysomnography on night seven. The slide gives a 30% reduction in awakenings; on the chart they fell from about 30 to about 21, read from the chart, where she said "around 30 to 22, something like that". On the Stroop test the Peptan group scored about 1.00 against about 0.97 for control, read from the chart; she said the Peptan group "performed perfectly, 100%" [00:10] (slide 13).
Rousselot offers roundtables on application advantages and help incorporating collagen [00:10] (slide 15).

Slides after the close: Nextida GC, which Rousselot says was "specifically developed to target post-meal glucose spikes & boost GLP-1 secretion". Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (pilot 2024: 16 people, 5 g or 10 g; confirmation 2026: 30 people, 10 g; each taken 30 minutes before a carbohydrate-rich meal). Citing the 2026 study, for 10 g against placebo the slides give a 37% lower glucose spike, a 47% lower glucose peak, 82% more total GLP-1 exposure, a 53% higher GLP-1 response, a 70% higher GIP response and a lower post-meal insulin response. A 2026 Ipsos consumer study for Rousselot in the US (5 g twice a day for six weeks, N = 181) found 80% felt fuller for longer and 55% reported weight loss; the slide says this "does not constitute a consumer-facing claim" (slide 17) (slide 19) (slide 20) (slide 21) (slide 22) (slide 23).

takeaways.text: Brands have three responses to whey costs: raise the price, shrinkflation, or smarter formulation with protein blends, which she called the most elegant and a way to stand out on shelf [00:10] (slide 5).

Launches combining whey and collagen grew at 17.44% a year from 2023 to 2026 to date, led by snacks, cereals and energy bars (39.7%) and nutritional and meal replacement drinks (36.4%); her example, Optimum Nutrition's clear whey isolate with collagen, has 10 g of each [00:10] (slide 6).
Collagen supply is spread across bovine, porcine, chicken and fish, and its historical prices fluctuate far less than whey's [00:10].
Whey and collagen are "no competitors": whey for muscle, Peptan (rich in hydroxyproline, glycine and proline) for ligaments, tendons, joints and bone [00:10] (slide 8).

In 22 men over three weeks of training, 25 g whey plus 20 g Peptan a day gave the same recovery and performance as 45 g whey; the slide says such blends "may provide broader support across the musculoskeletal system" [00:10] (slide 9).

2 × 10 g Peptan a day with vitamin C, for a week before 150 drop jumps and two days after, gave 28% less muscle soreness and 13% faster muscle recovery than placebo; the slide marks the soreness result as a likely benefit and the recovery result as significant [00:10] (slide 10).

quotes.text: "So people should no longer ask when will whey prices go down, but what can we do to work around this?" Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]

"...there are more and more launches of products combining whey and collagen, so steady increase over the last couple of years, and yeah, actually an average growth rate of 17.5 percent almost." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
"...these two are no competitors; these two already complementary, and when you add in both, you can have extra additional health benefits." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]
"So actually, the athletes, the recovery was the same, the performance was the same, but you also have more support in your movement system..." Speaker unknown (Tess Plaquet) [00:10]

followups: Find the papers the deck cites: Robberechts et al. 2023 (IJSNEM), Clifford et al. 2019, Taylor et al. 2022, Jiang et al. 2014 and Thomas et al. 2023. Slide 10 gives Clifford et al. the DOI that slide 8 gives Aussieker et al. 2025, so check which paper the soreness figures come from (slide 8) (slide 10).
Ask Rousselot which market the WPC80 price on slide 3 is for (slide 3).
Question for us: what head-to-head data would show a pea isolate replacing part of the whey without loss of performance? (my reading).

# Built in the gym: Turning athlete insight into sports nutrition innovation: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Marchon - Fireside - SNS", https://otter.ai/u/pZI1Kf2nvFAS-7PcfNZZlCOVpH0, recorded 9 Nov 2026 12:05, 23m 1s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Olivia Haslam - NutraIngredients: Welcome to the stage the team behind March on Ollie Marchon, founder and Liam Bones, head of product. Okay, guys. Thank you so much for joining us. Okay, God, I've got a million questions for you. Where to start? Okay, so we've we we both heard, and we know this already, about how performance nutrition is no longer the domain of these elite athletes and kind of serious bodybuilders. It's much more broader, much more mainstream consumers. From your perspective, both of you, what has fundamentally changed in the way that people think about nutrition and performance, and what new demands has created the industry?
[00:54] Speaker 1 (Ollie Marchon): I'll go first. We've seen the rise of the every athlete. I think this has been born more prominently probably over the last five years. We've seen the running boom. We've seen the boom of high rocks. We've seen increase in people participating in strength. Now that's something that everyone's kind of engaging with. Someone just before mentioned the GLP-1. So I think those three categories: sort of running, evolving into functional fitness competitions, and striving to achieve things outside the gym, plus people in the gym now thinking about sets and reps and objectively measuring their strength. We've seen this this rise of the everyday athlete, and we categorize it into into into three. We've got the the inspired by every athlete that's looking to build those habits and routines, getting into the gym 345 times a week. They're looking for feeling based improvements, and I think our nutrition and supplementation goes towards how do we make someone feel better. So we're thinking about micronutrient deficiencies. We think about the given multivitamin, the omega, improving their sleep, and we'll always go from a food-first approach. But for these people, it's just about building those those incremental improvements through habits and routines. The driven buy is they're looking for objectively how can I measure my progress inside the gym and outside of it. They're they're worrying about their marathon time. They're worrying about their high rocks time. They're thinking about their their personal bests inside the gym, and for those people, we're thinking about nutrition strategies that might involve nutrient timing. What do they do before they work out, during the workout, and post workout? So slightly more sophisticated goals for them. And the third category we see is like live by. So they are really the optimizer for everything. So they're thinking about this 24 hour clock. How can I think about my nutrition strategy, my recovery strategy, my supplement stack, my training goals, and for all like good intents and purposes, they might identify as a nine-to-five corporate person, but their their number one priority that day is is their health and wellness, and when they get their training session done. So, we've seen a big shift of people prioritizing their training session first thing in the morning. When we look across our sort of 8,000 people that use our training app every day, most of them are training at 6:00 in the morning. We look across 50 people that use our gyms every day. Again, most of them train first in the morning. So their nutritional performance at that time in the day that are slightly different to those that maybe train pre-COVID times, where they had less flexibility after work, where they're maybe in a better fed state. Yeah, I mean,

summary.Summary:
Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients talked with Ollie Marchon, founder of the UK brand Marchon, and Liam Holmes, its head of product, about what the rise of the everyday athlete means for sports nutrition.

Ollie described three kinds of consumer: those inspired by training, who want habits and to feel better; those driven by it, who measure progress and time their nutrients; and those who live by it, planning the whole day around training. Most people on Marchon's training app train at 6 in the morning, which changes what they need. Liam argued for situational formats, such as carbohydrate in a pre-workout for people who cannot eat first.

Ollie said awareness of supplements is high but understanding lags, so education, honest positioning and effective doses matter more than hype. Creatine shows how this works: decades of research and podcast voices did the selling, and it built the daily supplement habit. Liam sees creatine as here to stay and moving into cognition; for ingredient suppliers, the challenge is stability in water, gummies and other formats. Claims are a regulatory nightmare, so Marchon adds ingredients to products already in people's routines.

Asked where the category goes in five years, Liam answered: formats that improve compliance.

The founders of **Marchon** discussed the evolution of performance nutrition from an elite niche to a mainstream market driven by everyday athletes.

## Consumer Segments
**Ollie** and **Liam** identified three distinct consumer categories shaping the current industry landscape:
*   **Inspired Athletes**: Individuals focused on building habits and feeling better through micronutrients, sleep, and food-first approaches.
*   **Driven Athletes**: Goal-oriented consumers interested in objective metrics like marathon times or personal bests, requiring sophisticated nutrient timing strategies.
*   **Live-by Optimizers**: High-priority wellness seekers who view nutrition, recovery, and training as their central daily focus, often training early in the morning.

## Product Trends
The discussion highlighted shifts in how products are formulated and perceived by the modern consumer. 
**Liam** noted that while awareness of supplements like **creatine** is high due to influencers and longevity research, true scientific understanding still lags behind. **Ollie** emphasized "situational formulation," such as creating pre-workout fuels containing carbohydrates for those training at 5:00 AM or 6:00 AM when eating solid food is difficult. There is also a growing movement toward viewing gut health, immunity, and recovery as integral components of performance rather than just muscle growth.

## Industry Challenges
The speakers addressed several hurdles regarding compliance and scientific integrity:
*   **Education vs. Awareness**: Consumers often use products they see online without understanding efficacy or proper dosing, such as using electrolytes as a primary fuel source instead of carbohydrates. 
*   **Regulatory Compliance**: **Liam** mentioned the difficulty of communicating complex scientific benefits through marketing without violating regulations or oversimplifying claims.
*   **Future Innovation**: The team predicts that future growth will come from improved delivery formats—such as gummies, jellies, and ready-to-drink (RTD) options—designed specifically to increase user compliance and convenience.

How can brands effectively bridge the gap between high social media awareness and genuine consumer understanding to prevent "trend chasing"?

# Is the Juice Worth the Squeeze? Polyphenols in Performance and Recovery: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Mark Evans - SNS", https://otter.ai/u/czP9hEiBGV7ASrKyQI1pL4gsbTg, recorded 9 Nov 2026 14:04, 35s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: Case in point, my wife is an athlete herself, and as I was putting together this this presentation, you know, she was asking a lot of questions about it yesterday. She was like, "What's it about again?" And I was like, "Polyphenols." And she goes, "Oh, is that those things that all the influencers tell me to inject into my ass?" And I was like, "No, I think I think those are peptides." She's like, "Okay, are they different? Yeah, they're like a bit different." And then she texted me this morning saying, "Go look at the the polypeptide presentation

summary.Summary:
Mark Evans, a senior scientist at Holland & Barrett, asked whether polyphenols earn their place in sports nutrition. He began with a quiz. Protein, creatine and caffeine each have a known dose and timing. Polyphenols have general guidance too, but it leaves a question: milligrams of what?

Polyphenols are several thousand compounds, not one thing. The same figure on a label can mean a whole extract, a subclass or a single compound. They work less as antioxidants than as signals. Of the five ways they act, only raising blood flow through nitric oxide shows up consistently in people. Of the four best-studied sources, blackcurrant has the strongest evidence for performance and cherry for recovery.

His lesson came from outside polyphenols. Beetroot nitrate and a broccoli sprout extract built awareness by teaching a simple rule of use, not a mechanism. Brands are starting to name anthocyanins, and he asked whether consumers will learn the word.

His answer: for some polyphenols, yes. Cherry at over 1,000 mg a day for recovery and blackcurrant at about 300 mg before exercise are reasonably settled. The industry now has to standardise and declare what is in the product, fund better trials and communicate dose and timing.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The dose problem: guidance from fruit-polyphenol studies is about 300 mg 1 to 2 hours before exercise for performance and over 1,000 mg a day for at least 3 days around hard exercise for recovery, but the slide asks "mg of what?" (slide 3). A label figure can mean total polyphenols, a subclass or one compound; his three questions for any ingredient are which compound, how much and measured how (slide 5).
- Mechanism: blood levels are too low for polyphenols to act as direct antioxidants; they act as signals. Of five mechanisms, only increased blood flow (nitric oxide) is rated "consistent" in humans; the others are rated limited, mostly animal, inconsistent or mostly lab (slide 6).
- The big four: blackcurrant has the strongest evidence for performance and cherry for recovery; pomegranate (performance) and turmeric (recovery) are equivocal; 3 of the 4 share anthocyanins as a main polyphenol (slide 7).
- The lesson from nitrate and Nomio: make the dose and timing the message, and let credible users do the teaching. Beetroot nitrate became "one shot, 2–3 hours before and/or for 1 week prior to competition" (slide 11).
- A layered label: "Rich in polyphenols" on the front for awareness, "X mg anthocyanins per serving, standardised and batch tested" on the back for credibility (slide 12).
- His three asks of the industry: standardise and declare, fund the right trials (trained athletes, women, blood levels, real outcomes) and communicate dose and timing (slide 13).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: polyphenols are outside our range, but a Holland & Barrett scientist set out how he judges a sports ingredient: a declared, standardised dose, the right trials and a simple rule of use (slide 5) (slide 13). My reading: that is the bar CreaWin, IsoClr: Pea and Oxystorm will be held to at that retailer.
- Oxystorm: his model of success is dietary nitrate, sold as a standardised dose with a timing rule (slide 11), and the one polyphenol effect he rates consistent in humans is blood flow through nitric oxide (slide 6). My reading: lead Oxystorm, a nitrate-rich amaranth extract, with its nitrate dose and when to take it, not its mechanism.
- Stacking for pre-workout: blackcurrant's performance guidance is about 300 mg 1 to 2 hours before exercise (slide 13); nitrate's rule is 2 to 3 hours before (slide 11). My reading: an anthocyanin plus Oxystorm pre-workout fits one timing window, but no trial of the pair was shown.
- CreaWin and recovery: creatine is his example of an ingredient with a clear dose and timing, 3 to 5 g a day, daily and ongoing (slide 2). Cherry for recovery is over 1,000 mg a day for at least 3 days before and after hard exercise (slide 13). My reading: a daily recovery formula with CreaWin and tart cherry fits one routine; again, no combined evidence was shown.
summary.Quotes:
- "mg of what?" (slide 3)
- "Strong vascular, weak sport" (slide 8)
- "Neither led with mechanism. Both gave people a simple rule and a reason to trust it." (slide 11)
- "For some polyphenols, yes. Now the industry needs to prove it, and explain it." (slide 13)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Read Howatson and Clifford (2026), Experimental Physiology, doi:10.1113/EP093724, the review behind most of the deck, and Bowtell and Kelly (2019), Sports Medicine 49(Suppl 1):S3–S23.
- Ask Mark Evans what Holland & Barrett expects a supplier to declare for a standardised sports ingredient, and whether nitrate products are judged the same way.
- Ask for the final deck: the file has a placeholder for a second brand example on slide 12.
- Confirm whether Nathan attended and what was said in questions; only a 35-second clip was recorded.
summary.Detail:
- The quiz's reference doses: protein about 0.3 g/kg per meal (20 to 40 g) and about 1.6 g/kg a day for muscle gain, every 3 to 4 hours; creatine 3 to 5 g a day (or 20 g a day for 5 to 7 days to load), about 4 weeks to saturate muscle without loading; caffeine 3 to 6 mg/kg about 60 minutes before exercise (slide 2).
- Worked examples of the guidance: Montmorency cherry 600 mg twice daily for at least 3 days before and during recovery; pomegranate about 620 mg twice daily for 7 days before and after. Chronic dosing over 1 to 6 weeks showed no clear advantage over a single acute dose for performance. The source review (Bowtell and Kelly, 2019) appeared in a supplement sponsored by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute (slide 3).
- The four classes: flavonoids (anthocyanins, flavan-3-ols, flavonols such as quercetin, flavanones; the best active-nutrition evidence), phenolic acids, stilbenes (resveratrol) and lignans. Curcuminoids from turmeric do not sit neatly in any class (slide 4).
- Why label figures do not travel: quick "total phenolics" tests also react with vitamin C and can overstate content; variety, harvest and processing change the blend (cherry juice against powder); content varies by batch, so each batch should be tested; "standardised to X%" only helps if it says X% of what (slide 5).
- The five mechanisms by benefit: Nrf2 defences (recovery, limited in humans), blood flow (performance, consistent), new mitochondria (endurance, mostly animal), a shift towards fat as fuel (endurance, inconsistent), calming NF-κB inflammation (recovery, mostly lab) (slide 6).
- Ones to watch: cocoa flavanols improve blood vessel function (meta-analysis of 42 studies) and hold one of very few authorised polyphenol health claims, but 900 mg before a time trial gave no gain in trained cyclists; blueberry improves blood vessel function within about an hour at 0.3 to 1.9 g polyphenols, and 6 weeks of daily blueberries reduced oxidative stress after a 2.5-hour run, but few studies measure performance ("early: promising signals"); quercetin is easy to dose but human effects are small and inconsistent ("early: mostly animal data") (slide 8).
- Beyond sport, he sees strong signals and almost no consumer understanding: the first flavan-3-ol intake guideline (2022) and the cocoa flavanol claim for the heart; wild blueberry improved vascular function and cognition in older adults; most polyphenols reach the colon and interact with gut bacteria. The first to explain them well could lead well beyond sport (slide 9).
- What good evidence looks like: a standardised extract, total polyphenol and primary anthocyanin doses, trained athletes and women rather than recreational men, blood levels measured with outcomes, performance and strength recovery rather than biomarkers, and pre-registered, independent, properly powered trials (slide 10).
- Still open: what reaches the blood and does the work, the best dose for each source, and trials in women, older athletes and resistance training (slide 13).
- Nitrate history: University of Exeter research from around 2009 showed nitrate improved endurance efficiency, and products were standardised to a nitrate dose in a small shot. Nomio's sulforaphane is not a polyphenol but tells the same Nrf2 story; it built high awareness in its audience through endurance athletes and influencers, from a smaller evidence base. The slide cites Nomio as a communication example only (slide 11).
- Brand examples, read from the images: an AMACX cherry juice, a 500 ml ready-to-drink "improved formula" with 125 mg anthocyanins and 30 g carbohydrate at a 2:1 ratio; and a Flycarb "case study" post claiming a 5 km time trial 2.7% faster (2.8% in its body text), 37 seconds quicker, after a week of daily New Zealand blackcurrant (300 mg anthocyanins), with a comment imagining stacking Flycarb, ITC and anthocyanins. The slide shows them for illustration only, with no endorsement implied (slide 12).
- The 35-second clip on record is an anecdote: his wife, an athlete, confused polyphenols with the peptides influencers promote [00:00].

summary.Summary:
Dr Sharon Madigan (PhD, RD, FFSEM) started from the slide everyone knows: 1 to 1.2 g of carbohydrate per kg per hour for rapid recovery in the first four hours after exercise. That is correct, she said, but nowhere near the whole story.

Her case is that carbohydrate is a signal, not just fuel. When it is available, the body treats it as safe to invest in bone, iron handling, hormones, immunity and sleep. When it is short, those are switched off to protect muscle output. A glycogen debt shows up as heavy legs the next day. The other costs build silently for weeks, until they appear as a bone stress injury, low ferritin or menstrual dysfunction.

Bone, the forgotten tissue, responds to every session in the same window used to fuel muscle. Carbohydrate during running blunts a marker of bone breakdown, and enough energy overall can still leave bone at risk if carbohydrate is low. Back-loading food into the evening, training low and cutting weight carry the same hidden costs, and low carbohydrate also amplifies the hormone that blocks iron absorption after exercise.

She closed on the limits. Most bone-marker studies are in men and measure hours or weeks, not fractures, and the dose and timing that protect bone are not yet defined.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Carbohydrate is "a Signal, Not Just a Substrate": its availability is "an electrical green light" telling the body it is metabolically safe to invest in bone remodelling, iron handling and endocrine function (slide 3) (slide 4).
- Quick against quiet costs: a glycogen deficit shows as a flat session and heavy legs, usually fixed within a day of good fuelling; bone, iron and hormones give no immediate signal, and by the time a bone stress injury, low ferritin or menstrual dysfunction appears the debt has been building for weeks (slide 5).
- Bone markers: carbohydrate during running significantly reduces the acute rise in the resorption marker CTX, and carbohydrate with protein after exercise alters bone turnover markers favourably; about 3.5 weeks of a ketogenic diet in race walkers raised resorption and suppressed formation, with incomplete recovery once carbohydrate was restored. The slide notes these are acute responses over hours, mostly in men (Sale et al., 2015) (slide 8).
- The hidden risk zone: short-term carbohydrate restriction suppresses bone formation more than low energy availability does, so energy intake alone will not flag bone risk and practitioners must screen for carbohydrate availability (Heikura et al., 2020; Fensham et al., 2022) (slide 10).
- Timing: even with an identical daily total, within-day energy deficiency is linked to unfavourable hormonal profiles in female and male athletes (Fahrenholtz et al., 2018); "Daily totals cannot save a back-loaded schedule" (slide 12) (slide 20).
- Iron: a hard endurance session triggers an IL-6 spike and hepcidin rises over 3-6 hours; low carbohydrate availability amplifies this, "functionally blocking iron absorption", so iron-rich meals and supplements should be timed around carbohydrate-restored windows (slide 13).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: none of our ingredients was named, but the recovery window she redefines includes carbohydrate with protein, which she shows altering bone turnover markers favourably after exercise (slide 8). My reading: a carbohydrate-plus-clear-protein recovery drink (IsoClr: Pea) has a bone and recovery story beyond muscle, but only as education; her own caveat is that the data are acute markers, mostly in men (slide 8) (slide 19).
- Women's needs: the quiet costs she names (bone stress injury, low ferritin, menstrual dysfunction) are female-athlete concerns, and she lists athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction among the absolute contraindications for low-carbohydrate protocols (slide 5) (slide 16). My reading: products for active women should not lean on low-carb positioning.
- Two speakers, two emphases. Emily Jevons put adequate energy intake first (ISSN position stand) (fuelling-female-performance); Madigan argues that adequate overall energy "is insufficient to protect the system" if carbohydrate availability is chronically restricted (slide 9). My reading: the views add up rather than conflict.
- James Morton's figures (up to 120 g of carbohydrate an hour) are for fuelling during exercise (fuelling-the-female-runner-from-paper); Madigan's 1-1.2 g/kg/h is for recovery after it (slide 2). Different windows, not different advice.
- Creatine and collagen were not mentioned.
summary.Quotes:
- "Most bone-marker studies are in men; menstrual status adds complexity." (slide 19)
- "We measure markers over hours and weeks, not fractures over years." (slide 19)
- "How much carbohydrate, and when, is needed to protect bone isn't yet defined." (slide 19)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm her role and the institute's exact name (slide 21 gives an instituteofsport.ie address).
- Find the papers: Sale et al. 2015 and the Townsend paper on slide 8, Heikura et al. 2020, Fensham et al. 2022, Lodge et al. 2023, Fahrenholtz et al. 2018.
- Open question: has anyone tested carbohydrate with a plant protein, rather than the protein in the slide 8 studies, on bone turnover markers after exercise, and in women?
summary.Detail:
- The deck's subtitle: "Clinical Insights on Carbohydrates as a Systemic Survival Signal" (slide 1). Every slide except 19 is an image; the text below is read from the slide images.
- The traditional view treats carbohydrate as "gas in the tank" to refill muscle glycogen when the next session is close (slide 2). Her paradigm shift: from substrate to signal ("Governor of systemic safety"); from muscle and liver to bone, endocrine, immune and iron handling; from flat sessions tomorrow to stress injuries and hormonal dysfunction next month; from daily totals to intra-day timing (slide 4).
- Glycogen: under 8 hours to the next session, start early and feed often, speed being the main variable; over 24 hours, total carbohydrate over the day matters more than precise timing. Glucose-fructose blends restore liver glycogen more effectively than glucose alone (Burke et al., 2011; Fuchs et al., 2019) (slide 6).
- "Bone responds to every single session": exercise shifts bone turnover in the hours afterwards, the same window used to fuel muscle (slide 7).
- On slide 8, β-CTX reflects existing bone being broken down and P1NP new bone being laid down; the footnote's second reference is cut off after "Townse" (slide 8).
- The blind spot: low energy availability is measured to prevent the Female Athlete Triad and RED-S, but low carbohydrate availability is a compounding variable. Read from the chart: the low-energy bar is mostly carbohydrate, the low-carb high-fat bar is tall with a thin carbohydrate layer; the bars carry no values (slide 9).
- Lodge et al. (2023) note that low carbohydrate availability "operates as an independent risk factor" within RED-S, overlapping on glycogen stores, bone health (stress injuries), menstrual function and immunity (slide 11).
- Within-day fuelling, read from the chart: targeted fuelling spreads intake across the day with short deficits; back-loaded fuelling eats little around training and catches up in the evening, with long, deep deficits. The curves are illustrative, without values (slide 12).
- The switchboard: when carbohydrate drops, power stays with heart, lungs and muscle output, and is cut to bone formation, iron handling, hormonal reproduction and immune defence; this also drives immune disturbance in heavy blocks and disrupts sleep onset and quality (slide 14).
- Her diagnostic matrix rates targeted fuelling optimal or protected on every line; back-loaded fuelling sub-optimal, with P1NP suppressed, β-CTX elevated and hormones and iron disrupted; train-low variable or compromised, with P1NP highly suppressed and β-CTX highly elevated (slide 15).
- Train low "heavily suppresses bone formation and increases injury risk without consistent performance benefits in elite racing"; repeated weight cuts mean repeated exposure to low carbohydrate availability over a season. Absolute contraindications for low-carbohydrate protocols: adolescent athletes, athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction, and athletes with a history of bone stress injuries (slide 16).
- Two more quiet costs: carbohydrate availability influences immune disturbance after prolonged heavy exercise (high risk in heavy blocks, major competitions and travel; Walsh, 2019), and evening carbohydrate influences sleep onset and quality (high risk with late training and evening competitions; Halson, 2014) (slide 17).
- Making weight: carbohydrate is cut before the weigh-in to reduce glycogen, water and gut content, followed by a panicked refeed limited by gut tolerance (slide 18).
- Where evidence runs thin: female athletes (mostly male bone-marker studies), adolescents (peak bone mass being built, little direct data), outcomes (markers, not fractures) and dose and timing (slide 19).
- Her four pillars: protect more than glycogen; fuel recovery early to avoid the within-day deficit; treat low carbohydrate availability as an independent bone-health risk even when calories look adequate; periodise with intent and keep adolescent, low-energy and previously injured athletes off train-low protocols (slide 20).

# GLP-Won - Market Opportunities for the Active Nutrition Sector: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Morgan Griffiths - SNS - GLP-1", https://otter.ai/u/wvgHAxfP-V-tLHD4fpz8neQnxbw, recorded 9 Nov 2026 16:05, 18m 47s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:08] Speaker 1 (Morgan Griffiths): Afternoon, everyone. So GLP-1. Just my as a quick kind of show of thumbs. Give me a thumbs down if you've kind of heard of GLP-1, not really sure about it. Give me a middle thumb if you think you've got a decent understanding, and give me a thumbs up if you think you could do this presentation now. There are some confident people in the room. Okay, let's bit of a history lesson. Let's sort of set the stage, set the context for talking about GLP-1. So, as you might imagine I've been doing this presentation quite a lot, speaking about GRP one, often to the kind of food and drink sector. And if we look at the kind of last 50 years, it's actually been in the round quite a good time in the food and drink sector. And this is for a few reasons. First of all, as you can see, the population has been growing. So this is we just look at the UK, just just illustratively, but the population has been growing. So, as a food and drink business or as a nutrition business, you've had more people you can sell to. You've then also had more people consuming more things, consuming more calories. So, per person and at a population level, more people consuming more things, and then even adjusting for inflation, you've still got more people spending more, so more people consuming more products and spending more on them. That's pretty good context from a market perspective. Put those together, you can kind of see, broadly speaking, the line goes up. Now, I'm going to show one more of these line graphs, and this is from the US this time. So what this shows is the prevalence of obesity in the U.S., and this is when GLP-1 in their kind of weekly form was introduced. So semaglutide was introduced, and as you can see, that had a pretty much kind of immediate impact on obesity rates. And so what that would have impacted was that consumption graph, so the calories graph we were speaking about now? If you also add into the mix that we're obviously in a bit of a cost of living crisis, and to a lesser extent we're in sort of entering a bit of a population crisis, sort of those three lines that we're all going up start to be a bit more of question and start to be a bit more dramatic. Now the thing is, when I do this presentation for food and drink brands, this is the part of the presentation where I have to say, and now for the bad news. However, in this room, this is the opposite story. This is actually the fun part of the job, where I can actually say this is a real opportunity for you, and we'll come on to unpack why. Now, GLP-1 is, you know, as we as we saw from the kind of show of thumbs at the start, this is an issue which is still not super well known, super well understood, and it's also an issue which I think a lot of people think is quite horizontal. They think this is an issue that is that is coming down the line. And like I say, I'm still just the next two or three slides will still just be looking at UK data before we look at European wide data. What I should say is, is if you look at those percentages, we did a study over the summer, and we actually saw similar use of current usage of GLP-1 in Italy, France, Germany, and Spain. So, 6.1% of the UK population are currently taking GLP-1s. 5.7% of the population have previously used GLP-1s, and 15.1% of the population are considering using them. So that you know that point of friction, people not wanting to inject themselves, that went away, and you saw a lot more people willing to consider it. So if you put that into a bit of context, because often people see percentages, and you know they don't necessarily know what that means. You add all of those together. That's about 18 point 4 million people, which is the equivalent to every person in the UK born since the millennium, so since 2000, so effectively everyone who's 26 and under. It's the number of Netflix subscribers in the UK, and if you put it together as a national population, it'd be the 12th largest country in Europe. So these are significant numbers. And I think one more stat to kind of illustrate that, as I mentioned, 6.1% of the UK population currently use GLP-1. What percent of the population do we think are vegan and vegetarian combined? Do you think it's bigger or lower than 6.1%? We think lower. Correct, 5.7%. Now, the reason I show this, like I say often when I'm speaking to kind of food and drink brands, what I will say is, your teams will spend a lot of time investing in sort of product innovation into vegan and vegetarian food. And for a bit of context, so I I've been at Lumina for over a year, but prior to working at Lumina, I worked for an organization called Nesta, which is an innovation health innovation charity in the UK, and one of their missions is around obesity. So I've been looking at GLP ones for around six years, and when I first came across GLP-1s, they I only ever and policy had only ever designed them to be for people who were suffering with obesity to have a BMI of 30 or over. Now, what the data has shown following the boom of GLP-1s, and they've been pretty well established in the UK for the last two years, is that they are not being consumed largely by people who are suffering with obesity. So, if they were suffering with people, if they were largely being consumed by people suffering with obesity, you'd expect them to be predominantly male in terms of common usage, in their 50s or 60s, and in lower socio-economic groups. I think this is where there's some opportunity, partly because there's not really enough of a focus here, specifically on that kind of longevity piece, that kind of tail off piece, or kind of like I say, kind of a change of behavior, helping those consumers make those lasting changes, and I think also it's worth saying that there's, like I say, not enough signposting for people who are on GLP-1, and particularly for when you kind of come off the medication. And I think lastly, to sort of look at the current landscape of kind of GLP-1 innovation. There's some really interesting things going on. So Hule, for example, GLP-1. Cambridge Nutrition and Portion IQ got in quite early with their range of beverages, snacks, meal replacements, etc., targeted toward the GLP-1 user, and perhaps kind of most powerfully, and I say it kind of powerfully as a mainstream, obviously high street brands, Boots now target very much do specific callouts for GLP-1. So they have sort of bays, sort of with lots of different products in on GLP-1. They have little sort of clips on shelves as well, which says you know suffering from hair issues or you know skin issues when on GLP-1, so giving those specific callouts to people on GLP-1, I think that's also a real point of focus. Is because obviously when you sort of put GLP-1 on a pack or speak about GLP-1, you know that is a kind of a health claim, and so brands are being quite deliberate and quite careful about how they do their messaging so fast, and to have the support of a retailer like that kind of Boots example is particularly pertinent and particularly kind of worth focusing on. So, to leave on a very dramatic slide, I think hopefully one of the key things you're taking away from today is that GLP-1 is not an issue that you can afford to sleep on, or can afford to kind of defer for later on. Like I say, if you just think about current users, there are more than vegans and vegetarians. This is already a big cohort. Our data forecasts in the UK alone, it's going to grow to around 11% by 2031. Just current users. So this is something which is really worth focusing on and focusing on as soon as possible. Many thanks for your time, and I'm going to hand over you over to your next amazing speaker. Thank you very much.

summary.Summary:
Morgan Griffiths, Commercial Lead at Lumina Intelligence, argued that GLP-1 drugs, bad news for many food and drink brands, are an opportunity for active nutrition.

He started with scale. In the UK, almost 27% of people, about 18.4 million, are taking, have taken or are considering a GLP-1. A summer survey found similar use in Italy, France, Germany and Spain.

He then described the users. They are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: most are women, Gen X or Millennial and better off. They are already health-minded and happy to pay more for quality. Most European users spend the same or more on food and drink, and most have increased their supplement use. Proteins lead their supplement list; creatine ranked higher than he expected.

He saw three openings: side effects, access to nutrition (protein, nutrients, muscle loss) and lapsed users. Users are confident of keeping the weight off, but a BMJ study he showed found weight returns almost four times faster after the drugs than after diet and exercise. Huel, Cambridge Nutrition's PortionIQ and Boots are already moving, and Lumina forecasts that UK use will keep growing to 2031.

Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Morgan Griffiths presents an analysis of the growing GLP-1 consumer market and its significant commercial opportunities for the food and drink sector.

## Market Context
**Morgan** provides a statistical overview of the current GLP-1 landscape, emphasizing that it is a live issue rather than a future trend. In the UK, 6.1% of the population currently uses **GLP-1**, 5.7% have used it previously, and 15.1% are considering it. This cohort represents approximately 18.4 million people, making the group larger than the combined vegan and vegetarian populations in the UK.

**Key demographic findings:**
*   Users are predominantly female (56%).
*   The age profile consists mostly of Gen X or Millennials (63%).
*   Most users belong to higher socio-economic groups (63% are ABC1).
*   The consumer base is health-minded, values quality, and is willing to pay more for functional benefits.

## Consumer Behavior
Despite concerns regarding reduced food volume consumption, **Morgan** notes that roughly two-thirds of users spend either the same or more on food and drink compared to before starting treatment. Many users also increase their use of supplements, with nearly 90% maintaining or increasing usage.

**Innovation opportunities include:**
*   Addressing side effects such as nausea and reduced food enjoyment through specialized products.
*   Tackling nutritional gaps caused by lower calorie intake, specifically regarding protein intake and muscle loss prevention.
*   Providing support for "lapsed users" who face a high risk—four times higher than traditional methods—of regaining weight once medication is stopped due to unchanged behaviors.

## Industry Response
Current market players are already pivoting toward this demographic through targeted product innovation and retail positioning. Examples of existing industry movement include:

*   **Huel**: Moving into blended nutrition/supplement spaces with low-calorie versions of existing products.
*   **Cambridge Nutrition** and **Portion IQ**: Developing specialized beverages, snacks, and meal replacements for **GLP-1** users.
*   **Boots**: Implementing dedicated retail bays and shelf signage that addresses specific side effects like hair or skin issues associated with medication use.

Action items (Otter's): none.

# From hype to proof: the science behind GLP-1 targeted nutritional supplements: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "GLP-1 and Weight Management Trends - SNS", https://otter.ai/u/dBvLceBTr1YTpQ3D_hK0fHOy5uE, recorded 9 Nov 2026 16:24, 1h 1m; this is the talk, from [00:00] to [25:19] of the recording (the panel follows in beyond-the-glp-1-boom-nutrition). Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: Of Westminster, and Gulres is going to discuss the mechanisms through which functional ingredients may support endogenous satiety pathways and weight management. Over to you, Gorres.
[00:15] Speaker 2 (Gulrez Zariwala): Thank you, Morgan, for setting the scene, and thanks to Native Ingredients for having me here. I'd like to start by a very brief introduction. My background is in drug delivery and formulation science. Also, have background in obesity and metabolism. I'm currently the founder director of the Center for Nutraceuticals, and I just like take a couple of minutes to talk a bit about our work because our clinicals and all our research is based at the center, so it's a first of a kind initiative. One of objectives to add to the bridge between industry and academia to bring some credibility, independent research-based opinions. We're based in central London. That's us. That's not all of us. That's the BD Tower. It's just us on the the fourth floor of the building. Just make that clear. Okay, so we work in a range of disciplines from sports and exercise all the way to nutrition, metabolism, neurobiology, formulation science. We have quite a multidisciplinary team, and our research model is also quite vertically integrated. We work on the mechanistic side all the way to the clinical side. We work with developing formulation strategies for novel as well as existing molecules. We then carry out mechanistic studies to test them using the relevant cell lines. This then feeds into human intervention studies, which can be sponsored by the industry or they are open sky, blue blue sky, open-ended research. This may inform product development, which we have also worked on quite a bit. So, just to give you a bit of breadth of our work, there's a recent publications all the way from sports, exercise, nutrition. There's a lot of curcumin-based work. We did some quite pioneering clinical trials about five, six years back, and all the way to obesity and metabolism, which I'm going to talk about. We work with partners across the world, from UK SMEs to large companies, and we collaborate with a number of universities as well as advising governments on nutraceutical and supplement-related policies. Today, I'm going to focus on clinical trials we have done. Again, as I said, we are very much research-founded. It's all about conducting research, publishing papers, but we actually work with the industry because our objective is to bring the science as much as possible. So let's come to the topic at hand. Obesity is an academic. We know it's a public health crisis. The prevalence is quite widespread. These are the hotspots, as you can see, in developed as well as emerging economies, particularly let's say U.S., the incidence is high at 40%. Equally, you have the same in South America as well as some parts of Africa, almost 35 to 40%. So obesity is chronic and multifactorial. It would be hard to simplify it within the remit of this talk. You have socioeconomic factors, psychological factors, genetic factors. All of these come in play, and you have a lot of secondary diseases related to obesity. These may be metabolic as well as non-metabolic. Metabolic type two diabetes, non-metabolic neurodegeneration, dementia, all strongly correlated to obesity. Obesity is generally quite simplistically defined as BMI over 30. Now we know there are more complex measures and screening tools. BMI is the consensus. It's a very simple ratio of height and weight, and it's quite widely used. So it's over 30, which is defined as obesity, and you have lower cutoff for say overweight. You have higher cutoff for type one, type two, type three obesity. Quite simply, it may not be the best picture, but it's it's the wave balance at the bottom. It is energy imbalance. You're intaking excess energy in terms of calories than what your energy expenditure is. If you get that right, you have a lean body. If there is any kind of alteration due to the various factors, you're prone to obesity. So, talking about silver bullets and magic bullets, there's long been a surge all the way from the 20s and 30s. You have some quite questionable material there. Let's talk about in the next slide. These were called rainbow pills. But over time, the most kind of desirable approach has always been diet and exercise. A diet low in calories, high in protein, high in fiber, balanced in carbs, and low in fat is ideal. However, it is not practical and as feasible as we might want it to be. So then we have bariatric surgery, gastric banding, and so on. This is most effective and durable treatment. This is applicable to certain populations and carries its own risks and costs. We then have pharmacological approaches. We are going to talk about GLP ones. Again, these are quite beneficial to certain populations, as we know, but they require lifelong use and the risk profile is quite low at the minute, but there there is some potential. There are some studies to show some adverse effects, which we'll touch upon. So let's look at a brief history of obesity drugs before we go into supplements. Now, as you can see, there's long been a search for the silver bullet, and this has really been marked by failures, all the way from the 20s, where you had the rainbow pills. This was a cocktail of antidepressant diuretics and all sort of questionable drugs, thyroid extract, and then coming all the way to the GLPs, all the drugs marked in red were withdrawn, with the exception of olistat, which is a fat blocker acts on lipoprotein lipase. Most of them are centrally acting, meaning they act on the brain. So the issue with centrally acting drugs is highlighted by rimonaban, which was the most recently withdrawn drug. It acts on the endocannabinoid receptors, endocannabinoid system. It did have quite potent effects on reducing appetite, on weight loss. However, these centers in the brain are quite tightly wired to your centers of pleasure, your heteronistic centers, and any kind of tinkering which lead to an imbalance, which is what you can see here. There's a very high incidence of neuropsychiatric effects all the way to it being a suicide risk. So this was withdrawn, and this directed the focus to peripheral therapies, which is gut hormone-based approaches. So what are gut hormones? The gastrointestinal tract, GI tract, is interestingly one of the largest endocrine organ of the body. It has specialized cells both in the small intestine all the way to the large intestine. Now these are L cells, and they respond to dietary stimulus, different components of diet, qualitatively and quantitatively. Again, protein, carbs, fats. They will respond according to the let's say the proportion, the quality, in response to that, there will be a secretion of gut hormones, which will then signal directly and indirectly to the brain, and this will balance out to create your feeling of hunger or satiety. It's not just the gut which is secreting hormones. You have them coming from the pancreas. You have them coming from fat tissue. Focusing on the gut hormones, we have them coming from secreted from the stomach, from the small intestine, all the way to the large intestine. These are ghrelin, GLP-1, PYY, oxymodulin, GIP. Other than ghrelin, which gives a positive signal, it makes you feel hungry. So between meals, when your stomach is shrinking, ghrelin is secreted, goes to the brain, signals, makes you feel hungry. All the others give a negative signal to the brain, particularly PYY and GLP-1. So interestingly, it's PYY peptide YY, which is the more potent anorexigenic hormone, which causes you to eat less. But due to a combination of commercial and clinical reasons, it's the GLPs, which very came in first as a class. Let's talk about GLP-1. It's an incretin hormone. It's released directly in response to dietary intake of certain components of food, let's say protein, following its release, it will be secreted in blood, and it will act on the organs surrounding it. So it will go to the pancreas, cause it to release insulin, maintain insulin balance. It will go to the pancreas, cause the glucagon to go down, it will also signal to the brain directly and indirectly, directly through the local nerves and indirectly going through the bloodstream across the blood-brain barrier and signaling to the GLP-1 receptors to cause you to eat less. Now the issue with the GLP-1 as a molecule was that it's rapidly degraded in your body by the enzyme DPP4, and this frustrated attempts to develop therapeutics for for quite a long time. And the solution was until the answer was found in in this reptile. I think the people from North America might be familiar. So it's the the Gila monster. I think it's pronounced with the H, although it's G. So this is some classic blue sky research, curiosity-driven research, where the researchers observe that it eats only five to 10 times a day, and sorry, a year, and it has a very good metabolic profile. So there was a search for hormones within it, and it was found to be exendin four, which is a long-acting LP1 analog. This led to patenting by a researcher. Pharmaceutical companies were not interested. Ultimately, Emilin acquired it. This became BioTuff, short-acting, first of its class. It then went on to the longer-acting drugs, from once a day to once a week, and then we have the latest, which is once a week, and these are dual GLP-1 and GIP acting drugs. Okay, this is just because of structural modifications. You increase the resilience to DPP-4, stays longer in your body, creates the effects that you want. Some of them are available as oral pills as well, and there are other small molecules now which are again available as pills. So, because of these dramatic weight loss effects, as you can see, between five to 15%, you have the transition of a highly regulated prescription drug to become almost a lifestyle product, as was touched upon in the previous talk. This is due to a number of complex factors. Again, we can spend an entire talk on that. There's a ease of availability through digital pharmacies. There are cosmetic pressures, and again, there are some cost reductions compared to what it was originally. LP1 also. has quite a important role in sports nutrition, both in people who are elite athletes as well as educational athletes have noticed that there is reduction in inflammation. There's increased energy levels. There are mechanisms to to support this. Again, it has benefits in sports such as Marshall Sports, where tight cut-offs are required, and as you can imagine, it's it's not banned yet, but it's on the watch list for for this reason. The last point, again, it's been covered in depth in in the previous talk. It leads to good supplementation with a number of other supplements in in other categories. So just like all drugs, there's a balance between benefits and risks, and there is a side effect profile. So these are not all adverse effects occurring in all consumers and users. But these have been reported. The most prominent ones are the GI side effects, nausea vomiting. There are some cosmetic effects, such as when you lose the buckle, the facial fat pads, also the breakdown in collagen, so you have the sucking skin, and importantly, all GLP-1 based drugs cause a reduction in body weight, not specifically body fat. So you have a reduction in muscle mass, which can lead to sarcopenia. So this directed a lot of consumers to supplement based solutions, and this led to the GLP one boom. This is from Expo West last year, where everybody was talking everything was GLP-1, and there are some products with some scientific basis, but some of them are a bit of a stretch, and there are pitfalls to this. As you can see, there's some high-profile lawsuits, there's some regulatory clampdowns, and ultimately, and importantly, leads to lowering of the consumer confidence. So, are there any supplements that have a scientific basis? Looked at a few of them. Proteins have an undisputed effect on GLP-1 secretion, both mechanistically, animal models, human study. Depends on the quality of the protein. Depends on the amino acid profile. Both supplemental as well as dietary proteins. Just to clarify, so this is one of the 2015 studies: high protein versus high carb versus high fat, 60 to 70 percent in each. And as you can see, a very prominent post meal, significant increase in both GLP-1 and PYY. So again, proteins scientifically validated, and they can also support the muscle loss that occurs to the LP1, so it's got some good credentials as a supplement. Lipid-based compounds, OEA is a molecule produced by a body. It is rapidly degraded. It has direct effects on GPR119, which causes GLP1 secretion. So there's a very direct mechanism. As I said, it's rapidly degraded. So formulation strategies may improve its profile, and you have a molecule called tripty. This has been recently studied. There's a latest paper which shows a dose-dependent increase in post-meal GLP-1 secretion. Berberine, I'm sure everyone here is familiar. It's often referred to as iti. It's alkaloid compound from barberries. So berberine does have some GLP-1 effects, but they are indirect, and a lot of them have been shown in animal models, mainly rodent studies. There are a couple of human studies, but its main effects is on maintaining glucose metabolism in a positive way, maintaining fat balance, and this is through actions on AMPK. On GLP-1, it has indirect effects, and most studies have shown quite modest effects on GLP-1 as well as on weight loss. Cinnamon is often combined with berberine. Cinnamon is rich in cinnamondehyde, cinnamondeide has a mechanistic basis. It acts on the ion channel trip A1, and through that it can increase GLP1 secretion. But it has mild to modest effects, and there are very few human studies to substantiate this. Next, we have beta compounds. So this is a bit of a crossover because bitter compounds include alkaloids, polyphenols can include berberine, which we talked about. There is a mechanistic basis. Bitter compounds is part of your body's natural defense system. They act on the taste receptors, particularly TAS tubar, and through that, which is a G protein-coupled receptor, so mostly it will bring about calcium increase in your cells and kick out protein hormones. It brings about increased secretion of GLP-1, but there have been very few human studies, and again it's a mild to modest effect. So I'm going to talk about some of our primary work on appetite regulation. We've been working on it for about eight to 10 years. We started with a focus on dietary proteins. We did the first study comparing the metabolic profile of plant proteins. We worked with protein, potato protein as well as rice protein, comparing it to whey protein isolate. So until then, most of the work was looking at the anabolic profile. Very few studies had looked at the effect on glucose metabolism. This was quite a complex quadruple crossover study. There's some very interesting results which were published, and I'm proud of it. It featured on the cover page of a journal. But the main objective was to progress this into appetite study, which led us to the appetite study. So this was called appetite. So this is a triple crossover study. We compared the effects of potato protein versus whey protein isolate. Again, one of the first studies comparing plant as well as milk proteins and a placebo-controlled study, so three arms a crossover study. Participants come in on the day of the study, following an overnight fast, and they will consume breakfast. We try to make it as palatable as possible. This is spiked with protein. Okay, so this is isocaloric, isovolimic. So all proteins will be having the same calorie, the same protein content, and the the placebo is also matched to this. Following the consumption, we will connect them to a cannula. We'll draw blood every 30 minutes, and they will also complete an appetite code. Following that, three hours later, they'll have a meal ablibitum, which you can eat as much as you want, and that's a huge bowl of pasta. We try to make it again appetizing, so that doesn't have a confounding factor. So the idea is that if the protein is creating a satiety effect, you're going to eat less, and this is going to be matched by the the peptide hormone release. So it's quite a complex hypothesis, and we wanted to explore this. And interestingly, we got some really exciting results. So, firstly, we showed that both the plant as well as the biprotein analyst, because a significant increase in GLP-1. The second important and novel result is that the equivalent response on GLP-1, as you can see between the teal and the pink in the plant protein compared to the whey protein isolate. Again, it's one of the first times it's been shown. And the third result, which is particularly significant, is that although at 180 minutes post meal, you're not seeing a significant increase in in GIP. Whey protein is leading to a significant increase in GIP at 60 minutes. So GIP acts in a different way to GLP-1. It may act more instantly and directly on appetite as compared to GLP-1. So it makes sense to combine them. This is why you have the new class of pharmaceutical drugs, which are a combination of GLP and GIS on others. This is the first nutraceutical compound, whey protein isolate, which shows a similar effect, not to the same magnitude, but the same trend. So the next study was on botanical. This is just completed last month, and hopefully we will submit it for publication next week. We're very excited about it. The last study you saw was independent study, unfunded, conducted as part of a PhD project. We do a lot of studies which are industry sponsored, but there's a balance between the academic work we do and the sponsored work. So we try to feed in from our academic research into this. So this is a replicate of our academic study. This study was done with support from Finova. It's a UK-based company, and the molecule is called Redicools. Redi Cools is a standardized mulberry extract. It is available across the world. It's used in a number of finished products as an ingredient, combined with other ingredients as well. It has a number of studies showing it to have effect on glucose metabolism. Quite simply, it limits, it slows down the absorption of carbohydrates, prevents sugar spikes. The hypothesis is for us, if it's slowing down the absorption of carbs in the small intestine, they are likely to go in the large intestine, where through generation of short chain fatty acids, there should be hypothetically an effect on GLP-1, which is what we want to test out. So it's a triple crossover study. One arm was the placebo, the second was the radicos formulation, the third is a combination of radicos with two other compounds, and this is one of the leading U.S. GLP-1 brands, which we brought in the study, also funded. So we often do studies where we look at combination effects of supplements because it's easy to show isolated effects with one ingredient and so on, and you want to show a true effect of a finished product. You want to see if the ingredients are working in synergy. So that's why it was important for us to have this as an arm. Study design was similar to a previous study. We recruited in central London, so very much centralized as compared to a lot of trials which are decentralized these days. We like to do blood work through blood collections through cannulation in house. Also, we like to focus on having a diverse multi ethnic population with a good balance of female as well as male participants, as you can see. And the BMI cutoff is also relevant to the actual consumer. So the study is designed with the consumer in mind, not just an idealized population. Similar to the previous study, we had the participants coming in, taking the pill, consuming the breakfast. They filled appetite scores for three hours. Then every 30 minutes, we were collecting the the blood samples, and then they completed another questionnaire over 24 hours, which is called a food noise questionnaire, which I'm going to talk about, Muradal. So we didn't really know what to expect from this study because this kind of work hadn't been done before, even mechanistically. The results were quite exciting. So we saw the response of both the ingredient and the formulation on glucose response, which we expected. What we also saw was a statistically significant increase in GLP-1 secretion post meal at 180 minutes. Matched by that, we also saw a significant reduction in appetite. However, what is most interesting for us was a significant reduction in food noise. So, for those who are familiar, food noise is intrusive thoughts related to food, and these are often related to food cravings, binge eating, overeating, and so on. A lot of the the GLP-1 trials carried out food noise questionnaires. There's strong food noise data. This is one of the first supplemental nutraceutical studies that used food noise as an endpoint. The 24 hours following the supplementation intervention, we saw a significant reduction. That is 21, 19 to 21, 19 with one and 21 with the other, reduction in food noise. So a significant increase in GLP-1, increase sorry reduction in appetite and reduction in food noise. Hopefully, we're going to continue this study. We want to do it long term. If the industry partner supports, we'd like to see effect. We would like to explore effect on body weight composition as well. And hopefully, in 2728, we'll be carrying out two follow on studies with this molecule as well as the the finished product. So, just a quick summary of the key points from my perspective: GLP-1 drugs have transformed our approach to to obesity and appetite regulation. They provide dramatic effects. At present, the side effect profile is is quite favorable. It's it's not particularly negative, but they do carry the risk which needs to be recognized because ultimately it is it is a drug. It's a pharmacological drug. Supplements and nutritional and nutraceutical interventions may fill a gap, either with active users concurrently or with lapsed users. However, there needs to be some management of expectation. There is no natural supplement solution that can match the magnitude of response which you will get with a pharmacological drug, as as stands with with most natural supplements as compared to pharmaceutical formulations. There's a need for increased scientific validation. It's a crowded market, as we've seen. Everybody wants to jump on the bandwagon. There is a place for scientific validation. This is why we are seeing ingredient as well as product companies who want to do trials with us, not just in this area but across the board. We are doing multiple trials because, quite simply, products that have scientific validation increase market resilience, and we've seen that both commercially. Of course, for us, it's great to have the science in the product. As we have seen in the the previous, as we have heard in the previous talk, GLP-1 based products create a need for a secondary demand for supplement products. These may be probiotics, proteins, fiber, multivitamins, due to various reasons. As I said, they may be poor supplementation because there's less absorption, less intake food, or they may be like proteins, which are a true substitute to some extent to the GLP-1 drug. Thank you for your attention.

summary.Summary:
Professor Gulrez Zariwala, founder and director of the Centre for Nutraceuticals at the University of Westminster, asked which supplements aimed at GLP-1 and appetite have science behind them.

He began with the biology. Gut hormones such as GLP-1 and PYY signal fullness, and ghrelin signals hunger. Earlier obesity drugs that acted on the brain carried psychiatric risks, which turned the field to gut hormones. GLP-1 drugs bring dramatic weight loss, but about 40% of the weight lost is lean body mass.

The boom in GLP-1 supplements, he said, has brought lawsuits, regulatory clampdowns and lower consumer confidence. He then went through the candidates. Proteins have an undisputed effect on GLP-1 release. Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have plausible mechanisms but modest effects and few human studies. His centre's own trials, both still unpublished, found that potato protein raised GLP-1 comparably to whey protein isolate, and that Phynova's mulberry leaf extract, Reducose, raised post-meal GLP-1 by 140% and cut appetite by 23% against placebo.

His conclusion: supplements may fill a gap for current or lapsed users, but none can match a drug, so expectations need managing. Products with strong scientific substantiation stand out, and GLP-1 use creates demand for micronutrients, protein, fibre and probiotics.
summary.Key takeaways:
- GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of "between five to 15%" [00:15]; his table gives 3.6% for liraglutide, 11.4% for semaglutide and 15.0% for tirzepatide (slide 17).
- Up to 50% of users have GI symptoms and about 40% of the weight reduction comes from lean body mass (slide 20). He said muscle loss "can lead to sarcopenia" [00:15]; his slide lists sarcopenia with "insufficient evidence" (slide 20, read from the slide image).
- Proteins have an "undisputed effect" on GLP-1 secretion; high-protein meals trigger GLP-1 and PYY, and the effect depends on the amino acid profile, such as leucine [00:15] (slide 23).
- Berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have mechanisms but "mild to modest" effects and few human studies; berberine "does not directly bind to or activate GLP-1 receptors" [00:15] (slide 25) (slide 26).
- In his centre's APPETITE trial (12 participants; porridge alone, with potato protein or with whey protein), both proteins gave a comparable, significant increase in GLP-1 secretion (slide 28) (slide 30).
- In the SATISPHY trial of Reducose (40 participants), post-meal GLP-1 rose 140% and appetite fell 23% against placebo, with "a marked reduction in appetite as well as food noise"; both trials are unpublished, manuscripts in progress (slide 31) (slide 33).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- A plant protein matched whey protein isolate on GLP-1 in his trial; that was potato protein, not pea, and whey raised GIP more than potato did (slide 30). My reading: this opens a satiety angle for IsoClr: Pea, but only with our own data, and his centre runs exactly this protocol for industry partners [00:15].
- Lean mass is about 40% of the weight lost on the drugs (slide 20), and protein is the one supplement class he called validated on both satiety and muscle [00:15]. My reading: protein for GLP-1 users is a pitch with science behind it; CreaWin's place there would rest on its muscle evidence, which he did not discuss.
- His protein slide shows Applied Nutrition's "GLP1 Friendly" range, including Complete Protein and an Energy + Creatine product (slide 23, read from the slide image). My reading: a UK sports brand already pairs protein and creatine with GLP-1 positioning; worth a look as a customer.
- His warning on overclaiming (lawsuits, clampdowns, an FDA warning letter) fits EU claims rules [00:15] (slide 22). My reading: we should not let customers imply GLP-1 effects for our ingredients.
- Relevance high: GLP-1 nutrition and protein.

summary.Detail:
- He is Prof M. Gulrez Zariwala, Director and Founder of the Centre for Nutraceuticals and Professor of Translational Physiology at the University of Westminster (slide 1). The centre is at 115 New Cavendish Street, London (slide 29), on the fourth floor of the building by the BT Tower (Otter: "BD Tower") [00:15] (slide 2).
- The centre aims to bridge industry and academia and to be a source of trustworthy, scientifically validated information (slide 2). Its model runs from formulation through cell studies (Caco-2, MIN-6, SH-SY5Y) to clinical studies, including head-to-head comparisons (slide 4). Its counts: 6 funded projects, 2 products developed, 7 clinical trials, 6 pipeline contract or collaborative projects, 30+ publications, 25+ student placements (slide 7, read from the slide image).
- Partner logos include Phynova, Gencor, Avebe, Agropur, GNC, Nelsons, Pharmako, Axonova, Issa Group and several universities and governments (slide 6, read from the slide image). The deck does not say whose potato protein APPETITE used; Avebe makes potato protein (my reading).
- His papers on the research slide are mostly on iron, curcumin and nanocarriers, plus a mouth-rinse study in runners (slide 5, read from the slide image).
- Obesity: he put US incidence at 40% and parts of South America and Africa at 35 to 40% [00:15]; the map uses WHO 2022 data (slide 8). Obesity is a BMI of 30 or more (slide 9).
- Treatments: diet is the most desirable but often unsustainable; bariatric surgery gives durable loss of about 25% to 30%; drugs are long-term, often lifelong, and usually prescribed at a BMI of 27 or more (slide 10).
- Drug history: most obesity drugs were withdrawn; rimonabant ("rimonaban" in Otter) was withdrawn in Europe in 2009 for suicidal thoughts and depression (slide 11). In one year of trial data, psychiatric disorders affected 6.7% on 20 mg against 3.2% on placebo (slide 12, read from the slide image).
- Gut hormones: ghrelin signals hunger; GLP-1, PYY, oxyntomodulin, GIP and cholecystokinin signal fullness (slide 14). He said PYY is the more potent anorexigenic hormone, but GLP-1 drugs came first for commercial and clinical reasons [00:15]. GLP-1 is rapidly degraded by DPP-4 (slide 15).
- Exendin-4 came from Gila monster venom; exenatide (Byetta, Amylin) was its synthetic, injectable version (slide 16). Otter heard "BioTuff" and "Emilin". The chart notes GLP-1 drug sales of $22 billion in 2022 (slide 16, read from the chart).
- Consumerisation: online weight-loss services advertise "Less Strict Than NHS Criteria", a qualifying BMI from 25 and plans from £64 for the first month (slide 18, read from the slide image). He cited digital pharmacies, cosmetic pressures and lower costs [00:15].
- Sport: GLP-1 drugs found to reduce inflammation, micro-dosing to lose weight and enhance performance, and a WADA monitoring programme; he said they are not banned but on the watch list [00:15] (slide 19).
- His slide puts protein at about 50%, multivitamins about 50% and probiotics about 30% among supplements taken with or after the drugs, citing Lumina Intelligence (slide 19). Lumina's own deck in the 16:00 talk (glp-won-market-opportunities-for-the) gives proteins 51%, multivitamins 48% and probiotics 37%; the two differ on probiotics.
- Other side effects: nausea and vomiting, loss of facial fat pads and collagen breakdown [00:15], shown as "Ozempic face" (slide 20, read from the slide image).
- The boom: Expo West photos of a "GLP-1 Companion" supplement, Metabolaid's "GLP-1 Inducer", "GLP-1 friendly vegan chicken & waffles" and a "GLP-1 Boost" stand (slide 21, read from the slide image). He dated it to Expo West last year [00:15].
- Substantiation: press headlines "As weight-loss drug users turn to dietary supplements, doctors and regulators raise flags" (20 October 2026) and "Unverified GLP-1-Related Claims Flood Food, Supplement Markets" (13 July 2026), and an FDA warning letter (Veronvy, 10 December 2024) (slide 22, read from the slide image). He spoke of "some high-profile lawsuits" [00:15]; the slide shows no lawsuit.
- Proteins: a 2015 study of high protein against high carbohydrate and high fat meals showed a significant post-meal rise in GLP-1 and PYY [00:15]. The slide's charts show both hormones highest after the protein meal (slide 23, read from the chart); its reference is incomplete.
