# Holland & Barrett: how longevity science translates into consumer outcomes: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Alex Glover - H&B - Remedy CDMO", https://otter.ai/u/LXa2bHODxRY5s8up7grRiBmKTgI, recorded 22 Oct 2026 15:50, 10m 43s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: Factoring and all the decisions that go with it, and then finally the customer's first question is: Is it on offer? Our next session considers how long Gavity Science translates into the relevant consumer outcomes. From strategic partner Holland and Barrett, please welcome Alex Glover. Probably best use one of those that's up there, I think.
[00:25] Speaker 2: Thank you. Yes, great. Everybody can hear me. So, hello, everyone. My name is Alex. So, I lead the product formulation team at Holden Barrack Global. I'm responsible for all of the own label products that Holden Barrett formulate and develop across the globe. And I'm really happy that you started out there saying is we are with you saying about deciding what to buy because that's really the information that we get as a retailer all the time, is why a customer is choosing to buy our products and it's how we communicate that the border of being scientifically led, a clinical outcome, and combining it with a customer outcome because customers don't speak clinical language, so that's the agenda, which we will skip over. So, there's a photograph of a tortoise on the screen, and I really like this this analogy because it was one of the first lectures I ever had doing my master's program. Was this exact image put up on the screen? So, why is there a tortoise on the screen? This is why there's a tortoise on the screen? A tortoise's biology fundamentally challenges the way we look at aging. A tortoise will live the majority of its life without any disability or ailment. As you compare to a human, we live approximately between 10 and 12 years with either a disability or poor health. So a tortoise fundamentally will challenge the notion that biology is we are destined to age in a poor way. I'm not saying we're all going to live to 200 years, but actually there is a biological plausibility that we can all age better. So it's not just smoke and mirrors. Lifespan to health. Nick touched on this very nicely in his talk about the difference between the two, and it's a really important distinction because I think the category should almost be renamed, not just longevity, because actually, we're not in the business of making people live longer; we're making them live better. How do we do that from a product perspective? So, we're in a very, very fortunate position where we have data of millions of consumers across the globe, and we can see what they're buying and how frequently they're buying it, which is obviously the most important thing that we all, as brand owners, want. Is we want customers not just to buy the product once, we want them to keep buying the product. So, I see a lot of this in the kind of cellular health space and the more novels products in the in the longevity spaces. They promise a lot from mechanism. It's all about sirtuins and parts and telomere lengths, and I think I was on a really interesting panel last week in London with our with our own customers. So we were talking to all of our customers. We had customers from all of our key groups, and we had customers from each of our key markets. And something that really stood out to me was the way that customers talk to us about our products. So we think we can communicate to the customer with the science and the claims, but the way customers talk to us. For example, there was there was a lady in one of our customer groups called Stay Healthies. These are customers around the 50 age group, and she was just saying, "Well, actually, all I want to be able to do is play with my grandchildren, get up out of my chair without making a noise, go on that hike, travel without being uncomfortable, and this is not something that we've seen in clinical literature about how can how can I play with my grandchildren, but actually it's how we translate scientific evidence to help consumers with their problems, and not just looking at what the science is saying. And this really does retain customers. So we see the biggest sales that in our own label portfolio is products that have a clear communicated benefit to joint function, joint comfort, brain function, etc. These things like this, not just focusing on disseminating the clinical literature. So yeah, they do not buy. So this is a really interesting point, and I had a bit of a debate with our science team about this one last week. Customers are not buying into the mechanism. They are buying your product based off how they feel and how they continue to feel taking your product. So, common questions that we get as a retailer all the time is when timescale. summary.Summary:
Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett's Global Product Formulation Lead, runs the team that formulates its own-label products worldwide. He asked how longevity science becomes something a customer will buy. His answer: consumers may buy a story, but they judge a product on the outcomes they feel.

He opened with a tortoise to argue that ageing badly is not biologically fixed, so the category is about living better, not longer. H&B's data on millions of customers show that repeat purchase goes to products with one clearly communicated benefit, such as joint function or brain function. Shoppers ask when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs. His slides set the test an ingredient must pass: evidence, dose, outcome, communication and consumer relevance.

Two case studies followed. NAD boosters have a strong molecular rationale but very limited functional outcome data, and of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was. Curcumin, H&B's second best-selling ingredient, shows the other path: a meta-analysis of 11 trials found it improved knee osteoarthritis pain scores. He also named cheap basics with strong evidence: fibre, vitamin D, calcium and protein.

His conclusion for suppliers: bring ingredients with both a biological rationale and human outcome data, and help retailers translate the science without over-promising.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Mechanisms make promises and sell, but outcomes retain customers (slide 6). Shoppers ask whether and when they will feel it, whether they can measure it, and what it costs (slide 8); when trials show a benefit at four, six or eight weeks, H&B can sometimes put that on pack [00:25].
- H&B's test for an ingredient has five parts: evidence (high-quality science), dose (the effective, studied dose), outcome (which endpoint improves), communication (legal and responsible) and consumer relevance (does it matter in everyday life) (slide 6).
- The outcomes consumers buy are energy, memory, strength, mobility, sleep, appearance and feeling younger or better, not NAD+, sirtuins, telomeres or PARPs (slide 8). H&B's biggest own-label sellers carry one clear benefit, such as joint function, joint comfort or brain function [00:25].
- NAD: of over 1000 customers surveyed, not one knew what NAD was [00:25]. NR reliably raises blood NAD metabolites and NMN or NAM raise it in some studies, but functional outcome improvements are "very limited" (slide 13).
- Curcumin is the "tangible outcomes" case: a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs (n=1258) found curcuminoids improved VAS and WOMAC pain scores in knee osteoarthritis against comparators or placebo, and formulation matters because bioavailability varies widely (slide 15).
- Cheap interventions with strong evidence (fibre, vitamin D, calcium, protein) beat novel technologies on evidence and cost; US shelves are "protein plus fiber" [00:25]. None of this is on his slides.

Alex Glover discusses the necessity of translating complex scientific mechanisms into tangible consumer outcomes to drive product sales and customer retention.

## Consumer Insights
**Translating Science**
**Alex** emphasizes that while researchers focus on biological mechanisms like sirtuins, telomeres, or **NAD**, consumers prioritize functional benefits. Customers do not use clinical language; they want to know if a product will help them play with grandchildren, walk without pain, or sleep more refreshingly. **Alex** notes that the highest sales in the **Holland & Barrett** own-label portfolio come from products with clearly communicated benefits for joint function, brain function, and comfort.

**Market Realities**
**Alex** highlights a significant gap in consumer understanding regarding longevity science. In a survey of over 1,000 people, not a single respondent knew what **NAD** was. While there is high interest in "cellular health," consumer definitions are vague, covering everything from fertility to immunity. This suggests that marketing novel ingredients requires bridging the gap between clinical biomarkers and everyday feelings.

## Product Strategy
**Evidence Based Interventions**
**Alex** argues that cost-effective, traditional nutritional interventions often have stronger evidence bases than newer technologies. Examples include:
* **Fiber**: Reduces coronary heart disease risk by approximately 9% per seven grams of intake.
* **Vitamin D**: Highly cost-effective, costing roughly two cents per 10 microgram serving.
* **Curcumin**: A top-selling ingredient globally (one bottle sold per minute) that supports joint flexibility and reduces systemic inflammation.

**The Longevity Gap**
The discussion contrasts the "longevity" category—which implies living longer—with the goal of helping people "live better." **Alex** points out that many industry players get stuck in the "blue sections" of research, focusing on mechanisms and biomarkers rather than clinical outcomes. The primary questions from retailers and customers remain: "When am I going to feel a benefit?" and "How much is it going to cost?"

[00:13] Speaker 1: Manufacturing. How does this market actually work today? There are three sides: brands, manufacturers, and ingredient suppliers, working with each other every single day, from an idea to a finished product, from research to new formulations and new forms of production. One side places the orders; the other makes them a constant exchange of information between them. According to Grandview Research, all of this adds up to over 12 percent growth a year, and a forecast of more than 60 billion dollars by 2030. So, one more question: Why are we all here today to grow? The market works today; it grows as we have just seen. But are we using its full potential because the same problems come back again and again when looking for new partners and in the daily exchange between the three sides, no visibility in your category, no single format or offers, inquiries that arrive incomplete, one inquiry living in many threads, inquiries that do not fit what you do, and sometimes no answer at all.
[01:50] Speaker 2: Raise your hand if you see at least one of this at your company. Okay, thank you. I see some hands. All of this has a cost. There is, of course, wasted time that never turn into business. But there is also operational cost. These problems slows down every process. Hours spent organizing inquiries, searching for agreements across long email threads, and dealing with all the noise around them. And the second one, lost opportunity. Every offer you never received, every inquiry you never had a chance to answer, because of lack of visibility in your category.
[02:45] Speaker 1: It

That's a good question, but first let me introduce myself. My name is Viktor Tsevsky, co-founder of Two Waves, and as a product manager, I work on this side of the market every day. Contact with manufacturers, negotiation quoting, and that is where I started noticing all of this. This is Matthew Kwembowski, co-founder of Two Waves. He designs IT architecture and data security systems for industrial clients for some of the most demanding automotive and aerospace brands in the world. And someone who needs no introduction, the person thanks to whom we are all here today, Pavel Grushinsky, strategic advisor and board member of the project. Ladies and gentlemen, this industry grew up without a tool of its own, and now it has one, and it's called two ways. So, how do we unlock the full potential of this growth? The answer starts with module one: new partnerships, quoting, and negotiation. Today's market runs on three sides: brands, manufacturers, and ingredient suppliers, and everything that moves between them. Let's take one example. A brand has a new inquiry. How do you find the right manufacturer partner today? In most cases, you start with companies you already know. That means one inquiry goes to one manufacturer at a time. Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

**Two Waves** is a digital platform designed to streamline the manufacturing ecosystem between brands, manufacturers, and ingredient suppliers.

## Market Challenges
The manufacturing market is projected by **Grandview Research** to grow at over 12 percent annually, exceeding $60 billion by 2030. However, current processes suffer from significant inefficiencies:
* Lack of visibility in specific product categories.
* Incomplete inquiries and fragmented communication across multiple email threads.
* High operational costs due to wasted time organizing data and searching for agreements.
* Lost opportunities resulting from missed offers or inquiries that do not reach the right partners.

## Platform Solutions
**Viktor** and **Matthew** introduced **Two Waves** as a tool to centralize quoting and negotiation through several key modules:
* **New Partnerships**: Instead of one-to-one outreach, one inquiry automatically reaches all verified manufacturers within a specific category, allowing for rapid comparison of structured offers.
* **Standardized Quoting**: The platform uses structured templates tailored to product categories to eliminate "communication noise" and ensure all key information is present.
* **Negotiation Management**: Users can manage quoting variants and track the full history of negotiations in a single location. 
* **Feedback Loops**: If an inquiry or offer is declined, the system provides a specific reason to improve future interactions.

## Security Infrastructure
**Matthew** addressed the risks associated with traditional communication methods like phone calls and emails, where data control is easily lost once information enters an inbox. To mitigate these risks, **Two Waves** implements:
* Mandatory company verification for all users to ensure participants are interacting only with verified entities.
* Enhanced control over how sensitive information is shared during the initial stages of business relationships.

summary.Summary:
The day's closing panel brought together a retailer (Alex Glover, Holland & Barrett), a CDMO (Martina Pavlová, FAVEA), an ingredient company (Matts Johansen, chief executive of Aker BioMarine), a food lawyer (Joanna) and a pharmaceutical company (Alexandra). The moderator asked what each wants in the next two or three years, then turned to regulation, supply and AI.

They agreed that the consumer comes first. Alexandra wanted evidence-based claims and better communication, Martina a focus on what consumers actually need, and Alex a few claims done well, starting from the consumer's problem rather than piling on ingredients. Matts wanted a revolution in clinical trials: high-dose studies in people with real problems, published where consumers' chatbots will find them.

On regulation they differed in tone. Joanna wants food law to be a shield for innovators, though the claims system was written for vitamins. Matts was blunter: a three-year longer approval in Europe than in the US almost makes innovation impossible.

On supply, Matts warned of a fish oil shortage reaching shelves next summer. Alex described pre-bought stock and protecting the claim shoppers buy. Joanna said blaming the supplier is no defence.

On AI they wanted a human in the loop and peer-reviewed sources, and Matts warned that anyone who cannot use AI will not be able to work in two years.

The panel discussed the evolving landscape of the nutraceutical industry, focusing on scientific evidence, regulatory challenges, and technological integration.

## Industry Trends
**Alexandra**, **Matt**, and **Alex** highlighted the increasing demand for evidence-based products and high-quality communication.
*   **Alexandra** emphasized that consumers are increasingly well-informed but often rely on unqualified sources, necessitating better communication of factual ingredient claims.
*   **Matt** suggested a revolution in clinical trials, advocating for high-dose studies on individuals with actual health problems rather than healthy subjects to generate more meaningful data.
*   **Alex** noted that consumers prioritize solving specific problems and prefer clear, specialized messaging over brands that attempt to market too many ingredients or claims simultaneously.

## Regulatory Challenges
**Joanna** and **Martina** addressed the friction between innovation and legal frameworks.
*   **Joanna** explained that current food laws were designed for common ingredients like vitamin C and D, making it difficult for innovators to use clinical trial data to support new claims. She urged R&D teams to involve lawyers early in the development process to ensure compliance is a "shield" rather than a "heartbreak."
*   **Martina** observed that legislation often acts as an obstacle for CDMOs and advised businesses not to simply chase every market gap but to focus on deep understanding and consumer needs.
*   **Matt** raised concerns regarding the speed of European regulations compared to the **U.S.**, noting that a three-year delay in approval can make the net present value of new ingredients economically unviable.

## Supply and Technology
The discussion concluded with the impact of supply chain volatility and artificial intelligence.
*   **Matt** warned of a looming collapse in the fish oil supply chain due to aquaculture industry competition and potential traceability issues involving illegal fishing. 
*   **Alex** noted that retailers must proactively manage lead times and prepare for price increases or shifts in consumer preference if core ingredients like omega-3 become unavailable.
*   **Joanna** and **Alexandra** discussed the role of **AI**, noting its utility in searching peer-reviewed databases and managing factory sensors. **Joanna** stressed the importance of keeping a "human in the loop" to maintain legal integrity and trust, while **Matt** predicted that proficiency in operating **AI** tools will become a mandatory job requirement within two years.

sessions.transcript:
# HMT: beyond probiotics, four new rules for the category: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Marit - HMT - Remedy CMO", https://otter.ai/u/bK_DMxHJzVgH8AgUv_VzIp24x3Y, recorded 23 Oct 2026 10:03, 11m 31s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Speaker 1: Health and supplement brands. Its role is to help companies connect what they can develop with what consumers understand and value. So, to open our probiotic program with the landscape and trends from HMT, please welcome Marty Leibstra.
[00:24] Speaker 2: Thank you. Hello, good morning, everyone. I'm actually really happy to see that the room is quite full because after last night I was expecting less people to be here. To be honest, and thank you for the introduction. So my name is Marit Weinstra, and yes, I'm from H and D. So you said it very well. We do branding and innovation for food and supplements. And today I'm talking about beyond probiotics because when Paolo asked me, "Can you talk about probiotics?" First I thought, "Okay, in 10 minutes, what's there's only so much you can say in 10 minutes about probiotics." But I thought let's make it a little bit easier for myself, and let's talk about beyond the probiotics. Because in the end, if you work in probiotics, you also need to understand what's happening beyond probiotics. We have prebiotics, we have fibers, we have postbiotics. So the market is becoming much bigger. So it's important to understand what is happening. Yes. Okay. So I don't think I have to tell you that probiotics in general have increased in popularity in the past years. So both the sales have increased. Have increased. The consumption has has increased, and more and more people are aware of the effects of any type of biotic, basically, and the gut health. So this is of course really good for our industry. But when we look at the at the market, we see more and more products being launched every day in different formats, new ingredients, new health benefits, so it's becoming really a jungle of products. And imagine yourself as a consumer standing in front of the shelves or looking online for what products you want to buy. How can you understand which product you need to choose? Because there is so much available. And in the end, and I think Alex told that very well yesterday. In the end, the consumer just wants to understand which product is actually right for me, and this is where we can still do a lot of work in this industry because there are too many options out there, but there's not enough clarity in this industry. And consumers even say that they don't feel that informed about probiotics, maybe they know that it's good for them. They know they need to do something about their gut health, but do they really understand what it is and what it does? Well, we still have a lot to achieve here. So to talk about and to understand where we are today and what you need to be aware of to really win in this market today, I want to go a little bit back in time and also give you an understanding of how did we actually get here and what what happened in this in this whole category and how has the market evolved. So it actually started with Yakult and the understanding that there can be good and bad bacteria because initially it was okay, bacteria are bad for you, but then there came the understanding and especially the education that there can also be good bacteria. And actually, how the category was born was right away from a really good point of view because it was right away born as a daily ritual. And we all know that if you want the biotics to be successful in your body, you kind of need to take it on a daily basis. So the category was born as a daily ritual in a very convenient format, and yeah, something that you can easily take every day.
[03:52] Speaker 3: 10 o'clock already should be now.
[03:53] Speaker 2: But then the challenge was: okay, you have this benefit
[03:56] Speaker 4: of it supports your gut flora, which is very
[03:59] Speaker 2: intangible because of the bacteria, and this. where Danone Activia actually led that second wave, and they try to make the invisible benefits more tangible by talking about the digestion. And you see that in their old logo, the way that they branded their strains, and they really help to yeah educate more around the benefits that probiotics can have in your gut, but this also led to the competition of more bacteria is better, and where where brands started competing on the CFU count. And the third era, this is where we also started to understand. Okay, but if it doesn't arrive alive in your gut, then actually it doesn't really work. So this is where the technology became the story, and survival became the promise, so that it has to survive, arrive alive in your gut. But as you can imagine, we are moving now further away from the consumer and helping them understand, okay, but what does it actually do for you? And where we are now is where we shifted from adding to nourishing, and this is where the market now starts to educate on, okay, you already your gut is an ecosystem, and we need to nourish that, we need to strengthen that, and this is opening a whole new world because this is where we start creating new language in the category. So we move from strains and bacteria. We can actually talk about the ecosystem, the gut barrier. This is where fermentation becomes an important term, even a whole food approach. So the question is really changing from what is in the product to what does it actually do for me. And the gut also became the gateway because when we move the focus from just bacteria to actually the gut barrier and the whole ecosystem, the gut barrier is also where it meets the rest of your body. So this is where the story becomes much bigger, and this is also why the why the category really exploded because it's not only about digestion anymore. So this also means that now that the the market has become so much bigger, and we're not only talking about bacteria anymore, that there are also new rules that define actually what win in the category today. So I'm gonna show you the four different rules. I don't think you can see it very well, but the next slide you should see them. So the first rule is from more is better to quality and proven. And as I said before, you still have a lot of shelves where you see 50 billion, 80 billion, 100 billions of bacteria, and to be honest, it doesn't really mean anything to the consumer. They don't understand what is that difference, and they probably feel that more is better. But what we're seeing that numbers alone don't build trust anymore with the consumer, and how you can build trust with the consumer is also not to focus anymore on the generic gut benefits, but really try to be an expert in your own niche. And this is where this brand from the U.S. does a good job. So they they are based on the Acromancia strain, and they really focus on metabolic health and weight management. Then the second rule is from simply adding bacteria to feeding your whole ecosystem. And as I said before, this is really opening a new world and language that the consumer actually understands much better, because this is where we can talk about nourishing, nourishing what you already have, the diversity of plants that you need to actually feed the bacteria that are in your gut. So the language becomes more relatable for the consumer. You can actually see it because bacteria you don't see it, but when you start talking about fibers and plants, it becomes much more tangible. And this is also where you can be more in control as a consumer because you can actually proactively do something about it. You can proactively feed your gut yourself. So this is where you see now mainly the fiber brands that are talking about this, but also where it's not about having just one fiber, one prebiotic fiber anymore, but really have that diversity, and then we have the third rule, and that is from belief and promise to measurable and felt benefits. And for years, the benefit was quite invisible. It was about supporting a healthy gut flora, and that is relevant for those who actually understand a bit more about gut health and the importance of probiotics, for instance. But what we're seeing now is that early adopters they actually start measuring the benefits. So they do microbiome tests. They use different apps to actually measure the effect that it has on their on their body. And this is where we see the mass market consumers, so let's say most consumers that are out there, they want to feel the benefits. So for them, if they use it and they don't feel the benefits, they won't continue to use your products. So these are the consumers that will only continue to buy once they feel difference. And you don't see the example very well, but this is where you see brands that start communicating and creating the right expectations for consumers. So, what can you actually feel when you use this product for one week, for one month? summary.Summary:
Marit Veenstra of HMT, the Healthy Marketing Team, a food and health branding and innovation agency, opened the probiotic programme. Her question was how to win in a biotics market that has grown into a jungle of products. Use keeps rising, yet in seven of eight European countries consumers do not feel informed about probiotics.

She traced four eras. Yakult made good bacteria a daily ritual. Activia made the benefit tangible, and brands began competing on CFU counts. Then survival technology became the story. Now the shift is from adding bacteria to nourishing the gut ecosystem, with the gut barrier as the gateway to the rest of the body.

From that she drew four rules: quality and proof over "more is better", feeding the ecosystem, benefits consumers can measure and feel, and everyday food formats. Her examples were mostly American: Pendulum's Akkermansia products for metabolic health, a prebiotic fibre brand, a digestive brand that sets expectations week by week, and Poppi.

Her conclusion: in Europe most of these claims cannot be made, so the brand has to carry them. Value is moving from what is inside the product to what the consumer gets. A strong probiotic needs a "Double IP": the science and the brand.

- Rule 1, from "more is better" to quality and proof: a number on its own no longer builds trust, so be an expert brand in a niche (slide 14). Shelves show 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU [03:59]; her niche example is Pendulum, an Akkermansia-based US brand for metabolic health (slide 14) [03:59].
- Rule 2, from adding bacteria to feeding the ecosystem: "eat more plants" instead of strain names, plants and fibre consumers can see, and a gut they feed themselves (slide 15); fibre brands lead this language [03:59].

Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Marit Weinstra from **HMT** discusses the evolution of the probiotic market and shifting consumer expectations toward holistic gut health.

## Market Evolution
The probiotic category has moved through several distinct eras, transitioning from basic awareness to complex ecosystem management.
*   **First Era**: Focused on the concept of "good" vs "bad" bacteria, popularized by **Yakult** as a daily ritual.
*   **Second Era**: Led by **Danone Activia**, which focused on making intangible benefits like digestion more tangible via branding.
*   **Third Era**: Centered on technology and survival, where the primary promise was ensuring bacteria arrive alive in the gut.
*   **Current Era**: Shifting from simply adding bacteria to nourishing the entire gut ecosystem, focusing on terms like the gut barrier and fermentation.

## Strategic Shifts
To succeed in the current "jungle" of products, brands must follow four new industry rules to build consumer trust and clarity.
*   **Quality over Quantity**: Moving away from competing solely on high CFU counts (e.g., 50 billion or 100 billion) toward proven, niche expertise such as metabolic health.
*   **Ecosystem Nourishment**: Transitioning from adding single strains to providing plant diversity and fibers that proactively feed existing gut flora.
*   **Measurable Benefits**: Shifting from invisible promises to felt or measured results, utilizing microbiome tests or apps for early adopters while ensuring mass-market consumers feel immediate physical differences.
*   **Consumer-Centric Formats**: Moving from functional supplements toward desirable everyday food formats, similar to how **Poppi** approaches the category.

## Branding Strategy
Because many health claims are restricted in Europe compared to the U.S., brands must rely on emotional value rather than just rational science. 
*   Building a "double IP" involves combining rational scientific evidence with an emotional brand identity to ensure long-term protection and market presence. 
*   Success requires turning scientific innovation into a consumer-centric value proposition that provides clarity amidst excessive market options.

summary.Summary:
Sacco System's speaker presented the company as a family-owned probiotic maker and CDMO that sells speed and flexibility. The recording joins mid-introduction, and the slides do not name him. Sacco dates from 1872 and turned over €195 million in 2025.

He described its offer: probiotics, postbiotics and tailor-made mixtures, strains screened to EFSA safety requirements, custom fermentation at any scale, and next-generation strains developed for third parties. Sacco has recently invested in clinical studies and patents in two areas, women's health and healthy ageing, and he gave one strain for each.

CA15, a patented strain isolated from a healthy woman, was tested in two placebo-controlled trials in women with vaginal imbalance. He reported fewer symptoms after ten days, held a month after intake stopped.

Synbio, a patented mix of two strains isolated from elderly people in Marche, was tested over six months in 97 healthy people over 65. He reported more beneficial bacteria and butyrate, a 43% fall in a marker of inflammation, higher IGF-1, which he linked to muscle maintenance, and slower shortening of telomeres.

His close was an invitation: Sacco will take on unusual projects quickly and work closely with the customer.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Its pitch as a CDMO is speed and flexibility: a low time to market, agile family decisions, custom fermentation from 1 L to 40,000 L, and a new kind of production if asked (slide 6) (slide 8) [00:00].
- CA15 trials: two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies, 60 women in 2023 and 200 in 2025, one capsule of 10 billion CFU a day for 10 days and a 30-day wash-out (slide 14). They differ from the talk, which gave a six-woman exploratory study and "10 mil per capsule" [00:00].
- CA15 results: symptom scores fell 78% for discomfort, 66% burning, 64% itching, 62% secretions and 56% inflammation (slide 15). On the Amsel criteria 98% of women had a corrected pH, 92% a negative amine test, 79% no clue cells and 75% normal discharge, as labelled on the chart (slide 16); he gave the first three the same [00:00].
- Synbio trial: L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502, 5 billion CFU a serving for six months in 97 healthy people over 65, randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled (slide 21) (slide 23); spoken as "five mil" daily [00:00].
- Synbio results, end of study against start: hs-CRP down 43%, IL-8 down 83%, IL-6 67%, MIP-1α 60% and TNF-α 23% (slide 25); total short-chain fatty acids up 23% and butyric acid up 33% (slide 26) [00:00].
- Sacco says Synbio "increases IGF-1 levels", which it calls key for muscle maintenance in ageing, and that it slowed telomere shortening against placebo (slide 27) (slide 28) (slide 29) [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Medium relevance, unchanged by the slides. Sacco makes probiotics and runs a CDMO, so it is a possible partner, not a buyer of our ingredients.
- Synbio is pitched to over-65s on muscle maintenance, through IGF-1 and nutritional status (slide 27) (slide 29). My reading: a "gut plus muscle" healthy-ageing pairing with CreaWin or IsoClr: Pea is a possible co-formulation pitch.
- Sport is one of Sacco's ten therapeutic areas (slide 9), though the talk covered only women's health and healthy ageing. Worth asking what it has for sports nutrition.
- The claims are Sacco's. The hs-CRP, cytokine and fatty-acid charts compare the end of the study with its start; only the IGF-1, nutrition and telomere charts show the placebo group (slide 25) (slide 26) (slide 27) (slide 28). My reading: ask for the placebo comparison before citing any of it.

- "...we observe a 43 percentage reduction of the high sensitivity C reactive protein, which is a marker of inflammaging" Speaker 1 (Sacco System) [00:00]
- "...an improvement in the production of insulin growth factor one, that is a hormone correlated with the protein synthesis as well as the maintenance of the muscle mass, the so-called sarcopenia" Speaker 1 (Sacco System) [00:00]

summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm the speaker's name ("Simone"?) and role; neither the recording nor the slides give them.
- Ask Sacco for the CA15 trial papers (60 and 200 women) and the Synbio (ProBioSenior) paper, with the placebo-group results for hs-CRP, cytokines, fatty acids and telomeres.
- Ask what Sacco offers for sports nutrition (slide 9), and whether Synbio has been tested alongside protein or creatine.
summary.Detail:
- The deck is titled "From cell to scale: Patented strains & custom fermentation power", subtitled "Targeted solutions for healthy ageing & women's health" (slide 2). No slide names the speaker. No slide is marked confidential.
- Sacco's numbers: more than 6,500 strains in its bank, more than 600 people, 11 production plants, €195 million turnover in 2025, more than 110 export countries, more than 40 university collaborations (slide 4).
- Presence: headquarters in Italy (Sacco System and CSL, Centro Sperimentale del Latte), CSL USA, and Sacco System companies in France, the Nordics, Japan, China, Australia, Brazil and Uruguay (slide 5). He named plants in Como, Milan (CSL, pharmaceutical API probiotics) and Wisconsin, and a Brisbane pilot for next-generation and exotic strains [00:00].
- Offer: CultureScience, clinically documented strains; CultureSelect, strains screened for EFSA safety and function (at least 30 species); Made For You, development of next-generation probiotics and live biotherapeutics (slide 7) [00:00].
- Manufacturing: GMP pharma plants and pilot labs, qualified persons and validation experts, religious certifications, a hypoallergenic production system (slide 6); food-grade GMP, an anaerobic pilot plant for next-generation strains, and uses in supplements, pharma, food and drinks (slide 8).
- Therapeutic areas: gut, immune, skin, healthy ageing, metabolic, sport, women's, oral, infant and children, mental health (slide 9).
- CA15 is Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus CA15 DSM 33960, isolated in 2022 in Sicily from a healthy woman (slide 11). Otter's "in CCD" is Sicily [00:00].
- CA15 in vitro: more than 95% survival in simulated gut transit; adhesion of 36% to intestinal Caco-2 cells, 34% to vaginal VK2/E6E7 cells and 12% to intestinal mucus; produces lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide (slide 12).
- In the SHIME gut model a 10-billion capsule survived the small intestine and colon, fasted and fed, alone and with fluconazole 200 mg; the slide cites Vaccalluzzo A et al, Food Res Int (2025) (slide 13). He said the University of Catania ran the clinical studies [00:00]; the slides neither name Catania nor cite the trial papers.
- CA15 outcomes: primary, microbiota rebalance, no signs or symptoms of dysbiosis, normal Amsel and Nugent scores; secondary, quality of life (slide 14).
- Nugent score: CA15 moved women from the dysbiotic band (7 to 10) to normal (0 to 3) by day 10 and held at day 30, while placebo stayed in or near the dysbiotic band, read from the chart (slide 17).
- Vaginal counts: Lactobacillus rose from about 3.5 to about 7 log10 CFU/ml in 10 days; Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Gardnerella, Candida and E. coli fell, and both held 30 days after the last dose, read from the chart (slide 18) [00:00].
- CA15 key messages also claim better quality of life, resistance to fluconazole, and remission "not only maintained, but further increased" (slide 19).
- Synbio strains were isolated in 2021 in Marche from elderly people (slide 21); he said the ratio is 1 to 1 and the region has one of Europe's highest shares of centenarians [00:00]. The slide says Synbio is backed by "over 50 scientific publications" and more than 1,000 people in human studies (slide 21).
- The Synbio trial slide carries a "ProBioSenior" logo. Primary outcomes were hs-CRP, gut microbiota and fatty-acid production; secondary, cytokines, IGF-1 and nutritional status (slide 23).
- Gut changes after six months: Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus and butyrate up, inflammation down (slide 24) [00:00].
- Chart values, read from the charts: hs-CRP from about 4 to 2.3 mg/l (slide 25); fatty acids from about 57 to 70 µmol/g and butyric acid from about 9 to 12 µmol/g (slide 26). Each is marked significant by t-test (P<0.05).

The meeting presents the capabilities and patented probiotic solutions of **Sacco**, a family-owned CDMO specializing in pharmaceutical and food-grade active ingredients.

## Company Overview
**Sacco** is an agile, family-owned company with global operations including manufacturing plants in Italy (Como and Milan) and the US (Wisconsin). Their infrastructure supports various production needs:
*   **CSL** (Milan): Specialized in pharmaceutical API probiotics.
*   **Sacosystem Australia** (Brisbane): A pilot facility focused on next-generation bacteria, exotic strains, and LVPs.
*   **Quality Standards**: They offer both GMP pharma-standard facilities for high-end APIs and conventional GMP food-grade sites, supported by validation experts.
*   **Services**: Capabilities include providing probiotics, postbiotics, customized mixtures, and a "made-for-you" service for third-party strain development.

## Product Portfolio
The presentation highlights two primary areas of investment: women's health and healthy aging.

**Women's Health: CA15**
**CA15** is a patented strain isolated from vaginal samples in 2022. 
*   **Efficacy**: Clinical studies involving 200 women showed significant reduction in symptoms of bacterial vaginosis and vaginal candidiasis, such as burning, itching, and inflammation.
*   **Diagnostic Results**: Post-treatment (10 days) and one month after washout, 98% of subjects showed restored pH ranges and 92% had negative amine tests.
*   **Mechanism**: The strain survives gastrointestinal transit, colonizes the vagina, promotes natural lactobacilli like *G. acidophilus*, and reduces pathogens like *Gardnerella vaginalis*.

**Healthy Aging: Symbio**
**Symbio** is a synergistic mixture of *L. paracasi* and *L. rhamnosus* isolated from the Italian Marche region.
*   **Clinical Findings**: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 97 subjects over six months, **Symbio** increased gut microbiota diversity (Akkermansia, Bifidobacteria) and short-chain fatty acids like butyrate.
*   **Inflammation & Muscle Mass**: Results showed a 43% reduction in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and improved insulin growth factor one levels to combat sarcopenia.
*   **Longevity**: Blood analysis indicated a decrease in the rate of telomere shortening, a key marker of biological aging.

detail.text: The deck is titled "From cell to scale: Patented strains & custom fermentation power", subtitled "Targeted solutions for healthy ageing & women's health" (slide 2). No slide names the speaker. No slide is marked confidential.

Sacco's numbers: more than 6,500 strains in its bank, more than 600 people, 11 production plants, €195 million turnover in 2025, more than 110 export countries, more than 40 university collaborations (slide 4).

Presence: headquarters in Italy (Sacco System and CSL, Centro Sperimentale del Latte), CSL USA, and Sacco System companies in France, the Nordics, Japan, China, Australia, Brazil and Uruguay (slide 5). He named plants in Como, Milan (CSL, pharmaceutical API probiotics) and Wisconsin, and a Brisbane pilot for next-generation and exotic strains [00:00].

Offer: CultureScience, clinically documented strains; CultureSelect, strains screened for EFSA safety and function (at least 30 species); Made For You, development of next-generation probiotics and live biotherapeutics (slide 7) [00:00].

Manufacturing: GMP pharma plants and pilot labs, qualified persons and validation experts, religious certifications, a hypoallergenic production system (slide 6); food-grade GMP, an anaerobic pilot plant for next-generation strains, and uses in supplements, pharma, food and drinks (slide 8).
Therapeutic areas: gut, immune, skin, healthy ageing, metabolic, sport, women's, oral, infant and children, mental health (slide 9).
CA15 is Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus CA15 DSM 33960, isolated in 2022 in Sicily from a healthy woman (slide 11). Otter's "in CCD" is Sicily [00:00].

CA15 in vitro: more than 95% survival in simulated gut transit; adhesion of 36% to intestinal Caco-2 cells, 34% to vaginal VK2/E6E7 cells and 12% to intestinal mucus; produces lactic acid and hydrogen peroxide (slide 12).

In the SHIME gut model a 10-billion capsule survived the small intestine and colon, fasted and fed, alone and with fluconazole 200 mg; the slide cites Vaccalluzzo A et al, Food Res Int (2025) (slide 13). He said the University of Catania ran the clinical studies [00:00]; the slides neither name Catania nor cite the trial papers.
CA15 outcomes: primary, microbiota rebalance, no signs or symptoms of dysbiosis, normal Amsel and Nugent scores; secondary, quality of life (slide 14).
Nugent score: CA15 moved women from the dysbiotic band (7 to 10) to normal (0 to 3) by day 10 and held at day 30, while placebo stayed in or near the dysbiotic band, read from the chart (slide 17).

Vaginal counts: Lactobacillus rose from about 3.5 to about 7 log10 CFU/ml in 10 days; Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Gardnerella, Candida and E. coli fell, and both held 30 days after the last dose, read from the chart (slide 18) [00:00].
CA15 key messages also claim better quality of life, resistance to fluconazole, and remission "not only maintained, but further increased" (slide 19).

Synbio strains were isolated in 2021 in Marche from elderly people (slide 21); he said the ratio is 1 to 1 and the region has one of Europe's highest shares of centenarians [00:00]. The slide says Synbio is backed by "over 50 scientific publications" and more than 1,000 people in human studies (slide 21).
The Synbio trial slide carries a "ProBioSenior" logo. Primary outcomes were hs-CRP, gut microbiota and fatty-acid production; secondary, cytokines, IGF-1 and nutritional status (slide 23).
Gut changes after six months: Akkermansia, Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus and butyrate up, inflammation down (slide 24) [00:00].

Chart values, read from the charts: hs-CRP from about 4 to 2.3 mg/l (slide 25); fatty acids from about 57 to 70 µmol/g and butyric acid from about 9 to 12 µmol/g (slide 26). Each is marked significant by t-test (P<0.05).

IGF-1 rose from about 118 to 145 pg/ml with Synbio and from about 118 to 120 with placebo; normal nutrition on the questionnaire rose from about 28% to 57% of the Synbio group, and malnourished fell from about 18% to 7%, with placebo little changed, read from the charts (slide 27) [00:00].

Telomere length (estimated marginal means): placebo fell from about 1.025 to 1.00 and Synbio rose from about 1.018 to 1.027 over 180 days, read from the chart; the chart carries no significance mark (slide 28). He said there was "a decrease in the reduction in the length" [00:00].
Otter heard the mix as "Symbio" [00:00]; the slides spell it SYNBIO (slide 20). He used Gemini to find the shoelace metaphor for telomeres, which the slide repeats (slide 28) [00:00].

takeaways.text: Its pitch as a CDMO is speed and flexibility: a low time to market, agile family decisions, custom fermentation from 1 L to 40,000 L, and a new kind of production if asked (slide 6) (slide 8) [00:00].

CA15 trials: two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies, 60 women in 2023 and 200 in 2025, one capsule of 10 billion CFU a day for 10 days and a 30-day wash-out (slide 14). They differ from the talk, which gave a six-woman exploratory study and "10 mil per capsule" [00:00].

CA15 results: symptom scores fell 78% for discomfort, 66% burning, 64% itching, 62% secretions and 56% inflammation (slide 15). On the Amsel criteria 98% of women had a corrected pH, 92% a negative amine test, 79% no clue cells and 75% normal discharge, as labelled on the chart (slide 16); he gave the first three the same [00:00].

Synbio trial: L. rhamnosus IMC 501 and L. paracasei IMC 502, 5 billion CFU a serving for six months in 97 healthy people over 65, randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled (slide 21) (slide 23); spoken as "five mil" daily [00:00].

Synbio results, end of study against start: hs-CRP down 43%, IL-8 down 83%, IL-6 67%, MIP-1α 60% and TNF-α 23% (slide 25); total short-chain fatty acids up 23% and butyric acid up 33% (slide 26) [00:00].
Sacco says Synbio "increases IGF-1 levels", which it calls key for muscle maintenance in ageing, and that it slowed telomere shortening against placebo (slide 27) (slide 28) (slide 29) [00:00].

"...we observe a 43 percentage reduction of the high sensitivity C reactive protein, which is a marker of inflammaging" Speaker 1 (Sacco System) [00:00]

"...an improvement in the production of insulin growth factor one, that is a hormone correlated with the protein synthesis as well as the maintenance of the muscle mass, the so-called sarcopenia" Speaker 1 (Sacco System) [00:00]
"Rapid effect, making asymptomatic 6 out of 10 women in 10 days" (slide 19)

followups: Confirm the speaker's name ("Simone"?) and role; neither the recording nor the slides give them.
Ask Sacco for the CA15 trial papers (60 and 200 women) and the Synbio (ProBioSenior) paper, with the placebo-group results for hs-CRP, cytokines, fatty acids and telomeres.
Ask what Sacco offers for sports nutrition (slide 9), and whether Synbio has been tested alongside protein or creatine.

summary.Summary:
Two suppliers shared this slot. Miguel of SPI Pharma, an ABF Ingredients company, presented "From platform to product". His case: consumers buy formats first, so the gap is not another active but a format people will take. Last year SPI Pharma showed probiotics can be tableted. This year it showed what that tablet becomes.

He showed three concepts, each on an SPI platform. A mint chewable probiotic for adults, pressed gently on a low-moisture platform so the cultures survive. A fizzy electrolyte and energy stick for sport, kept stable by a modified sodium bicarbonate; a light fizz also masks bitterness. A vanilla fast-melt for healthy ageing that needs no water. The packs were illustrative concepts. His close: do not ask the consumer to swallow another capsule. The deck also asked the room for ideas, as SPI Pharma looks to grow in nutrition.

Mihail Jakubowski of Nordic Biotic then presented a supplier of clinically tested probiotic strains, sold with exclusivity by territory. He showed a stress and sleep blend tested on 227 students at exam time, saying the results, received the week before, proved efficacy on sleep quality and stress. He also showed a blend aimed at microplastics, with its human study still in progress. He closed with an invitation to develop products together.

- Fast-melt: Advantol 300 with Effer-Soda 12 disintegrates in under 10 seconds, 20–40% faster than typical direct-compression competitors, and uses standard packaging, not lyophilised blisters (slide 14) (slide 15). It is aimed at children and older people who cannot or will not swallow [00:01].

files.text:
Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

The meeting focused on innovative probiotic dosage forms and clinically tested probiotic strain technologies.

## Dosage Form Innovation
**Miguel** from **SPI Pharma** presented advanced delivery systems designed to improve consumer experience and stability.
*   **Composol Pro Tab**: A polyol-based, low water activity platform used to create chewable probiotic tablets with low compression forces to ensure probiotic survival.
*   **Effer Soda**: A partially transformed sodium bicarbonate product that creates a protective layer, enhancing stability in effervescent tablets, stick packs, or sachets. This technology can also produce a "delicate fizz" in fast-melting solutions to mask bitterness.
*   **Orally Disintegrating Tablets (ODT)**: Fast-melting platforms designed for populations with dysphagia, such as children and the elderly, allowing for consumption without water.

## Probiotic Research
**Mihail Jakubowski** of **Nordic Biotic** detailed scientific advancements in specialized probiotic strains and their metabolic functions.
*   **Northbiotic Mental Balance**: Developed with the **Polish Academy of Sciences**, this blend uses **Lactobacillus plantarum 140** (producing GABA) and **Bifidobacterium breve 010** (producing vitamin B free). An eight-week study of 227 students demonstrated statistical efficacy in improving sleep quality and managing stress.
*   **Microplastic Management**: A novel approach using two specific strains for gut cleansing:
    1.  **Lactobacillus acidophilus 120**: Aggregates and binds microplastic particles.
    2.  **Lactobacillus fermentum 160**: Pushes microplastics away from the mucosal lining to facilitate removal.
*   Human studies regarding the microplastic-binding technology are currently in progress.

## Strategic Partnerships
Both speakers emphasized opportunities for collaborative development between manufacturers and researchers. 
*   **Miguel** invited participants to use **SPI Pharma's** concept-driven approach to expand existing portfolios into new dosage forms like hydration sticks or chewable probiotics. 
*   **Mihail Jakubowski** proposed the **Plastic Gut-Free Initiative**, inviting brand owners and CDMOs to participate in co-development projects centered on microbiome research and genomics.

Action items: none returned.

sessions.to_check: Who wrote this report and when (no author, publisher or date is stated; it is a secondary synthesis, not a talk); where its market figures come from (no source is given for the USD 30.6 billion and USD 28.4 to 37.8 billion figures, which do not agree with each other). The advance programme bills Prof. James Morton (SiS, Chief Scientific Officer) in Day 2's "The Female Athlete" block, and the women-in-sports-nutrition panel's James is taken as Morton; it bills An Maris, PhD (Rousselot, EMEA Business Development Manager H&N) in Day 2's "Active Nutrition and Health Weight Management" block, with no talk title, and we hold no material for it; Perfect Day is not in the programme. summary.Summary:
This is a secondary synthesis of the whole summit, not a talk. It is a 20-page written report of unknown authorship and date that says it "synthesizes all presentations". Its figures are the report's own, as it states them, not the speakers' figures as given in the room.

It groups the summit into themes: market dynamics and consumer trends, gut health and the microbiome, weight management and GLP-1, female athlete nutrition, personalisation and AI, longevity and "ageless" consumption, mind health, and regulation and trust. It closes with white spaces, investment areas and an outlook.

It opens with a global market of USD 30.6 billion in 2024, Europe at 19%, and growth projected from USD 28.4 billion to USD 37.8 billion by 2028; the two figures do not agree and no source is given. It then summarises most named talks, from Paul Cotter's athlete microbiome research to Luca Bucchini's regulatory update.

It is useful as a map of the programme and of talks with no session of their own. Some attributions are loose: buyer figures from Biogena's talk also appear under the Avea talk, and some sections reword the hosts' closing recap.
summary.Key takeaways:
- By generation, the report names creatine as a hero ingredient for Millennials and Generation Z, with protein for all four generations (page 2).
- Euromonitor data as the report gives it: new product launches up 33%, electrolytes and creatine leading, milk protein supplements down 21%, "no added sugar" claims up 32% (page 2) (page 3).
- Rousselot's Nextida GC collagen peptides, which the report says boost GLP-1 secretion, with a 42% reduction in glucose spike taken before a meal (page 6).
- Creatine as a semi-essential nutrient for the general population, with food fortification as a public health route (Ostojic, as the report puts it) (page 11).
- Misinformation figures attributed to Alice Millbank: only 2.1% of social media nutrition content aligned with public health guidelines; 59% of the accounts studied had no formal health qualification (page 14) (page 15).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Creatine appears as a growth segment, a hero ingredient for younger buyers and a candidate for food fortification (page 2) (page 11). My reading: three angles for CreaWin, to check against the talks themselves.
- Rousselot positions a collagen peptide directly for GLP-1 and glucose control (page 6). My reading: a competitor claim to watch in the GLP-1 companion space.
- Citicoline appears among the mind-health ingredients (page 12). My reading: a prompt for CogniWin, with the talk (singer-biogena-cognitive-health) as the better source.
- Relevance is medium: a useful map of the summit, but secondary and unsourced; leaders should rely on the session records.
summary.Quotes:
- "This comprehensive report synthesizes all presentations, research findings, and industry insights organized by key topic areas" (page 1)
- "Global market size: USD 30.6 billion (2024)" (page 1)
- "Projected growth: $28.4B to $37.8B by 2028" (page 1)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Nathan who wrote the report, and when.
- Find the source of its market size figures.
- Check whether Rousselot gave a talk on Nextida GC and whether James Morton spoke in the female athlete session.
summary.Detail:
- The original is filed unchanged: files/active-nutrition-summit-2025-key-insights-industry-trends.pdf. It names no author, publisher, date or sources for its market figures (page 1).
- Talks the report covers that have no session of their own in this event: Rousselot's Nextida GC collagen (page 6); Professor James Morton's evidence-based fuelling framework for female athletes, which may belong to the women-in-sports-nutrition session (page 7); Perfect Day, named as a mature precision-fermentation example under investment areas, not clearly a talk (page 19). Professor Susan Jebb is quoted inside the Gilbert section, not as a speaker (page 6).
- Talks it covers that are filed here: Cotter (cotter-athlete-microbiome, page 3); minutia.ai (minutia-gut-microbiome-sports, page 5); Mark Gilbert (gilbert-weight-loss-long-term, page 5); Balchem (balchem-branded-ingredient-partnerships, page 7); Nathan Price (price-ai-scientific-wellness, page 8); Mariette Abrahams (abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition, page 9); Marimiina Pykälistö (pykalisto-nutrigenomics, page 9); Sophie Chabloz (chabloz-avea-longevity-supplements, page 10); Sergej Ostojic (ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition, page 11); Kristiina Singer (singer-biogena-cognitive-health, page 12); Eric Puro of Nordic Mushrooms (nordic-mushrooms-functional-mushrooms, page 13); Alice Millbank (millbank-nutrition-by-algorithm, page 14); Marit Veenstra (veenstra-hmt-branding, page 15); Luca Bucchini (bucchini-essna-regulatory-update, page 16). The NutraIngredients Global Survey (page 1), the generational segments (page 2) and the Euromonitor data (page 2) match consumer-health-survey, holland-barrett-fitness-generations and euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends, though the report names no speaker for them.
- Sessions filed here that the report does not name: lux-functional-ingredient-trends, neutral-labs-startup-pitch, sports-nutrition-innovation-panel, personalised-health-panel and tonic-health-fireside (its "social media regulation gaps" section may draw on the fireside, page 16).
- Market: Europe 19% of the global market, over 80% of it Western Europe; Latin America the highest two-year growth, then Europe (page 1).
- Generations, as the report segments them: Baby Boomers (protein, calcium, vitamin D, probiotics, omega-3); Generation X (protein, collagen, omega-3s, curcumin); Millennials (protein, adaptogens, magnesium, curcumin, creatine); Generation Z (creatine, caffeine, electrolytes, ashwagandha) (page 2).
- Euromonitor data, as the report gives it: plastic packaging claims down 76%, flexible packaging up; small "shot" formats gaining; gels and creams an emerging focus (page 2) (page 3).
- Cotter: the Clarke et al. (Gut, 2014) study of 40 elite male athletes against 46 controls; correlations of 0.76 (Oscillospiraceae and creatinine) and up to 0.89 between taxa and pathways in Penney et al. 2020 (page 3) (page 4).
- minutia.ai: 20 male runners and triathletes, 8-week interventions tailored to each microbiome profile, VO2max 49±7 ml/kg/min, age 46±12 (page 5).
- Gilbert: fat-free mass was a similar share of weight lost with rapid (0.42) and moderate (0.44) loss; Susan Jebb quoted that the claim that rapid initial loss means rapid regain "is false" (page 6).
- Price: 5,000 participants, about 1,200 analytes; a USD 52 million NIH grant for a personalised healthspan optimiser; 50% of microbiome diversity variance predicted from 11 blood metabolites; 18% of circulating metabolites made or co-made by the microbiome (page 8).
- Abrahams: fewer than 5 companies offer true digital twins; generative AI nutrition companies grew from 5 (July 2024) to 20 (April 2025) (page 9).
- Chabloz: mainstream longevity buyers are 45 to 65; the report also gives "16% of customers now aged 25-35" and "60% over 45" here (page 10). In the recordings those are Biogena's buyer figures from Singer's talk, which the report repeats under Chabloz's name (page 12) (page 13).
- Nordic Mushrooms: lion's mane, chaga, reishi and cordyceps with their compounds and claimed benefits, which are the report's wording; quality standardisation and beverages as priorities (page 13) (page 14).
- Millbank: 57% of Gen Z and Millennials influenced by TikTok nutrition content; 96% of accounts studied monetised; 7 of 53 verified medical doctors; one carnivore post with 3.7 million likes against 82 million engagements for a two-year UK COVID campaign (page 14) (page 15).
- Veenstra: 80% of innovations fail, the report says through irrelevance; four consumer mindsets, need, want, solution and normal (page 15).
- White spaces and outlook: active parenting, gender-specific formulas, cellular health, AI personalisation, wearables, precision probiotics, bioavailability, upcycled ingredients and precision fermentation (page 17) (page 18) (page 20). The active parenting point echoes the editors' recap (editors-recap).
- The report ends mid-line on page 20 ("Preventive medicine: Nutrition as primary intervention") (page 20).

files.text:
--- page 1 ---
Active Nutrition Summit 2025: Comprehensive Industry Report
Executive Summary
The Active Nutrition Summit 2025, held in Vienna from June 23-25, explored eight transformative themes
driving the industry's evolution. This comprehensive report synthesizes all presentations, research
findings, and industry insights organized by key topic areas, providing actionable intelligence for strategic
decision-making.
Key Market Metrics:
Global market size: USD 30.6 billion (2024)
Europe: 19% market share (>80% Western Europe)
Projected growth: $28.4B to $37.8B by 2028
Highest growth: Latin America, followed by Europe
MARKET DYNAMICS & CONSUMER TRENDS
Global Market Overview
Regional Distribution & Growth:
North America: Largest market share with established consumer base
Europe: 19% global market share, dominated by Western European countries
Asia Pacific: Steady growth trajectory with emerging opportunities
Latin America: Highest 2-year CAGR, driven by increasing health awareness
Australia/Middle East/Africa: Smaller but developing markets
Market Expansion Drivers:
Expanding consumer base beyond traditional athletes
Holistic health and wellness trends mainstreaming
Social media influence driving product discovery
Innovation in formats and delivery systems
Aging population embracing active lifestyles
Consumer Behavior Evolution
Mindset Shift Analysis (NutraIngredients Global Survey):
Evolution from long-term prevention to immediate performance enhancement
Growing demand for both physical and mental performance benefits

--- page 2 ---
Health apps becoming primary data collectors and personal advisors
Increasing consumer sophistication in ingredient knowledge
Rising expectations for personalized solutions
Generational Market Segmentation:
Baby Boomers (Health Maintenance Focus):
Primary concerns: Mobility, cognition, immunity, bone health
Hero ingredients: Protein, calcium, vitamin D, probiotics, omega-3
Format preferences: Fortified foods, ready-to-drink products
Shopping behavior: Traditional retail, expert-guided decisions
Generation X (Longevity Optimization):
Primary concerns: Longevity, joint health, mobility preservation
Hero ingredients: Protein, collagen, omega-3s, curcumin
Format preferences: Powders, tablets, capsules
Shopping behavior: Research-driven, value-conscious
Millennials (Convenience & Recovery):
Primary concerns: Convenience, recovery, stress management
Hero ingredients: Protein, adaptogens, magnesium, curcumin, creatine
Format preferences: Powders, bars, drinks
Shopping behavior: Online-first, brand-loyal
Generation Z (Energy & Cognition):
Primary concerns: Energy optimization, cognitive enhancement, focus
Hero ingredients: Creatine, caffeine, electrolytes, ashwagandha
Format preferences: Ready-to-drink, gummies, shots
Shopping behavior: Social media-influenced, convenience-driven
Innovation Trends Analysis (Euromonitor Data)
Product Launch Dynamics:
33% overall increase in new product launches across category
Highest growth segments: Electrolytes and creatine supplements leading expansion
Declining categories: 21% decline in milk protein supplements (market saturation)
Emerging formats: Significant focus on gels and creams

--- page 3 ---
Packaging evolution: 76% decline in plastic packaging claims, flexible packaging trending upward
Health Claims Progression:
Protein focus: Sustained emphasis on "high-protein" positioning
Clean labels: 32% increase in "no added sugar" claims
Dietary accommodations: "Gluten-free" and "lactose-free" gaining traction
Fortification: Rising trend across multiple nutrient categories
Natural positioning: Natural claims driving innovation growth
Sustainability: Steady growth in organic and sustainable sourcing claims
Format Innovation Drivers:
Convenience prioritization: Small-volume "shot" formats gaining popularity
Jar packaging dominance: Traditional formats maintaining market share
Flexible packaging growth: Though innovation lagged in 2024
Novel delivery systems: Advanced encapsulation and bioavailability enhancement
GUT HEALTH & MICROBIOME RESEARCH
Groundbreaking Athlete Microbiome Research (Professor Paul Cotter)
Professor Paul Cotter (Teagasc Food Research Centre, APC Microbiome Ireland) presented comprehensive
research establishing the diet-exercise-microbiota triad as fundamental to athletic performance and
health optimization.
Landmark Elite Athlete Study (Clarke et al., Gut 2014):
Study design: 40 elite male athletes vs. 46 controls (23 lean BMI <25, 23 higher BMI >28)
Age range: 18-37 years
Data collection: Fasting blood samples, clinical markers, dietary assessment, body composition, fecal
microbiome sequencing
Key Research Findings:
Microbiome Diversity Differences:
Elite athletes showed distinct microbiome profiles compared to controls
Beta diversity analysis revealed clear clustering patterns (though with exceptions)
Taxonomic analysis identified specific bacterial families significantly increased/decreased in athletes
Higher microbial diversity generally associated with athletic status
Functional Health Connections: The gut microbiota influences multiple performance-relevant functions:

--- page 4 ---
Vitamin synthesis: Enhanced production of essential vitamins
Weight regulation: Improved satiety signaling and weight management
Immune system optimization: Strengthened immune response and stimulation
Digestion & absorption enhancement: Improved nutrient bioavailability
Disease-causing microbe control: Better pathogen resistance
Energy harvest optimization: Enhanced efficiency from ingested food
Intestinal health: Improved epithelial cell proliferation and pH balance
Gut-brain signaling: Direct communication affecting stress, anxiety, and mental health
Microbiome Modulation Factors:
Exercise: Direct influence on composition and function
Diet: Particularly fiber and fermented foods
Probiotics/Prebiotics: Targeted interventions
Antibiotics: Negative impact on diversity
Stress levels: Affecting microbial balance
Environmental factors: Housing, lifestyle influences
Advanced Microbiome-Metabolite Research (Penney et al. 2020)
Sophisticated Analytical Approach:
Objective dietary assessment using WHO guidelines
1H-NMR urinary profiles for dietary habit classification
Models comparing extremes of dietary habits, exercise, and combined effects
Focus on gut microbe-host co-metabolism relationships
Clinical Correlation Analysis: Robust statistical associations identified between:
Taxonomic data and clinical markers: f__Oscillospiraceae vs. creatinine (0.76 correlation)
Functional pathways and clinical parameters: Various metabolic pathway correlations
Taxa and functional pathways: Strong correlations (up to 0.89) between specific bacterial families
and metabolic functions
Gut-Brain Axis & Sports Performance
Comprehensive Health Impact Areas:
Musculoskeletal development & growth
Bone health & injury prevention

--- page 5 ---
Female athlete health & performance optimization
Hematological function enhancement
UTI prevention strategies
Optimal cardiovascular function
Immune and endocrine response optimization
Skeletal muscle metabolism improvement
Optimal neurocognitive function
Sleep, recovery, and performance optimization
Mental health and motivation support
Precision Microbiome Interventions (minutia.ai Research):
Study population: Runners & triathletes (N=20)
Design: 8-week targeted nutritional interventions
Measurements: VO2max, body composition, blood biomarkers, gut microbiota testing
Approach: All interventions tailored based on individual microbiome profiles
Demographics: All males, VO2max 49±7 ml/kg/min, Age 46±12
WEIGHT MANAGEMENT & METABOLIC HEALTH
The GLP-1 Revolution
The summit extensively covered how GLP-1 agonist drugs have fundamentally disrupted traditional
weight management, creating new opportunities across active nutrition.
Market Disruption & Opportunities:
Traditional sector upheaval: GLP-1 drugs challenging conventional weight management
approaches
Protein repositioning: Products being reformulated to support muscle mass during weight loss
Natural alternatives market: Significant demand for non-pharmaceutical options
Side effect management: Consumer interest in supportive products
Post-GLP-1 support: Market for metabolic health maintenance after discontinuation
Revolutionary Weight Loss Science (Mark Gilbert Presentation)
Challenging Established Paradigms: Mark Gilbert presented University of Oxford research overturning
conventional wisdom about rapid weight loss:
Traditional Assumptions Questioned:

--- page 6 ---
Previous belief: Rapid weight loss leads to increased lean body mass loss
Previous belief: Higher likelihood of weight regain
Previous belief: Generally detrimental to long-term health
New Research Evidence:
Professor Susan Jebb (University of Oxford, Chair UK FSA): "Research shows clearly that the
common claim that more rapid initial weight loss is associated with more rapid regain is false"
Rapid weight loss group: More likely to achieve target weight loss and stick with programmes
Sustained maintenance: Nearly all initial weight loss maintained over three-year periods using
intermittent cycles
Lean body mass preservation: Proportion of weight loss as fat-free mass similar between rapid
(0.42) and moderate (0.44) approaches
Clinical Implications:
Intermittent cycles of weight loss and gain can be effective long-term strategies
Rapid approaches may be more effective than previously thought
Individual responses vary significantly
Need for personalized approaches based on individual profiles
Next-Generation Metabolic Interventions
Nextida GC Collagen Innovation (Rousselot):
Mechanism: Naturally boosts GLP-1 secretion through specialized collagen peptides
Clinical evidence: 42% reduction in glucose spike when taken pre-meal
Target audience: Active lifestyle consumers interested in carbohydrate control
Performance integration: Supports weight management while fueling performance
Scientific validation: Evidence-based ingredient for post-meal glucose management
GLP-1 Companion Product Ecosystem:
Supplements: Supporting metabolic function during treatment
Nutritional products: Addressing specific dietary needs
Recovery solutions: Supporting active lifestyles during weight management
Precision targeting: Products matched to individual symptoms and needs
FEMALE ATHLETE NUTRITION
Addressing the Gender Gap

--- page 7 ---
The historic 50/50 gender split at recent Olympics highlighted critical gaps in female athlete nutrition
understanding and product development.
Unique Physiological Considerations:
Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S):
Growing awareness of prevalence and impact
Prevention strategies becoming priority
Need for specialized screening and intervention
Integration with performance optimization programs
Hormonal Health Integration:
Menstrual cycle impacts: Performance variations throughout cycle
Hormonal fluctuations: Affecting energy, recovery, and performance
PCOS considerations: Specialized nutritional approaches required
Menopause factors: Supporting active aging in female athletes
Behavioral Change Challenges:
"Carbohydrate fear" culture: Particularly prevalent in certain sports
Educational gaps: Bridging science to practical implementation
Individual variation: Moving beyond generic sex-specific guidelines
Cultural factors: Addressing sport-specific nutrition beliefs
Scientific Framework Development (Professor James Morton)
Evidence-Based Fueling Strategies:
Framework focusing on athlete demographics rather than gender-specific rules
Assessment of energy requirements and habitual intake patterns
Bridging gap from recommendations to sustainable behavior change
Education-focused approaches addressing carbohydrate misconceptions
Performance Optimization Areas:
Energy availability: Ensuring adequate fuel for training and recovery
Nutrient timing: Optimizing intake around training and competition
Recovery protocols: Gender-specific recovery considerations
Supplement strategies: Addressing female-specific nutrient gaps
Industry Partnership Opportunities (Balchem)

--- page 8 ---
Collaborative Innovation Model:
Partnerships between ingredient companies, brands, and sports teams
Evolution of sports nutrition market with female-focused products
High-quality ingredients supporting active women's unique needs
Focus on performance, recovery, and overall health optimization
Nutrient Gap Analysis:
"Getting back to nutrient basics" for elevated performance
Latest identified nutrition gaps affecting physical and mental performance
Prevention of common issues: stress fractures, muscle cramps, irritability
Endurance athlete focus and training optimization
PERSONALIZATION & AI TECHNOLOGY
Scientific Wellness Revolution (Nathan Price, Thorne/Buck Institute)
Nathan Price presented groundbreaking research from the Pioneer 5000 study, demonstrating how AI
and deep data are transforming personalized nutrition.
Personal Dynamic Data (PD3) Clouds:
Comprehensive data collection: Genome sequencing, detailed lab tests, microbiome analysis, self-
tracking
Scale: 5,000 participants in longitudinal study
Measurements: ~1,200 analytes including clinical chemistry, metabolites, proteins
Publication: Nature Biotechnology 2017, establishing scientific foundation
AI-Driven Personalization Capabilities:
$52 million NIH grant: Developing personalized healthspan optimizer
Agentic AI integration: Moving beyond pattern recognition to deep reasoning
Individual mechanistic understanding: Leveraging large language models for personalized insights
Continuous refinement: Machine learning improving recommendations over time
Gut Microbiome-Metabolite Connections:
Predictive power: 50% of microbiome diversity variance predicted from 11 blood metabolites
Health condition correlations: Relationships across abdominal pain, antibiotics, constipation,
diarrhea, Type II diabetes
Metabolite significance: 18% of circulating metabolites made or co-made by microbiome

--- page 9 ---
Obesity breakdown: Complete relationship obliteration in extreme obesity (BMI >35)
Clinical Implementation Framework:
Database development: 200 actionable possibilities, continuously expanding
Biomarker integration: Combining genetics, metabolomics, microbiome data
Wearable technology: Continuous physiological and lifestyle monitoring
Personalized recommendations: AI-driven, individually optimized interventions
Market Reality & Technology Adoption
Digital Twins Market Assessment (Mariette Abrahams, Qina):
Current scale: Less than 5 companies offering true digital twins
Medical applications: Primarily diabetes-focused implementations
Consumer confusion: Many companies misrepresenting basic apps as digital twins
Cost barriers: Very expensive, limiting access to populations most in need
Future potential: Promising for healthcare applications but early-stage
Generative AI Proliferation:
Rapid growth: From 5 companies (July 2024) to 20 companies (April 2025)
Consumer appeal: Easy answers and simple scoring systems
Scientific concerns: Recommendations not always representative or relevant
Ethical challenges: AI Act implementation creating compliance requirements
Trust building: Need for demonstrated nutritional and behavioral outcomes
Wearable Technology Integration:
Healthcare disruption: Potential to reduce traditional doctor visits
Vital sign monitoring: Comprehensive health tracking capabilities
Real-time feedback: Immediate intervention and adjustment possibilities
Consumer adoption: Growing acceptance across demographics
Nutrigenomics & Precision Nutrition (Marimiina Pykälistö)
Scientific Foundation:
Genetic testing applications expanding beyond medical settings
Professional training and education initiatives growing
Integration with microbiome and lifestyle data
Practical applications for personalized supplementation

--- page 10 ---
Consumer & Professional Adoption:
Oncologists and specialized doctors requesting genetic testing tools
Patient-driven demand for personalized health solutions
Genetic testing as one component of comprehensive personalization
Professional validation supporting consumer confidence
LONGEVITY & AGELESS CONSUMPTION
Beyond Biohacking: Mainstream Longevity (Sophie Chabloz, Avea)
Distinguishing Market Segments:
Extreme Biohackers:
Bryan Johnson example: 105 pills daily, extensive monitoring
Ray Kurzweil approach: 200 daily supplements, singularity preparation
Not target customers: Extreme approaches not representative of mainstream

--- page 11 ---

Autophagy enhancement: Cellular "housecleaning" processes
Senescent cell targeting: Reducing inflammation drivers
Creatine for General Population (Dr. Sergej Ostojic)

athletic performance:
Healthy Aging Benefits:

Cellular Health Innovation
Scientific Wellness Integration:
21st Century Medicine: From genetics & environment to disease prevention

Longevity optimization: Data-driven healthspan extension

NAVIGATING REGULATORY & TRUST CHALLENGES
