summary.Summary:
Alice Millbank, co-founder and chief scientific officer of Rooted Research Collective, asked what goes wrong when people take their nutrition advice from social media algorithms rather than from dietary guidelines.

Their starting point is that guidelines are evidence-based but rarely followed, while social media reaches far more people: one pro-carnivore post drew 3.7 million likes, against 82 million engagements for a two-year UK COVID campaign. Millbank then presented their group's study of 53 nutrition "super-spreaders" with a combined reach of over 24 million, sorted into three personas: the Doc (borrowed authority), the Rebel (counter-culture) and the Hustler (quick-fix wellness). Most had no health qualifications and nearly all had a financial incentive. Their themes were carnivore and keto diets, anti-seed-oil messages, distrust of institutions, and the demonisation of "fake meats", legumes, grains and milk alternatives.

Their conclusion for industry: this noise shapes how consumers see functional ingredients and the whole sector. Brands should simplify without denying complexity, avoid silver-bullet promises, tell the truth, use storytelling ethically and check the values and credibility of the influencers they pay.
summary.Key takeaways:
- 57% of Gen Z and Millennials are influenced by TikTok nutrition content, and "only 2.1% aligned with public health guidelines", in the slide's words (slide 9).
- One pro-carnivore post drew 3.7 million likes; a two-year UK COVID social media campaign drew 82 million post engagements (slide 10).
- Of 53 super-spreader profiles, 59% had no formal health qualifications, only 7 were verified medical doctors, and 96% had clear financial incentives, many selling their own supplements or programmes (slide 14) (slide 18) (slide 19).

summary.Summary:
The Vitamin Shoppe, a US supplement retailer with over 635 stores, published its fourth annual trend report in 2025. Nathan filed it with this summit; whether it was presented there is not known. Its figures are the report's own: the retailer's sales and site searches, SPINS industry data, and a survey of 2,000 US adults by Talker Research in May 2025.

The report finds a proactive consumer: 69% of Americans take supplements, and 35% have used AI tools for their health. It names five trends. Protein is moving from powders into drinks, bars and snacks. NAD+ has gone mainstream for longevity. Peptides are the next frontier in sports nutrition. Formats are moving beyond pills and powders, to liquids, gummies, chews, beadlets and topicals. And shilajit is finding a new generation of buyers.

Creatine runs through two of the trends: the category has grown over 320% at the retailer since 2019, and searches for creatine gummies are up over 1,300% this year.

It closes on trust: TikTok drives curiosity, but friends, news and doctors still build credibility, and only 11% of people find influencers very trustworthy.

Health & Wellness
Trend Report 2025

--- page 2 ---
2 3
Introduction
Driven by scientific innovation, highly engaged consumers, and a heightened focus on active lifestyles
and performance, the health and wellness sector is evolving in dynamic ways in 2025. The Vitamin
Shoppe’s fourth annual Health & Wellness Trend Report provides a data-rich analysis of this evolution,
powered by proprietary insights from our 635+ retail locations and vitaminshoppe.com, as well as
industry-wide data from SPINS.
T o further contextualize these insights, The Vitamin Shoppe commissioned an exclusive 2025 Consumer
Survey of 2,000 U.S. adults, conducted by leading market research firm T alker Research. *
This year’s report reveals a highly proactive wellness consumer, with 69% of Americans currently taking
dietary supplements to support their health and well-being. Motivations range from energy and stress
management to longevity, cognitive health, and weight management. Over half of Americans (56%) are
very or somewhat likely to try new trends to reach their wellness goals. Yet consumers are divided on
the overall trajectories of their personal health: 31% believe they are healthier than they were five years
ago, while 35% report feeling less healthy and 30% see no change, according to the survey.
“The insights from our Health & Wellness Trend Report 2025 underscore the challenges and complexities
of modern wellness, as well as the strong demand for the trusted products, tools, and expertise that
can help individuals optimize their unique wellness journeys, ” says Sharon Leite, CEO of The Vitamin
Shoppe.
Notably, AI is playing an increasingly vital role in that pursuit. Over one-third of Americans (35%) have
already used AI tools to manage or learn about their health, and another 27% would consider doing so in
the future. Among those who have used AI, popular applications include researching medical or wellness
topics (31%), meal and recipe planning (25%), weight-loss program design (24%), and learning about
supplement usage (21%).
Amid the myriad emergence of wellness trends online and in the media,
The Vitamin Shoppe’s Trend Report identifies five standout movements that
reflect a deeper convergence of scientific innovation, shifting consumer
priorities, and changes in lifestyle-driven wellness:
1. Protein Shifts to Functional Foods and Beverages
Once relegated to powders and gym routines, protein is fast expanding into anytime and anywhere
consumption through convenient bars, ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages, and snackable functional
foods.
2. The NAD+ Revolution for Longevity
Previously the domain of biohackers, NAD+ (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) has entered the
mainstream as a powerful supplement supporting cellular health, energy production, and anti-aging
goals.
3. Peptides: The Next Frontier in Sports Nutrition
Already well-known for their applications in the beauty and skin-care space, these potent, bioactive
compounds are emerging as a breakthrough innovation in sports nutrition for their performance-
enhancing and recovery benefits.
4. Delivery Formats Move Beyond Pills and Powders
Consumers are gravitating toward convenient and enjoyable supplement formats—such as liquids,
gummies, chews, beadlets, and topicals—that fit seamlessly into modern lifestyle routines.
5. A New Generation of Wellness Seekers Discovers Shilajit
Driven by social media, this time-honored adaptogen is experiencing renewed relevance among
modern consumers seeking its holistic wellness benefits.
About The Vitamin Shoppe®
Since its founding in 1977, The Vitamin Shoppe has grown into the leading
destination for health and wellness solutions, providing millions of customers
with innovative nutritional supplements and trusted expertise from its
knowledgeable Health Enthusiast® store associates. The Vitamin Shoppe
offers the largest assortment of vitamins, supplements, and sports nutrition
at retail in the U.S., including national brands and an expanding portfolio of
proprietary brands. In the U.S., customers can shop over 635 stores under
The Vitamin Shoppe and Super Supplements® banners, as well as online at
vitaminshoppe.com and on the The Vitamin Shoppe app.
*About The Vitamin Shoppe Consumer Survey
The Vitamin Shoppe commissioned leading market research company T alker Research to conduct a survey on health and
wellness behaviors and attitudes. T alker Research completed a random, double-opt-in survey of 2,000 general population
Americans from May 16 to May 22, 2025. The margin of error is +/- 2.2% at 95% confidence.

--- page 3 ---
54
Trend #1
Protein Demand Shifts to Functional
Foods and Beverages
Once dominated by powders, the protein category is being redefined as consumers increasingly look to
on-the-go, lifestyle-friendly formats that include protein-enhanced, ready-to-drink (RTD) beverages,
bars, and snacks.
In 2025, The Vitamin Shoppe has seen year-to-date sales increases of 20% in RTD protein beverages
and 28% in protein bars and snacks, signaling a shift in consumer behavior toward convenience, taste,
and macro-balanced nutrition. Protein powders decreased by 12% in the same period.
“Bars and drinks are outpacing powders for the first time in years, with innovation, great taste, and
sharp macros driving momentum in these categories, ” says Jack Gayton, VP and General Merchandise
Manager at The Vitamin Shoppe. “Protein continues to dominate wellness routines, but RTDs have
emerged as a convenient alternative to the shaker cup, highlighting changing consumer patterns and a
growing demand for grab-and-go options. ”
Industrywide, Americans’ growing demand for all things protein helped drive a 9.1% increase in the
protein supplement and meal replacement category in 2024, according to SPINS data. Searches for
“protein” on vitaminshoppe.com jumped 81% this year, a sign of the widespread demand for this hero
macro.
In The Vitamin Shoppe Consumer Survey, 66% of respondents said they are actively trying to add more
protein to their diets.
As protein supplementation has evolved from the occasional post-workout shake to a mainstream
performance and wellness tool, consumers are seeking format flexibility to match their busy lives. RTD
protein beverages are growing due to convenience, flavor variety, and advanced formulations; protein
bars are emerging as meal replacements and even dessert alternatives; and protein snacks are replacing
high-calorie, nutrient-poor chips and sweets with healthier, functional nutrition.
Searches for “protein” have jumped 81% on vitaminshoppe.com
this year, as sales of ready-to-drink protein beverages increased
20% and on-the-go protein bars and snacks gained 28%.
A breakout trend this year in RTDs is clear protein—a lighter, more refreshing alternative to traditional
creamy shakes, offering hydration and post-workout recovery in a single drink. A top seller at The
Vitamin Shoppe is Clean Simple Eats Clear Protein, available in prickly pear and dragonfruit flavors,
delivering 20 grams of whey isolate per can. Also making a splash is RYSE Clear Protein in nostalgic
flavors like Kool-Aid Tropical Punch and Country Time Lemonade, with 22 grams of whey isolate per
bottle.
While a longtime favored protein format, bars are noticeably surging this year, driven by superior
macros, better textures, and more indulgent flavors. Barebells continues to excel in the category, up
97% year-to-date and the #1 selling protein bar out of 30 brands at The Vitamin Shoppe. Known for
indulgent flavors, such as caramel cashew, salted peanut caramel, key lime pie, and chocolate dough,
Barebells exemplifies how great taste combined with nutrition can help dominate a category.
Another hot seller is the new David bar—named after the Michelangelo statue and wrapped in
glamorous gold foil—which first launched at retail with The Vitamin Shoppe this year. David offers
category-leading macros (28g of protein, 150 calories, 0g sugar) and has already become the #2 selling
bar at The Vitamin Shoppe in just a few short months.
5

--- page 4 ---
6
Built “Puff” bars are also coming on strong. They have a delectable marshmallow-style texture and blend
whey and collagen proteins for a softer bite. The bar quickly reached the #5 spot at The Vitamin Shoppe
this year.
Beyond bars, the protein snack category is exploding as consumers seek better-for-you replacements
for salty chips and sweet treats. At The Vitamin Shoppe, top sellers include Legendary Foods Popped
Protein Chips, a crispy, satisfying snack with bold flavor and 20 grams of protein per bag. A well-known
pioneer in the high-protein snack category, Quest continues to roll out in-demand new products and
flavors, such as its Spicy Sweet Chili T ortilla Style Protein Chips and Hot & Spicy T ortilla Style Protein
Chips.
For sweet snackers, recently-launched Vaughn’s Protein Pretzels are enrobed in chocolate and deliver
12g of protein and just 1g of sugar per single-serving bag. They combine indulgence with smart macros
and are quickly becoming a customer favorite.
As consumers increasingly view protein as essential to their daily health and wellness goals, the demand
has ignited one of the most exciting growth opportunities in functional nutrition—pushing brands to
innovate with crave-worthy foods and beverages that deliver serious levels of protein.
76

Trend #2
The NAD+ Revolution for Longevity
Fueled by social media buzz, research breakthroughs, and brand marketing campaigns, NAD+
(nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide) has become one of the biggest longevity and cellular health trends
of the past year. Once the domain of biohackers and scientists, NAD+ is now gaining widespread
traction among health-conscious consumers seeking to optimize energy, slow the aging process, and
support metabolic function.
Case in point: Searches for NAD+ on vitaminshoppe.com skyrocketed nearly 500% this year. In total
sales, the cellular health and healthy aging category grew by 91% in Q1 at The Vitamin Shoppe, and
NAD+ products contributed 90% of that growth.
Why the immense interest? NAD+ is a coenzyme found in every living cell and is essential for numerous
biological functions, including energy production, DNA repair, and cellular resilience. It acts as a critical
molecule in metabolism because it helps to convert nutrients into cellular energy, which is fundamental
to all functions of the body. As we age, however, NAD+ levels decline—by up to 50% between 40 and 60
years old—which can lead to fatigue, reduced metabolic efficiency, cognitive decline, and other signs of
aging.

Interest in NAD+ has surged dramatically, with searches on
vitaminshoppe.com skyrocketing nearly 500% this year.
Enhancing longevity and healthspan is a major concern for most Americans, with 75% of respondents
in The Vitamin Shoppe consumer survey “very” or “somewhat” concerned about the impact of aging on
their health. A full 21% also said they are doing “everything possible to fight aging, ” while 23% are doing
“a few things that fit into my lifestyle. ” T aking vitamins and supplements is the most popular longevity
and anti-aging activity (cited by 43% of respondents), even ahead of seeing a doctor regularly (40%) and
exercising regularly (39%).
Americans are seeking not just to live longer, but to experience healthier and more active lives—and
NAD+ supplements are well-positioned to meet these goals with a range of benefits that span energy,
cognition, cellular repair, and metabolic health.
11
With NAD+ supplementation, users aim to counteract this decline by improving overall cellular
function, thus enhancing vitality and healthspan. These supplements can be NAD+ itself—which can be
challenging for the body to absorb due to the digestion process—or formulas that focus on precursor
nutrients that the body converts into NAD+, such as NR (nicotinamide riboside), NMN (nicotinamide
mononucleotide), and NAM (nicotinamide).
“There are many more human studies on precursors versus direct NAD+ supplementation, ” says
Brittany Michels, a Registered Dietitian Nutritionist at The Vitamin Shoppe. “The pro of taking NR, for
example, is that it’s well-absorbed and efficiently converted to NAD+ through established metabolic
pathways. The pro of taking NMN is that it’s one step away from becoming NAD+, which may result
in faster or more direct conversion. Making a choice between these supplements may come down to
specific health goals, formulation quality, preferences, and emerging research. While NAD+ precursors
currently offer the most reliable and accessible path to raising NAD+ levels, evolving formulations and
research may soon reshape the landscape. ”
Life Extension is the current NAD+ sales leader at The Vitamin Shoppe, posting 127% growth in Q1
2025. Its NAD+ Cell Regenerator is formulated with Niagen®, a patented and clinically studied form of
NR.
Tru Niagen, developed by Niagen Bioscience—which is the patent holder for Niagen—is another top
brand, combining leading-edge science with robust marketing campaigns that have helped grow the
entire NAD+ category.
New market entrants like Codeage Liposomal NAD+ are addressing the absorption challenge with
liposomal delivery systems, increasing cellular uptake and product efficacy.
The surge in NAD+ is not just a reflection of interest in anti-aging; it aligns with broader demographic
and wellness trends. “Look for supplements, ingredients, and foods that support healthy aging to
continue to prosper in 2025 as the population gets older, ” says Scott Dicker, Senior Director of Market
Insights at SPINS. According to S&P projections, the 65-and-over age group is experiencing the fastest
growth rate among all demographics in the U.S.

Trend #3
Peptides: The Next Frontier in Sports
Nutrition
As science and consumer demand drive innovation in sports nutrition, a new class of bioactive
ingredients called peptides is poised to redefine the category. These powerful signaling molecules are
emerging as a breakthrough addition to traditional sports nutrition formulas because of the unique way
they support performance, recovery, and overall muscle health.
While peptides have already gained traction in beauty and wellness through the collagen boom, they are
now making significant inroads into performance nutrition. So, what exactly are peptides? In a nutshell,
they’re short chains of amino acids that act as biochemical messengers in the body, regulating processes
such as metabolism, appetite, blood sugar, inflammation, and muscle regeneration. Unlike amino acids
or proteins that serve as structural components, peptides influence how and when the body uses these
building blocks.
In the context of sports nutrition, peptides play a pivotal role in:
• Enhancing muscle protein synthesis
• Accelerating post-exercise recovery
• Improving endurance and strength
• Reducing fatigue and muscle soreness
Over the past year, The Vitamin Shoppe has been a leader in introducing peptide formulas within the
sports nutrition category—and customers have responded with robust interest. Searches for peptides
on vitaminshoppe.com have exploded over 550% in 2025.
Searches for peptides on vitaminshoppe.com have exploded
over 550% in 2025—and 41% of all consumers are “a lot” or
“somewhat” more aware of peptides versus five years ago.

This robust interest is reflected in consumers’ overall awareness of peptides, with 41% of consumers
“a lot” or “somewhat” more aware of peptides versus five years ago in The Vitamin Shoppe Consumer
Survey—a significant figure given the specialized, scientific nature of these compounds.
Since its launch this year, AN Performance Creatine + Peptide has been the brand’s top-performing SKU
at The Vitamin Shoppe. Combining creatine monohydrate with PeptiStrong®—a patented, plant-based
peptide complex developed by Nuritas using proprietary AI technology—this formulation merges a
time-tested performance enhancer with next-generation peptide signaling. The result is a synergistic
blend clinically proven to maximize strength output, enhance endurance, and support faster recovery.
Several other increasingly popular products also leverage PeptiStrong in their formulations, including
Force Factor Anabolic Muscle Builder, dubbed “the future of muscle building” by the brand, as well
as GLP-1 Support Protein from Whole Health Rx™ , which is formulated to address the unique muscle
preservation needs of GLP-1 medication users as they lose weight—demonstrating the versatility of
peptides across diverse health goals.
“While your protein powder provides the raw materials for muscle building, PeptiStrong can help
optimize the body’s natural muscle maintenance processes, potentially enhancing the overall
effectiveness of your nutrition strategy, ” explains Dr. Andy Franklyn-Miller, Chief Medical Officer
at Nuritas. “We conduct extensive clinical research on our peptide ingredients, with PeptiStrong
specifically demonstrating significant benefits for muscle health in three different human clinical trials. ”
In response to growing consumer demand and promising clinical data, The Vitamin Shoppe is
accelerating its peptide strategy with a range of exclusive and innovative offerings coming this year.
Several new peptide products from MuscleT ech will launch exclusively at The Vitamin Shoppe this
summer, including a creatine product and a DL185™ dileucine peptide formula, that offers 159% greater
activation of muscle protein synthesis.
In addition, The Vitamin Shoppe’s proprietary BodyT ech Elite® brand is getting into the peptide game
with three key launches in the fall: an anabolic peptide complex (with DL185™ and myHMB™ for muscle
health), a nitric oxide booster and vasodilator formular (with VasoDrive AP™ proprietary peptide), and a
muscle recovery formula (with PeptiStrong™ and MalT or™ for muscle pain and soreness).
“The latest trend is peptides from specific plants that have targeted functions in the body, including
muscle protein synthesis. Stay tuned, because there is much more to come in this category, ” says
Brian T anzer, Director of Scientific and Regulatory Affairs at The Vitamin Shoppe and a member of its
Wellness Council.
This compelling area of innovation represents a significant shift in how the sports nutrition industry
thinks about muscle health, recovery, and performance. Not solely focused on substrate products,
brands and retailers are now tapping into bioactive signaling pathways with targeted, functional
ingredients that optimize results. This next-generation approach to muscle optimization is capturing
the attention of athletes, fitness enthusiasts, and weekend warriors seeking the next edge in nutrition
science.

Trend #4
Beyond Pills and Powders: The Rise of
Alternative Delivery Formats
While pill and powder formats have long dominated supplement sales, today’s wellness consumers are
actively seeking more convenient, enjoyable, and personalized ways to integrate supplements into their
routines. This growing demand has sparked a wave of innovation across the supplement industry, with
brands embracing new delivery systems that are both functional and user-friendly —from liquid vitamins
and gummies, to chews, beadlets, and even topical applications.
One of the most dynamic trends in supplement delivery is the surging popularity of liquid vitamins.
Sales in this category have jumped 50% year-to-date at The Vitamin Shoppe, led by category leader
MaryRuth’s, which has played a central role in mainstreaming liquid multivitamins in recent years.
MaryRuth’s has expanded its reach with innovative liquid offerings that feature additional targeted
health benefits. For instance, the top-selling Multivitamin + Hair Growth, plus an assortment of new
herbal tinctures targeting immune health. The brand’s impressive growth of 90% this year at The
Vitamin Shoppe underscores the widening appeal of liquid vitamins and supplements in expanding use
cases.
This momentum has inspired category stalwarts like New Chapter to enter the liquid space for the first
time. The launch of its Liquid Multivitamins in appealing berry and mango flavors marks a strategic
move to capture share in this growing format, supported by a robust national marketing campaign and a
strong retail presence.
Searches for “liquid multivitamin” on vitaminshoppe.com continue to grow, up 31% year-to-date in
2025.
Brands are also reimagining how consumers can experience functional ingredients in ever more creative
and flavorful ways. The new plnt® Shilajit Syrup offers an adaptogenic boost in a mixable liquid format,
while the BetterAlt KSM-66 Honey Sticks deliver organic ashwagandha in a delicious, spoon-free
dose that supports sleep, stress relief, and focus. These emerging product types elevate the consumer
experience, making supplementation feel more like a treat than a task.
Similarly, gummies and chews have emerged as major disruptors in categories historically dominated
by pills and powders—notably, creatine, a fast-growing cornerstone of sports nutrition (the category
as a whole multiplied over 320% since 2019 at The Vitamin Shoppe). While creatine powder remains a
mainstay, consumers are now gravitating toward gummies and chews for their convenience, portability,
and flavor.
This trend can be seen in searches on vitaminshoppe.com for “creatine gummies, ” which have rocketed
over 1300% this year. Industrywide, SPINS data shows that liquid, chewable tablets, and gummies are

were one of the first to launch at The Vitamin Shoppe, with sales up over 100% this year. Since then,
a host of other brands have launched creatine chews and gummies, including Force Factor, Legion,

Additionally, the BetterYou Magnesium Oil Spray, launching later this year at The Vitamin Shoppe, will

While pills and capsules still dominate overall sales—65% of supplement users take them, according
to The Vitamin Shoppe Consumer Survey—the supplement industry is focused on innovating and

delivery formats would make it easier to take them, and 20% said it would help them be more consistent.
From the expansive growth of liquid vitamins to the rise of creatine chews and the sophistication of

Trend #5
Shilajit: Modern T akes on an Ancient
Wellness Treatment
For centuries, shilajit has been used as a traditional Ayurvedic wellness treatment. Now, a new
generation of health seekers has rediscovered it, making it one of the past year’s trendiest—if also
stickiest—supplements. Shilajit sales were up over 40% in Q1 of this year at The Vitamin Shoppe, driven
by social media attention, a spate of new product launches, and renewed interest in its time-honored
wellness benefits.
Commonly sourced from mountainous regions like the Himalayas, this resin-like substance is formed
from the natural decomposition of plants and minerals. With its high concentration of fulvic acid—a
potent antioxidant that fights free radicals—and over 80 essential minerals like iron, magnesium,
potassium, and zinc, shilajit is a highly versatile supplement that can benefit a wide range of
demographics. Its users include older women seeking longevity and bone health benefits, men looking
for testosterone support, athletes aiming to enhance energy and muscle recovery, and people coping
with chronic stress or fatigue.
With these wide-ranging benefits, searches for shilajit have surged on vitaminshoppe.com, up 52% year
to date.

its potential benefits to energy levels, mental clarity, and hormonal health, ” says Brittany Michels, a
Registered Dietitian Nutritionist at The Vitamin Shoppe.
Launched in February at The Vitamin Shoppe, BetterAlt is redefining the category with modern
branding and innovative delivery systems. In just a few months, it has captured 25% of shilajit sales at
The Vitamin Shoppe, with product formats that include capsules, honey sticks, and gummies. The brand
has also combined shilajit with other trending ingredients, such as sea moss, ashwagandha, and tongkat
ali, offering synergistic benefits for testosterone, mood, and overall vitality. For purists, BetterAlt also
offers a resin product intended to be mixed into warm water or milk.
A new wave of health seekers and brand launches has driven
shilajit sales up over 40% in Q1 of 2025 at The Vitamin Shoppe.
BetterAlt joined established and emerging shilajit innovators on The Vitamin Shoppe’s shelves, including
category pioneer Cymbiotica. The Vitamin Shoppe recently brought in a slew of new products in this
space, including Force Factor and Trace Minerals capsule formulas, Atlantic Naturals 5-in-1 superfood
blend with shilajit, and an option from plnt, The Vitamin Shoppe’s proprietary, whole food-based brand.
As shilajit has grown in visibility, brands are adding it as a hero ingredient to other core products, such
as JYM’s Alpha Advance T estosterone Optimization formula and Codeage’s GLP-Harmony Companion+
metabolic formula for those on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.
The multifaceted benefits of shilajit address a cross-section of the wellness concerns that consumers
are most interested in improving in 2025, according to The Vitamin Shoppe Wellness Survey, including
boosting energy (49% of respondents), immunity support (38%), cognitive function (37%), and bone
health (35%). As a science-backed, heritage-rich supplement, shilajit stands out as a high-potential
product for innovation and is well-positioned to become a staple in functional wellness.

NAD+ and peptides underscores the mainstreaming of science-backed longevity and performance

Vitamin Shoppe Consumer Survey revealed that traditional information sources still hold significant
sway. 15% of respondents cite TikT ok as a source of wellness discovery, but traditional touchpoints

summary.Summary:
An unnamed presenter shared results from a consumer survey run in November in nine countries with 6,000 people, covering health goals, health tech, biotics and sports nutrition. Otter heard the team as "our women and Intelligence Team"; the survey matches Lumina Intelligence's, but the company is to confirm. The presenter said they were not the data person and pointed to a colleague, Ed, for questions.

Getting better sleep was the top health goal overall. Sleep and stress lead for younger people; healthy ageing rises with age. Younger consumers track themselves: the presenter said 78 to 79% use a fitness tracker, and 91% of app users buy an app-recommended product at least once a year, mostly in physical stores.

Six percent of respondents said they regularly take GLP-1 drugs, more than the presenter expected outside the US.

On sports nutrition, 36% in Europe take none, against under 20% in the US. Protein leads everywhere. Consumers buy for muscle, but the room's guess that consumers understand creatine's benefits was wrong: they did not know, which the presenter called an opportunity. Price is the second reason for not buying in every country.

Their close: sports nutrition is broadening, consumers still think it is about muscle, and women are an underserved group who want more products.

summary.Summary:
Dr Mark Evans, a Senior Scientist at Holland & Barrett and a sports nutritionist by training, followed the Euromonitor overview with a retailer's view: who buys active nutrition at each age, and how to formulate and talk to each group.

Evans argued that active nutrition is now for everyone, not only athletes, and that one message does not fit all ages. Boomers want mobility and ageing well, Gen X longevity and joints, Millennials convenience and recovery, and Gen Z energy and focus. Supplement use is high in every group, but Gen Z finds products on TikTok and distrusts polished brand content.

Protein was their first example: one nutrient, told differently at each life stage, from growth to muscle repair to sarcopenia and bone health. Creatine was their second. Evans called the evidence for cognition in healthy people very preliminary, noted there is no EFSA claim for it, and showed how brands stack creatine with ingredients that do carry claims so that packs can suggest the link without stating it.

Their close: communication should be planned from the start of product development, and the science team should set efficacious doses.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Hero ingredients shift by generation: Boomers protein, calcium, vitamin D, probiotics and omega-3; Gen X protein, collagen, omega-3 and curcumin; Millennials protein, adaptogens, magnesium, curcumin and creatine; Gen Z creatine, caffeine, electrolytes and ashwagandha (slide 11).
- Supplement use is high across ages: 79% of Boomers, 78% of Gen X and 81% of Millennials (CRN 2023 survey), and 70% of Gen Z in the US and UK call TikTok their most valuable source of food recommendations (Statista 2024) (slide 9) (slide 10).
- On creatine and cognition, Evans said there is "very preliminary evidence" in healthy people and that the strongest evidence is in cognitively impaired people; their slide says there are no EFSA-approved claims for creatine and cognition [00:00] (slide 13).
- Their stacking table: creatine 3 to 5 g/day (no EFSA claim); L-theanine 200 to 250 mg/day with 150 mg caffeine; caffeine over 75 mg a serving; B vitamins at 20% RI; Rhodiola rosea 576 mg/day for mental energy and attention (no EFSA claim); pantothenic acid at 15% NRV for normal mental performance (slide 14).
- Protein is one nutrient with many stories: growth for children, muscle repair for adults, convenient high protein, mobility, sarcopenia and bone health for older adults [00:00].
- Plan communication from the start: "start with the end in mind" (slide 16) [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- A large retailer's scientist set the bar for creatine cognition claims: preliminary in healthy people, no EFSA claim, and irresponsible to lean on studies in patients [00:00] (slide 13). My reading: CreaWin's cognition story should follow the same hedge and cite studies in healthy adults only.
- Their answer to the missing claim is stacking with ingredients that carry claims (B vitamins, pantothenic acid, caffeine) at efficacious doses (slide 14). My reading: a CreaWin plus B-vitamin concept is a pitch Holland & Barrett's own team already uses.
- Rhodiola rosea sits in their stacking table at 576 mg/day for mental energy and attention, without an EFSA claim (slide 14). My reading: a direct opening for our rhodiola in focus and pre-workout stacks; check our dose against theirs.
- Creatine appears for both Millennials and Gen Z, collagen for Gen X (slide 11). My reading: CreaWin's audience reaches beyond the gym, and the protein message for older adults (sarcopenia, bone) suits IsoClr: Pea in RTDs [00:00].
- Relevance is high: a retailer with over 1,600 stores, as introduced, set out how it judges ingredient science and claims [18:24].

- "...there's very preliminary evidence to show that may have some cognitive benefits in healthy individuals. I would say that the strongest evidence for creatine in humans you would see in cognitively impaired individuals." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans) [00:00]
- "No EFSA approved health claims for creatine and cognition." (slide 13)
- "This kind of packaging does help people to make that link of Crete into cognition without outwardly stating it." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans; "Crete" is Otter's word for creatine) [00:00]
- "...start with the end in mind the product communication should be part of how you're thinking about it at the very at the beginning..." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans) [00:00]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Find Konstantinos et al. 2018 (creatine and cognition in healthy individuals) and check what CreaWin's own evidence says against it (slide 13).
- Check whether an EFSA claim on creatine and cognition was submitted and rejected, as Evans thought [00:00]. Cross-check with ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition and bucchini-essna-regulatory-update.
- Contact Dr Mark Evans (Holland & Barrett science team) about CreaWin and rhodiola stacks at their doses (slide 14).
summary.Detail:
- The deck is filed as received (files/holland-barrett-fitness-across-generations-deck.pdf, 17 pages); slide numbers here are the file's pages. Most slides carry the footer "Strictly confidential proprietary to Holland & Barrett International and not for onward distribution". Slides 3, 4, 7, 12, 15 and 16 are images with only a title in the file's text.
- Timestamps: [18:24] is in part 1 of the transcript (the chair's introduction); all other cites are in part 2, where Otter puts the whole talk in one turn at [00:00].
- The chair introduced Holland & Barrett as having over 1,600 stores across 19 countries; Evans said it was their third time speaking at the summit [18:24] (part 1).
- The science team: the slide says 15 scientists with nearly 150 years of combined experience (biomedical scientists, nutrition and sports scientists, registered nutritionists, pharmacists, dietitians); Evans said it was two to three people 12 to 18 months earlier and 19 on the day, with the ambition of "being known for science" (slide 2) [00:00].
- Market size: Statista's sports and active nutrition market, USD 28.4 billion in 2023 and USD 37.8 billion in 2028 (slide 6). Evans said numbers differ by source [00:00]. Euromonitor's figure in the talk before was USD 30.6 billion for 2024 (euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends); both are kept.
- Drivers on the slide: expanding consumer base, holistic health and wellness, social media, innovation and formats, and active ageing (slide 6). Evans mentioned encapsulated ingredients and gummies growing [00:00].
- Health areas mapped to active nutrition: joint, bone and muscle; energy; immunity; stress and anxiety; sleep and relaxation; heart health; cognitive health; gut health (slide 5). Evans noted sleep ranked first as a reason to take supplements in global data but low in purchases, and asked whether consumers are underserved there [00:00].
- Generations (slide 8): Boomers (1946 to 1964) health-conscious, brand-loyal, ageing well and mobility; Gen X (1965 to 1980) time-poor, practical, holistic wellness and longevity; Millennials (1981 to 1996) digital natives, convenience, transparency; Gen Z (1997 to 2012) social-first, trend-driven, highly visual, sustainability and identity.
- Formats by generation: fortified foods and RTDs (Boomers); powders, tablets and capsules (Gen X); powders, bars and drinks (Millennials); RTDs, gummies and shots (Gen Z) (slide 11). Spoken, Evans spoke of nootropics, ashwagandha and mushrooms trending with younger groups [00:00].
- Gen Z: polished or scripted content from traditional brands gets rejected; an academic's myth-busting content for a sports nutrition brand drew comments calling it paid and scripted. Unpolished, quick myth-busting content is what holds attention [00:00]. Evans spoke of 75 to 79% of Boomers taking supplements; the slide says 79% [00:00] (slide 9).
- On creatine Evans said it is one of the most researched ingredients in the market with demonstrated safety, and thought an EFSA claim on creatine and cognition may have been submitted in the last couple of years but rejected [00:00].
- Creatine for cognition is reaching non-exercisers: a friend who does not train was taking it, having "heard all about brain health" [00:00].
- Slide 13 cites Konstantinos et al. 2018 for oral creatine possibly improving short-term memory and intelligence or reasoning in healthy individuals, with effects on other cognitive domains unclear (slide 13).
- Pack examples: a Holland & Barrett creatine pack ("Shameless plug") with creatine on front and back and "supports mental performance" tied to the B vitamins on the back; and a brand heard as "my brain co micronized creativity", which names no benefit but links creatine to the brain through its name [00:00].
- Older adults: communication may need in-store POS and education materials rather than social media [00:00].
- The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md).

# Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

## "Generational Trends in Nutrition" (https://otter.ai/u/hGW_YzPhcwWc92zSzE83n-XuR2I)

The discussion on generational trends in nutrition highlighted the growth of the science team at Holland Bars from 3 to 19 members, focusing on active nutrition for all ages. Key missions include joint, bone, muscle, and energy support. Consumer trends show high engagement across generations, with Gen Z particularly influenced by TikTok for food recommendations. Protein remains a major industry driver, with creatine showing potential cognitive benefits. The importance of scientific backing, responsible communication, and tailored product development for different age groups was emphasized, along with the need for transparency and effective marketing strategies.

Action items:
- Speaker - : Evaluate the current science team and capabilities to ensure the brand can effectively communicate the science behind products.
- Speaker - : Analyze the target consumer base and their specific health and lifestyle needs to inform product development and marketing.
- Speaker - : Explore opportunities to stack creatine with other ingredients like L-theanine and B-vitamins to support cognitive claims, while ensuring efficacious dosing.
- Speaker - : Review current product packaging and marketing communication to ensure transparency and responsible claims about ingredient benefits.

detail.text: The deck is filed as received (files/holland-barrett-fitness-across-generations-deck.pdf, 17 pages); slide numbers here are the file's pages. Most slides carry the footer "Strictly confidential proprietary to Holland & Barrett International and not for onward distribution". Slides 3, 4, 7, 12, 15 and 16 are images with only a title in the file's text.
Timestamps: [18:24] is in part 1 of the transcript (the chair's introduction); all other cites are in part 2, where Otter puts the whole talk in one turn at [00:00].
The chair introduced Holland & Barrett as having over 1,600 stores across 19 countries; Evans said it was their third time speaking at the summit [18:24] (part 1).

The science team: the slide says 15 scientists with nearly 150 years of combined experience (biomedical scientists, nutrition and sports scientists, registered nutritionists, pharmacists, dietitians); Evans said it was two to three people 12 to 18 months earlier and 19 on the day, with the ambition of "being known for science" (slide 2) [00:00].

Market size: Statista's sports and active nutrition market, USD 28.4 billion in 2023 and USD 37.8 billion in 2028 (slide 6). Evans said numbers differ by source [00:00]. Euromonitor's figure in the talk before was USD 30.6 billion for 2024 (euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends); both are kept.

Drivers on the slide: expanding consumer base, holistic health and wellness, social media, innovation and formats, and active ageing (slide 6). Evans mentioned encapsulated ingredients and gummies growing [00:00].

Health areas mapped to active nutrition: joint, bone and muscle; energy; immunity; stress and anxiety; sleep and relaxation; heart health; cognitive health; gut health (slide 5). Evans noted sleep ranked first as a reason to take supplements in global data but low in purchases, and asked whether consumers are underserved there [00:00].

Generations (slide 8): Boomers (1946 to 1964) health-conscious, brand-loyal, ageing well and mobility; Gen X (1965 to 1980) time-poor, practical, holistic wellness and longevity; Millennials (1981 to 1996) digital natives, convenience, transparency; Gen Z (1997 to 2012) social-first, trend-driven, highly visual, sustainability and identity.

Formats by generation: fortified foods and RTDs (Boomers); powders, tablets and capsules (Gen X); powders, bars and drinks (Millennials); RTDs, gummies and shots (Gen Z) (slide 11). Spoken, Evans spoke of nootropics, ashwagandha and mushrooms trending with younger groups [00:00].

Gen Z: polished or scripted content from traditional brands gets rejected; an academic's myth-busting content for a sports nutrition brand drew comments calling it paid and scripted. Unpolished, quick myth-busting content is what holds attention [00:00]. Evans spoke of 75 to 79% of Boomers taking supplements; the slide says 79% [00:00] (slide 9).

On creatine Evans said it is one of the most researched ingredients in the market with demonstrated safety, and thought an EFSA claim on creatine and cognition may have been submitted in the last couple of years but rejected [00:00].
Creatine for cognition is reaching non-exercisers: a friend who does not train was taking it, having "heard all about brain health" [00:00].

Slide 13 cites Konstantinos et al. 2018 for oral creatine possibly improving short-term memory and intelligence or reasoning in healthy individuals, with effects on other cognitive domains unclear (slide 13).

Pack examples: a Holland & Barrett creatine pack ("Shameless plug") with creatine on front and back and "supports mental performance" tied to the B vitamins on the back; and a brand heard as "my brain co micronized creativity", which names no benefit but links creatine to the brain through its name [00:00].
Older adults: communication may need in-store POS and education materials rather than social media [00:00].
The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md).

takeaways.text: Hero ingredients shift by generation: Boomers protein, calcium, vitamin D, probiotics and omega-3; Gen X protein, collagen, omega-3 and curcumin; Millennials protein, adaptogens, magnesium, curcumin and creatine; Gen Z creatine, caffeine, electrolytes and ashwagandha (slide 11).

Supplement use is high across ages: 79% of Boomers, 78% of Gen X and 81% of Millennials (CRN 2023 survey), and 70% of Gen Z in the US and UK call TikTok their most valuable source of food recommendations (Statista 2024) (slide 9) (slide 10).

On creatine and cognition, Evans said there is "very preliminary evidence" in healthy people and that the strongest evidence is in cognitively impaired people; their slide says there are no EFSA-approved claims for creatine and cognition [00:00] (slide 13).

Their stacking table: creatine 3 to 5 g/day (no EFSA claim); L-theanine 200 to 250 mg/day with 150 mg caffeine; caffeine over 75 mg a serving; B vitamins at 20% RI; Rhodiola rosea 576 mg/day for mental energy and attention (no EFSA claim); pantothenic acid at 15% NRV for normal mental performance (slide 14).
Protein is one nutrient with many stories: growth for children, muscle repair for adults, convenient high protein, mobility, sarcopenia and bone health for older adults [00:00].
Plan communication from the start: "start with the end in mind" (slide 16) [00:00].

quotes.text: "...there's very preliminary evidence to show that may have some cognitive benefits in healthy individuals. I would say that the strongest evidence for creatine in humans you would see in cognitively impaired individuals." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans) [00:00]
"No EFSA approved health claims for creatine and cognition." (slide 13)
"This kind of packaging does help people to make that link of Crete into cognition without outwardly stating it." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans; "Crete" is Otter's word for creatine) [00:00]
"...start with the end in mind the product communication should be part of how you're thinking about it at the very at the beginning..." Speaker 1 (Dr Mark Evans) [00:00]

followups: Find Konstantinos et al. 2018 (creatine and cognition in healthy individuals) and check what CreaWin's own evidence says against it (slide 13).
Check whether an EFSA claim on creatine and cognition was submitted and rejected, as Evans thought [00:00]. Cross-check with ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition and bucchini-essna-regulatory-update.
Contact Dr Mark Evans (Holland & Barrett science team) about CreaWin and rhodiola stacks at their doses (slide 14).

summary.Summary:
Harini Venkataraman, Associate Research Director at Lux Research, mapped where functional health ingredients are going. Lux is a research and advisory firm that tracks innovation signals such as patents and investment.

Venkataraman opened with three areas gaining momentum: phytochemicals, the gut-brain axis and small "shot" beverages. The space is crowded. Different ingredients can deliver the same benefit, so choosing between them is hard for brands and consumers, and ingredients with several benefits have an edge.

Venkataraman then took three consumer areas. Performance is mainstream: consumers agree it means building, sustaining and recovering muscle, and Lux expects strong growth over the next one to two years. Protein is table stakes, and precision fermentation may diversify protein sources over about five years, with more than 30 startups working on dairy proteins. Beauty from within is moving towards mainstream acceptance. Immune health is still at early consensus, because consumers see it as personal.

Their closing advice was to back ingredients with science and clinical evidence, solve formulation and flavour problems, partner with established ingredient players, and check what consumers mean by "performance" or "beauty" before building a product for it.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Three momentum areas: rising phytochemicals, growing interest in the gut-brain axis, and small-volume "shot" beverages (slide 5) [02:19].
- Connected impacts: different ingredients can confer the same benefit, which makes ingredient selection complex; ingredients addressing several benefits "can provide an edge" (slide 7) (slide 33).
- Performance is in mainstream consensus, with strong growth expected over the next 1 to 2 years. Consumers see it as building, sustaining and recovering muscle; the ingredients they name are protein, creatine, beta-alanine, curcumin and CBD (slide 14) (slide 15).
- Precision fermentation: more than 30 startups focus on dairy proteins; Perfect Day is the most mature, followed by ReMilk and Formo; DSM and Fonterra's Vivici targets beta-lactoglobulin, including for sports nutrition. Venkataraman doubted it would hit the price now; Venkataraman saw it as a path over "the next, let's say, five years or so" (slide 16) (slide 17) [02:19].
- Beauty from within is moving from early consensus to mainstream acceptance; immune health stays in early consensus with steady growth expected, because consumers see it as personal (slide 20) (slide 26).
- Their takeaways: back ingredients with clinical evidence that overcome formulation and flavour hurdles, collaborate with established ingredient players, and check how consumers define the category (slide 33).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: a trends map, not data on our ingredients, but it places performance as the mainstream, growing need and names creatine as a performance ingredient consumers look for (slide 14) (slide 15). My reading: support for pitching CreaWin to performance brands.
- Consumers "seek complete protein, comparing plant and animal sources" (slide 15). My reading: the IsoClr: Pea pitch should answer the completeness question directly.
- Precision-fermented dairy protein is a longer-term entrant in sports nutrition; Venkataraman did not expect it to be price-competitive yet (slide 17) [02:19]. My reading: worth watching for plant protein, not a near-term threat.
- My reading: their point on multiple benefits and consumer meaning favours pitches that state each benefit within its own evidence, in the consumer's words (slide 33).
summary.Quotes:
- "...if there are so many different ingredients that could confer same benefit consumer, what will he or she go after?" Speaker 1 (Harini Venkataraman) [02:19]
- "...the way protein is creating table stakes. Everybody buys it." Speaker 1 (Harini Venkataraman) [02:19]
- "Pro and probiotics are still leading the game." Speaker 1 (Harini Venkataraman) [21:14]
- "Performance = increasing gains" (slide 13)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Lux's consumer maturity work on performance and protein (Venkataraman invited questions after the talk) [00:00].
- Watch Vivici's scale-up and pricing for sports nutrition (slide 17).
- Related sessions: nordic-mushrooms-functional-mushrooms (mushrooms), minutia-gut-microbiome-sports (AI microbiome profiling, which Venkataraman trailed).
summary.Detail:
- Lux: founded in 2004, research hubs in Boston, Toronto, Amsterdam, Singapore and Tokyo, more than 3,000 syndicated reports a year (slide 2). Venkataraman said they lead consumer product innovation research and previously worked at DSM [00:00] [02:19].
- The bioactive "boom" (slide 6): phytochemicals and plant extracts, antioxidants (including CoQ10 and glutathione), functional proteins and peptides (collagen, casein, elastin, plant proteins, amino acids), functional sugars and HMOs, prebiotics, probiotics, vitamins and minerals, lipids (omega-3, -6, -9, DHA, phytosterols).
- Phytochemicals: extraction and processing innovations aim to improve yield, purity and bioavailability of flavonoids, terpenoids and carotenoids for metabolic health (slide 8). Venkataraman called getting them out in high quantities, formulating them and achieving bioavailability the biggest challenge [02:19].
- Other technology areas Venkataraman named: microbiome modulators, including fibres effective at lower doses; fermentation-derived ingredients (lipids, proteins), if EU regulation and scale allow; AI for microbiome profiling, where Venkataraman said earlier movers such as Day Two were not successful; encapsulation and new processing for bioavailability [02:19].
- Lux's consumer method maps conversations on a maturity curve from ideas to early consensus, mainstream acceptance and established ideas; performance shows strong consensus [02:19] (slide 14).
- Consumer voices on performance: recovery to sustain gains, and muscle and strength from training and high protein intake (slide 13). Venkataraman said protein is "probably less than $10 per kilogram" [02:19].
- Beauty from within: consumers want natural ingredients that work with the body; named ingredients are adaptogens, botanical extracts, spices (cumin, cinnamon, turmeric), collagen and ceramides, and omega-3 (slide 19) (slide 21).
- Functional mushrooms: most developers focus on lion's mane and reishi, almost all target more than two types, mainly fruiting bodies; beverages are a key application (slide 22).
- The Every Company and Landish: a protein and adaptogen coffee premix with fermentation-derived ovalbumin, 8 g protein a serving, sold direct to consumer at $49; Lux's take is that it should strengthen its B2B strategy (slide 23). The spoken price is unclear in the recording [21:14].
- Immune health consumer ingredients: probiotics, prebiotics, vitamins A, C and D, zinc and enzymes (slide 27). Venkataraman sees potential in enzymes, and said large corporates, IFF among them, are moving into postbiotics because they ease formulation, while consumers struggle to tell them apart [21:14].
- Prebiotics: immune-modulating, naturally sweet prebiotics are moving beyond gut health; Lux advises upcycled soluble fibre with several benefits (slide 28). Example: NutriLeads' BeniCaros, a carrot-derived polysaccharide described as clinically backed for immune health, distributed exclusively in the US and Canada (slide 29).
- Outlook: discovering and scaling a novel ingredient is still risky and takes years (slide 31). Venkataraman expects metabolic and digestive health to evolve further with GLP-1 [23:04].
- Marking: every slide carries "Lux Proprietary and Confidential". This is the company's own marking on a talk given at a public conference (slide 1).

The discussion focused on consumer product innovation, emphasizing functional ingredients, consumer trends, and future innovation. Key points included the resurgence of phytochemicals, the growing interest in gut health and the gut-brain axis, and the potential of sustainable protein production through precision fermentation. The conversation highlighted the importance of consumer insights, regulatory readiness, and the need for clear communication of product benefits. Specific trends mentioned were the rise of prebiotics, probiotics, and postbiotics, and the potential of enzymes and microbiome modulators. - Speaker 0 - : Investigate the intersection between upcycling and prebiotics, and how the claims are validated.
- Speaker 0 - : Follow the trends in metabolic health and digestive health, particularly the gut-one trend.

Venkataraman sees potential in enzymes, and said large corporates, IFF among them, are moving into postbiotics because they ease formulation, while consumers struggle to tell them apart [21:14].

Prebiotics: immune-modulating, naturally sweet prebiotics are moving beyond gut health; Lux advises upcycled soluble fibre with several benefits (slide 28). Example: NutriLeads' BeniCaros, a carrot-derived polysaccharide described as clinically backed for immune health, distributed exclusively in the US and Canada (slide 29).
Outlook: discovering and scaling a novel ingredient is still risky and takes years (slide 31). Venkataraman expects metabolic and digestive health to evolve further with GLP-1 [23:04].
Marking: every slide carries "Lux Proprietary and Confidential". This is the company's own marking on a talk given at a public conference (slide 1).

takeaways.text: Three momentum areas: rising phytochemicals, growing interest in the gut-brain axis, and small-volume "shot" beverages (slide 5) [02:19].
Connected impacts: different ingredients can confer the same benefit, which makes ingredient selection complex; ingredients addressing several benefits "can provide an edge" (slide 7) (slide 33).

Performance is in mainstream consensus, with strong growth expected over the next 1 to 2 years. Consumers see it as building, sustaining and recovering muscle; the ingredients they name are protein, creatine, beta-alanine, curcumin and CBD (slide 14) (slide 15).

Precision fermentation: more than 30 startups focus on dairy proteins; Perfect Day is the most mature, followed by ReMilk and Formo; DSM and Fonterra's Vivici targets beta-lactoglobulin, including for sports nutrition. Venkataraman doubted it would hit the price now; Venkataraman saw it as a path over "the next, let's say, five years or so" (slide 16) (slide 17) [02:19].

Beauty from within is moving from early consensus to mainstream acceptance; immune health stays in early consensus with steady growth expected, because consumers see it as personal (slide 20) (slide 26).

Their takeaways: back ingredients with clinical evidence that overcome formulation and flavour hurdles, collaborate with established ingredient players, and check how consumers define the category (slide 33).

summary.Summary:
Silvia Barbaresi, founder and chief scientific officer of Minutia.AI, presented as one of the summit's startup award winners, followed by questions from the moderator. Minutia uses probabilistic AI to predict how individuals respond to nutrition, starting with athletes.

Their argument: the gut microbiome is a network, so single biomarkers miss the picture. The gut connects to muscle, joints, brain and blood, and may shape performance and injury risk. Minutia tests stool samples with shotgun metagenomics, adds questionnaires and blood data, and returns performance and injury indices with a tailored diet. A digital twin of the athlete's gut is the goal for the next two to three years; Barbaresi called the platform "under construction".

Barbaresi showed early pilot results. Of 20 runners and triathletes, 12 completed: six on a personalised diet with prebiotics and probiotics for eight weeks, six controls. Some blood markers moved in the intervention group, but Barbaresi said 12 people is not enough for big conclusions.

Minutia sells B2B to clinics and sports centres in several countries, is moving into longevity, and plans larger studies, transfer to the general population and partnerships with wearable makers. It does not work with brands yet but has not ruled it out.

This updates their February 2025 Probiota talk (probiota-2025 / minutia-gut-microbiota-sports).
summary.Key takeaways:
- The thesis: the gut-muscle and gut-joint axes "play a key role" in performance and injury prevention, and interventions "are always customized" (slide 6) [06:33].
- The service: stool kit, shotgun metagenomics, anamnesis, ideally blood, urine and VO2max, then a report with performance and injury indices and dietary advice (slide 7) (slide 8) [06:33].
- The pilot: 20 recruited, 6 intervention and 6 control analysed, all male, VO2max 49 ± 7 ml/kg/min, age 46 ± 12, eight weeks of tailored diets with pre- and probiotics (slide 11) [06:33].
- Results: Barbaresi said TIBC, total proteins, glucose and monocytes fell after the intervention [06:33]; the slide marks TIBC decreasing at adjusted p < 0.05 and shows no VO2max effect (slide 13). Barbaresi said the sample is not enough "to make big assumption" [06:33].
- The digital twin is an ambition for "maybe two, three years"; the intelligent platform is under construction [06:33].
- Next: the largest gut microbiota collection in sport, transfer to the general population and longevity, and wearable partnerships (slide 16) [20:02].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: sports is our core market and the talk ties gut health to performance and recovery, but none of our ingredients is named and the evidence is a pilot of 12.
- Barbaresi said performance nutrition companies are "within our range of interest" and is not ruling out working with brands [06:33] [26:21]. My reading: a personalised-advice platform could one day recommend specific ingredients; a contact to keep, not a channel yet.
- My reading: nothing here supports a claim for us; no performance effect was reported (slide 13).
summary.Quotes:
- "we are just 12 people, so six participants in the intervention. And we are aware that it's not enough to make big assumption, but it's still something." Speaker 3 (Silvia Barbaresi) [06:33]
- "...for me, the best marketing that we can do is running a clinical trial showing that what we do make sense" Speaker 3 (Silvia Barbaresi) [28:46]
- "Gut Microbiota-based interventions" (slide 6)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Check whether the pilot results have been published since June 2025.
- Possible contact: Silvia Barbaresi, on whether brands or ingredient suppliers can work with Minutia [26:21].
summary.Detail:
- Team: founder and CSO with a PhD in sports nutrition; an AI team with backgrounds in computer science, molecular biology, physics, microbiology, immunology and bioinformatics (slide 2). Barbaresi said the company has nine people, began in Singapore five or six years ago with their co-founder, a data scientist, and that this is its first year in sport [03:52] [22:54].
- Barbaresi mentioned a project in Singapore with Danone in the dairy field, as Otter heard it [03:52].
- Lab partner: cmbio for shotgun metagenomics (heard as "cm bio") [06:33].
- Correlations in the pilot (Spearman, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted): Oscillospiraceae with creatinine 0.76 (p < 0.01); Bifidobacteriaceae with the Bifidobacterium shunt 0.89 (p < 0.001) (slide 12). Barbaresi linked Oscillospiraceae and creatinine to high protein intake [06:33].
- Taxa: the slide marks Eggerthellaceae decreasing in two columns and Lachnospiraceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae, Coriobacteriaceae, UBA1381 and Butyricicoccaceae decreasing in one; which column is which group is unclear in the PDF (slide 14). Barbaresi said some Lachnospiraceae may matter for cardiovascular health and that species-level work is still to do [06:33].
- In the control group, Barbaresi said, cholesterol increased [06:33]; the slide shows LDL and cholesterol increasing (slide 13).
- Clients: clinics and sports rehabilitation centres in Spain, Andorra, Italy and Australia; a US longevity clinic and one in Poland; performance athletes in soccer, tennis and motor sport, including Superbike champion Jules Cluzel (slide 10) [06:33].
- Choosing supplements: Barbaresi picks strains from the literature, naming Lactobacillus plantarum for iron, and also uses cross-feeding between bacteria when a strain is not sold in a country [24:08] [26:21]. Barbaresi recommends a retest after three months [20:02].
- Market sizing on slide 9 shows four segments (performance nutrition, sport and rehabilitation centres, fitness apps, human microbiome); the figures are not labelled clearly in the PDF (slide 9).
- Their February 2025 talk differs: the pilot was then 10 intervention and 10 control, VO2max above 45, and the twin was presented as an existing product, Minutia Twin; here 6 and 6 were analysed and the twin is a goal (probiota-2025 / minutia-gut-microbiota-sports) (slide 11) [06:33].
- Marking: the closing slide carries "Minutia.AI Proprietary & Confidential information". This is the company's own marking on a talk given at a public conference (slide 17).

# Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Recording "Startup Presentation and Q&A" (https://otter.ai/u/8WmLTwoKAbPvZ8QbHihI7dRxZdw). It covers both talks in the recording.

## Summary

Neutral Labs, co-founded by Harry, expanded from a 11,000 sq. ft. facility in Worcestershire to a 24,000 sq. ft. operation across two sites by year-end. Specializing in oils, capsules, gummies, and powders, they hold double A grade BRC, Soil Association, and Informed Manufacturing certifications. Their best-sellers include hemp oils, mushroom capsules, and adaptogen capsules. The company aims to diversify into traditional supplements and has secured two significant contracts. Minutiae AI, represented by Sylvia Barbaressi, uses probabilistic AI to predict individual responses to interventions, particularly in sports and nutrition. They collaborate with major companies like Danone and are developing a digital twin for personalized nutrition and performance optimization.

## Action items

- Minutiae AI - : Conduct more comprehensive studies with larger cohorts of different athlete populations to build a comprehensive database of gut microbiome data.
- Minutiae AI - : Translate the knowledge gained from athlete studies to develop solutions for improving general population health.
- Minutiae AI - : Explore partnerships with wearable companies to integrate Minutiae AI's digital twin technology and leverage wearable data.
- Minutiae AI - : Secure funding from investors or strategic partners to scale up the research and development efforts.

detail.text: Team: founder and CSO with a PhD in sports nutrition; an AI team with backgrounds in computer science, molecular biology, physics, microbiology, immunology and bioinformatics (slide 2). Barbaresi said the company has nine people, began in Singapore five or six years ago with their co-founder, a data scientist, and that this is its first year in sport [03:52] [22:54].
Barbaresi mentioned a project in Singapore with Danone in the dairy field, as Otter heard it [03:52].
Lab partner: cmbio for shotgun metagenomics (heard as "cm bio") [06:33].

Correlations in the pilot (Spearman, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted): Oscillospiraceae with creatinine 0.76 (p < 0.01); Bifidobacteriaceae with the Bifidobacterium shunt 0.89 (p < 0.001) (slide 12). Barbaresi linked Oscillospiraceae and creatinine to high protein intake [06:33].

Taxa: the slide marks Eggerthellaceae decreasing in two columns and Lachnospiraceae, Peptostreptococcaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae, Coriobacteriaceae, UBA1381 and Butyricicoccaceae decreasing in one; which column is which group is unclear in the PDF (slide 14). Barbaresi said some Lachnospiraceae may matter for cardiovascular health and that species-level work is still to do [06:33].
In the control group, Barbaresi said, cholesterol increased [06:33]; the slide shows LDL and cholesterol increasing (slide 13).

Clients: clinics and sports rehabilitation centres in Spain, Andorra, Italy and Australia; a US longevity clinic and one in Poland; performance athletes in soccer, tennis and motor sport, including Superbike champion Jules Cluzel (slide 10) [06:33].

Choosing supplements: Barbaresi picks strains from the literature, naming Lactobacillus plantarum for iron, and also uses cross-feeding between bacteria when a strain is not sold in a country [24:08] [26:21]. Barbaresi recommends a retest after three months [20:02].
Market sizing on slide 9 shows four segments (performance nutrition, sport and rehabilitation centres, fitness apps, human microbiome); the figures are not labelled clearly in the PDF (slide 9).

Their February 2025 talk differs: the pilot was then 10 intervention and 10 control, VO2max above 45, and the twin was presented as an existing product, Minutia Twin; here 6 and 6 were analysed and the twin is a goal (probiota-2025 / minutia-gut-microbiota-sports) (slide 11) [06:33].
Marking: the closing slide carries "Minutia.AI Proprietary & Confidential information". This is the company's own marking on a talk given at a public conference (slide 17).

takeaways.text: The thesis: the gut-muscle and gut-joint axes "play a key role" in performance and injury prevention, and interventions "are always customized" (slide 6) [06:33].
The service: stool kit, shotgun metagenomics, anamnesis, ideally blood, urine and VO2max, then a report with performance and injury indices and dietary advice (slide 7) (slide 8) [06:33].
The pilot: 20 recruited, 6 intervention and 6 control analysed, all male, VO2max 49 ± 7 ml/kg/min, age 46 ± 12, eight weeks of tailored diets with pre- and probiotics (slide 11) [06:33].

Results: Barbaresi said TIBC, total proteins, glucose and monocytes fell after the intervention [06:33]; the slide marks TIBC decreasing at adjusted p < 0.05 and shows no VO2max effect (slide 13). Barbaresi said the sample is not enough "to make big assumption" [06:33].
The digital twin is an ambition for "maybe two, three years"; the intelligent platform is under construction [06:33].
Next: the largest gut microbiota collection in sport, transfer to the general population and longevity, and wearable partnerships (slide 16) [20:02].

quotes.text: "we are just 12 people, so six participants in the intervention. And we are aware that it's not enough to make big assumption, but it's still something." Speaker 3 (Silvia Barbaresi) [06:33]
"...for me, the best marketing that we can do is running a clinical trial showing that what we do make sense" Speaker 3 (Silvia Barbaresi) [28:46]
"Gut Microbiota-based interventions" (slide 6)

followups: Check whether the pilot results have been published since June 2025.
Possible contact: Silvia Barbaresi, on whether brands or ingredient suppliers can work with Minutia [26:21].

NootroLabs, one of the summit's two 2025 Start-Up Stars, is a UK contract manufacturer (Otter heard the name as "Neutral Labs"). Its co-founder and CEO, Cary Holmes (heard as "Harry"), could not attend and sent a short video, played before the Minutia.AI pitch.

Holmes set the company up in Staffordshire in 2021 and moved to a larger site in Worcestershire a year later, after winning retail contracts. The current site is 11,000 square feet, extended by another 3,000, and a second site of 10,000 square feet is being taken on, for 24,000 square feet across two sites by the end of the year.

It makes oils, capsules, gummies and powders. Best sellers are hemp oils, mushroom, magnesium and adaptogen capsules. Holmes said hemp is contracting for now and the adaptogen market is growing. The company is moving towards sports powders such as protein and pre-workouts, and aims to win large contracts, hence the new site. Holmes described it as debt free, with automated machinery and strong investors and mentors.

summary.Summary:
A panel on the first afternoon, after the Euromonitor and Holland & Barrett talks: Nick Morgan, introduced as founder and managing director of Nutrition Integrated; Luca Bucchini, ESSNA's chair and a food supplement regulation expert; and Dr Mark Evans of Holland & Barrett. The chair is not named.

Morgan said protein and pre-workout remain the pillars of sports brands, but protein now runs through every format, and the further it spreads the simpler its message becomes. Protein waters were Morgan's model of simple innovation, and creatine Morgan's case study of an old ingredient reinvented through communication. Evans added that the science for premium protein forms over others is thin, and that sourcing quality ingredients is harder than Evans expected.

Bucchini covered regulation: claims rules differ by member state, and the Commission's coming maximum levels for vitamins and minerals look very low for several nutrients. Bucchini saw promise in botanicals but no convincing pro- or postbiotic sports products yet.

On white spaces, the panel named GLP-1 users, longevity and endurance, which Morgan said has never been unlocked. Their advice to founders: focus, believe in the product, and know the rules.

summary.Summary:
Aishwarya Rajpara, a Beauty and Health Consultant at Euromonitor International, opened the first day with the state of the European sports nutrition market, drawn from Euromonitor's market data, its 2025 consumer survey and its tracker of new product launches.

The global market reached USD 30.6 billion in 2024, and Europe holds 19% of it. Protein powder is still the largest category in Europe, but ready-to-drink protein grew fastest. Consumers now link health to mental wellbeing and stress, and European women report more stress than men and are turning to strength training.

Launches tell the same story. Low sugar is the feature consumers want most, convenience is their top priority, and clean-label and "free from" claims grew fastest. Sports supplements were the fastest-growing launch area, led by electrolytes and creatine, while milk protein supplement launches fell. Creatine use rose in every age group.

Rajpara closed on three trends: convenience, transparency and a holistic approach that reaches beyond protein, with women as the clearest group to grow. In questions Rajpara said consumers expect sustainability as standard rather than pay a premium for it.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The global sports nutrition market was USD 30.6 billion in 2024; Europe holds 19% of sales, over 80% of that from Western Europe, and Europe has the second-highest two-year growth after Latin America (slide 9).
- In Europe, protein powder is 43% of sports nutrition sales; protein bars grew 11% a year from 2022 to 2024 against an 8% global average, and RTD shows the highest growth (slide 12).
- Sports supplement launches rose 33%, with the highest increase in electrolytes and creatine, while milk protein supplement launches fell 21% (slide 17).
- The slide says creatine is "Building momentum in post-workout routine" (slide 18). Rajpara said its use rose in all age groups, and that "new studies that claim" effects beyond muscle, on cognitive function and memory, are one reason [00:00].
- Low sugar is the product feature most wanted, convenience the top priority and clean label still in demand; word of mouth and web browsing drive awareness more than experts or celebrities (slide 14).
- European women report 21% higher stress than men, physical activity is the first way consumers tackle stress, and more women do strength training (slide 11) [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Creatine is named twice in Euromonitor's data, as a top launch area and as rising use across ages (slide 17) (slide 18). My reading: this supports CreaWin as the creatine to pitch to European sports brands, including those reaching older users.
- The cognitive angle is reported as "new studies that claim" [00:00]. My reading: any CreaWin cognition story should stay at that hedge; see holland-barrett-fitness-generations on how a retailer handles it without an EFSA claim.
- Milk protein supplement launches fell 21%, and Rajpara linked the shift to "plant based" options (slide 17) [00:00]. My reading: a tailwind for IsoClr: Pea, especially in RTD, the fastest-growing protein format (slide 12).
- Electrolytes and hydration are the other launch leader (slide 17). My reading: worth checking where our range fits hydration and endurance stacks; the innovation panel the same day called endurance a white space (sports-nutrition-innovation-panel).
summary.Quotes:
- "There are new studies that claim to have positive effects are created on not just for muscle building, but also better support for COVID function and memory enhancement." Speaker 1 (Aishwarya Rajpara; Otter's "COVID" is probably cognitive) [00:00]
- "Word of mouth and web browsing drive sports nutrition awareness in Europe; expert and celebrity influence remains limited." (slide 14)
- "Creatine: Building momentum in post-workout routine" (slide 18)
- "...sustainability is something that they want as a standard feature and not a trend that they really want to pay for." Speaker 1 (Aishwarya Rajpara) [17:19]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Ask Euromonitor (Aishwarya Rajpara) for the chart values behind slides 11, 14 and 18, especially creatine use by age for 2024 and 2025 (slide 18).
- Check whether we have access to Passport Innovation's sports nutrition launch data for the 15 European countries (slide 15).

- Sources named on the slides: Euromonitor Passport Consumer Health (market sizes and shares); Voice of the Consumer: Health and Nutrition Survey, fielded February 2025 (n=21,207 overall; n=15,727 for female exercise; n=2,299 for desired product features; n=9,877 for consumption reasons; n=3,571 for creatine use); Passport Innovation, launches 2022 to 2024 across 15 countries in the UK and Europe (slides 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18).

This talk gives Euromonitor's USD 30.6 billion for 2024 (slide 9). The two use different sources and definitions; both are kept.
