# Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

## "European Sports Nutrition Trends" (https://otter.ai/u/utmmLl7JOqwbHdgoLoLtlkcvX3g)

The discussion on European sports nutrition trends highlighted the market's growth, exceeding $30 billion in 2024, with double-digit annual increases. Key trends include a shift towards multi-functional, protein-centric products, and a focus on convenience. Women are particularly stressed and engage in weight training and cardio exercises. Protein-based products dominate, with whey accounting for 40% of sales. Innovation emphasizes low sugar, clean labels, and sustainability. Consumers prioritize convenience, transparency, and holistic health benefits, particularly for women. The market is evolving towards more plant-based and functional ingredients, with a significant rise in creatine consumption.

Action items:
- Speaker 0 - : Analyze consumer trends around physical fitness and stress management.
- Speaker 0 - : Investigate opportunities to better cater to women's needs in the sports nutrition market.
- Speaker 0 - : Explore innovative product formats and packaging solutions to address consumer demand for convenience.
- Speaker 0 - : Develop sports nutrition products with a focus on clean label, no added sugar, and targeted benefits like hydration and energy.
- Speaker 0 - : Assess the potential to expand the consumer base for sports nutrition products, particularly among women.

detail.text: The deck is filed as received (files/euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends-deck.pdf, 21 pages); slide numbers here are the file's pages. Each page carries "© 2024 Euromonitor International. All rights reserved." The last slide offered a QR code to download the presentation (slide 21).

Sources named on the slides: Euromonitor Passport Consumer Health (market sizes and shares); Voice of the Consumer: Health and Nutrition Survey, fielded February 2025 (n=21,207 overall; n=15,727 for female exercise; n=2,299 for desired product features; n=9,877 for consumption reasons; n=3,571 for creatine use); Passport Innovation, launches 2022 to 2024 across 15 countries in the UK and Europe (slides 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18).
Passport Innovation covers 54 categories in 32 countries and over 400 attributes in 6 groups (slides 5, 6).

Another speaker's market size: Dr Mark Evans (Holland & Barrett, holland-barrett-fitness-generations) showed Statista's sports and active nutrition market at USD 28.4 billion in 2023 and USD 37.8 billion in 2028. This talk gives Euromonitor's USD 30.6 billion for 2024 (slide 9). The two use different sources and definitions; both are kept.

Spoken, Rajpara said the market is "doing postpartum double digit growth every year" (Otter's words) and that protein powder is "about 40%" of European sales; the deck says 43% (slide 12) [00:00]. Europe's main markets, as said: the UK, Germany, France, Spain and Italy [00:00].
Health perception: 60% associate health with mental wellbeing and 44% recognise low stress as vital to good health (slide 10).

Women's exercise types are compared for 2023 and 2025 (walking, at-home workouts, cycling, running, weight lifting, group classes, yoga, team sports); the chart values are not in the deck's text (slide 11). Rajpara said more women are doing weight training and cardio [00:00].
Desired features, in the chart's order: low in sugar, ready-to-drink, bar format, clean ingredient list, portable, powder, electrolytes, caffeine, free from animal products, gel (slide 14).
Launches: over 8,000 new and sub-brand launches in sports nutrition in Europe in 2024; clean label claims grew over 100%; health claims and flavour lead innovation (slide 15).

Claims: sustained focus on high-protein claims, fortification rising, "no added sugar" claims up 32%, gluten-free and lactose-free gaining; natural claims drive growth, with organic and sustainable sourcing growing steadily (slide 16).

Packaging and format: jar packaging dominates; plastic packaging claims fell 76%; flexible packaging is trending up but innovation lagged in 2024; new formats such as gels and creams (slide 17). Rajpara said new formats are "still underdeveloped" [00:00].

Consumption reasons: performance is the key reason; beyond protein, the focus is hydration and recovery speed (slide 18). Rajpara said strength and muscle tone remain the first reason and hydration is rising [00:00].

Their three closing trends: convenience (accessibility, flexible packaging), transparency (nutrition information, ingredient awareness, sustainability impact) and a holistic approach (broader consumption, beyond protein) (slide 20).

Q&A: asked whether longevity interest has shifted from cardio to muscle gain, Rajpara pointed to running as the number one physical activity in the data (Otter's text is garbled) [00:00]. Asked about a sustainability premium, Rajpara pointed to beauty, where consumers pay for naturally driven formulas, as a contrast [17:19].
The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md); its line that whey is 40% of sales is Otter's reading, not the speaker's or the deck's.

takeaways.text: The global sports nutrition market was USD 30.6 billion in 2024; Europe holds 19% of sales, over 80% of that from Western Europe, and Europe has the second-highest two-year growth after Latin America (slide 9).
In Europe, protein powder is 43% of sports nutrition sales; protein bars grew 11% a year from 2022 to 2024 against an 8% global average, and RTD shows the highest growth (slide 12).
Sports supplement launches rose 33%, with the highest increase in electrolytes and creatine, while milk protein supplement launches fell 21% (slide 17).

The slide says creatine is "Building momentum in post-workout routine" (slide 18). Rajpara said its use rose in all age groups, and that "new studies that claim" effects beyond muscle, on cognitive function and memory, are one reason [00:00].
Low sugar is the product feature most wanted, convenience the top priority and clean label still in demand; word of mouth and web browsing drive awareness more than experts or celebrities (slide 14).
European women report 21% higher stress than men, physical activity is the first way consumers tackle stress, and more women do strength training (slide 11) [00:00].

quotes.text: "There are new studies that claim to have positive effects are created on not just for muscle building, but also better support for COVID function and memory enhancement." Speaker 1 (Aishwarya Rajpara; Otter's "COVID" is probably cognitive) [00:00]
"Word of mouth and web browsing drive sports nutrition awareness in Europe; expert and celebrity influence remains limited." (slide 14)
"Creatine: Building momentum in post-workout routine" (slide 18)
"...sustainability is something that they want as a standard feature and not a trend that they really want to pay for." Speaker 1 (Aishwarya Rajpara) [17:19]

followups: Ask Euromonitor (Aishwarya Rajpara) for the chart values behind slides 11, 14 and 18, especially creatine use by age for 2024 and 2025 (slide 18).
Check whether we have access to Passport Innovation's sports nutrition launch data for the 15 European countries (slide 15).

# AI, Scientific Wellness and the Future of Personalised Health: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "AI, Wellness, and Personalized Nutrition - Nathan Price - ANS", https://otter.ai/u/Y8mjte52uDOpW4X56rJCCDKq87E, dated 24 Jun 2025 in Otter (Otter's clock time is not local time), 28m 52s. The recording starts a few words into the talk. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Nathan Price (Thorne): About some of the things that we're doing across both those enterprises at the moment and building a bit on the science side here. So we're at this really interesting moment in history, which I think all of us are aware of. Towards the birth of AI, there's a lot of questions and discussions about what this is going to mean for the future of our industry as we start to see the beginnings of this, one thing that is very clear is that AI helps us on at least two major fronts. One is that we're clearly entering an era where we can drive personalization at a level that was never before possible. I had started a company some years ago called arivale, which has generated a lot of new data. We'll talk about a little bit of that today, and got out of business back then. This was we started about, well, about 10 years ago. And it's interesting that when I get back with my former colleagues and so forth in that area, we like to chat about you, imagine we had a magic box that understood every language in the world, if they'd answer any question that you asked, or whether they could dive in right? We now, of course, have that so that ability for us to do personalization now is massive, and we're all aware of the other thing that it really does is it unlocks the ability to delve very deeply into the wealth of information that we have for interpretation of what's going on in biology. On the science side, we just got a $52 million grant from the market age in the United States, and part of that is to build out something that we call the personalized health span optimizer, or the end point analyzer. And the idea here in AI is that rather than having to just utilize patterns are something that we've seen before. You can actually take very deep information from a single individual and dive in and leverage tools like large language models, agentic AIS, to try to understand what's happening in that person. From a very mechanistic point of view, in essence, you can go from just pattern recognition into what we call, what we might call deep reason. So this new world of AI is really opening up for us, not only the ability to dive deep into trying to understand complexity, but also the ability to deliver that complexity in a way that's incredibly simple for the end user. And Mary did a beautiful job talking about how we want that to look at the end of the day and what's happening in the marketplace. So as we think about this, you know, the abundance of health would be, you know, the greatest achievement I would, I would think of the greatest good that we could get from this. AI, technologies that we have, which I think we all be agreed with in this particular audience. The way I came into this started about 12 years ago, in an area that we followed scientific wellness. This was at the time I was Professor and Associate Director of Institute of persistent biology, working closely with really great friend and colleague at Lee hood. So if you don't know, is one of the greatest scientists of the 20th century, and now into the 21st I haven't won the national medical science and President Obama sort of things, but what we really got interested in here was to try to understand how we could take the same sort of level of scientific rigor that had been built for the study of disease and try to think about that in terms of The study of health. And so this led to pushing for some of the first cohorts where we were making 1000s and 1000s of measurements on 1000s of people and monitoring them through health, which I'll get into this, and gathering really deep data across time as it's become more and more prevalent, it really allows us to now apply AI driven personalized strategies. I wrote a book on this last couple of years of our progress about the age of scientific wellness. So we are starting to see the shift in healthcare change, and it's very much for the benefit of people in this room, in the sense that we are seeing less of a focus on disease and more of a shift towards wellness for some of the early stages of this, but it is something we're starting to see. Deloitte did this report in 2022 with the forecast here. This is using money in the in the United States, so I'll use this because that's the data that I've got. So basically where we've been spending something like the vast majority of the $4 trillion that are spent in the US, and it's it's almost all spent on treating sickness and trying to delay symptoms a little bit. Alzheimer's is a great example of this. You know, we wait until people are far along, once your brain has started to disintegrate, and you want to think about, how do you reverse that, or treat that? There's no small molecule drug in the world that simply grow your brain once you've lost, like, billions of synapses. I think that's a pretty fanciful kind of idea. Prevention, however, is very doable, and nutrition and personalized approaches to that can make an incredible difference. I was one of the three keynote speakers for combination therapies and Alzheimer's disease from National Institutes of Health in the US recently, and you just couldn't help but notice, first talk was from pharma, beautiful, beautiful talk. Great. P value statistics, 20 to $40,000 a year, and you get a couple of months of delay in the progression of your disease. Second talk was on prevention, nutrition and lifestyle. You get years, sometimes many years, even a decade, of benefit at very low cost. Certain populations are incredibly responsive to this as well. The Hispanic population, there are genetics reasons for this. The Hispanic population, for example, in the United States, 45% of all dementia are preventable by lifestyle and nutrition. And so you can dive in there, and really big way, and you see effect sizes that are much bigger. So because of these many trends, what we're seeing in Deloitte is forecasting this for by 2040 is they're seeing a shift of a massive amount of this towards the wellness space towards prevention. I just did a thought. They were symposium for Al catterton, who has put 10s of billions of dollars now in the wellness space, including they bought farm a couple of years ago. So there are ones now and more, different term anyway. So they are great, but they are a big force in this. But anyway, as I was speaking there, since the $2 trillion pivot, right, which healthcare us is going for, and you can amplify that, if you will, look more worldwide. And Marion again, gave a really nice view of kind of how this is manifest in the marketplace. I also wrote this piece for Scientific American a couple years ago, going through like this, emergence of the wellness space, of the science based wellness industry, which so many people in here are aware of going through about that would be about 50 ish startups or so to come out of here. So coming back to this notion of scientific wellness, and getting involved in this, one of the first things we did was to launch a program where we measured deep data on about 5000 people. This started in 2014 to cover Nature Biotechnology in 2017 in the early days, and then we've basically been studying a lot of this ever since, and I'm going to share a little bit about what we've learned from doing this. So the kind of measurements that are in here, got the survey right. All of our genomes are 99.9% similar. We have whole genome sequencing you can do on people that still leaves you with about a million snip differences between any two humans. So we look at those. We've been analyzing data from about 1200 analytes in the early days, out of the blood, you can do a lot more than that. Now, gut microbiome on these individuals, and then also continual tracking of where it applies. The idea is that if you take this kind of data, and especially now with our AI tool, we can deliver that actual possibilities at a tremendous scale and depth now, and if people stay with you that over time, you can create what we call personal, dense, dynamic data clouds or typing and so just observe what's happening in a health trajectory for an individual. So I just want to share a little bit about what we learned from analyzing data on these 5000 people, and then relate that back to what are the opportunities we have for ourselves in AI today, as we're able to deliver much more of this kind of insight to a consumer base. So one of the first things I just want to emphasize, and I'll just give one quick example of this, is whether you can predict outcome of lifestyle and dietary interventions from a genome. So I'll just use a familiar example. So LDL cholesterol. And LDL cholesterol very commonly, something that we would, we would go against. It's a common for the prescription of status in healthcare. It's also a use for various different supplements as well red to use, rice, burger and things like that. So if we just look at the level of LDL cholesterol that's in all of our blood, if I don't know anything about your own your diet or your lifestyle, nothing, all I have is your genome, I can capture about 12% of that variance and predict something about what the level of LDL cholesterol that you're likely to have. So we took these 1000s of people, we bucketed them into five groups on this x axis here. summary.Summary:
Nathan Price, Chief Scientific Officer of Thorne and a professor at the Buck Institute, argued that AI lets personalised nutrition use very deep data on one person and still give that person simple advice.

Their evidence comes from scientific wellness work on about 5,000 people, each measured for their genome, about 1,200 blood analytes, gut microbiome and self-tracking. First, genetics. A polygenic score explains about 12% of LDL cholesterol. People whose measured level sat well above their genetic prediction lowered it in a lifestyle programme; people whose genes predicted a high level did not. Price calls that gap the "Modifiability Gap", a guide to where advice is most likely to work.

Second, the microbiome. Blood metabolites predict about half the variation in gut diversity. The microbiome's gene content was the only measure that predicted weight loss once BMI was accounted for. And some gut bacteria turn phosphatidylcholine into TMAO, so a supplement taken for the brain could harm the heart in those people.

Price called for trials that test a personalisation algorithm rather than one nutrient at a time. Their conclusion: AI powered by deep phenotyping will transform personalised nutrition, and genetics are not destiny.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Genetics predicted who lowered LDL cholesterol in a personalised programme: those measured well above their genetic prediction came down "very substantially"; those predicted high showed no significant change [00:00] (slide 11).
- The "Modifiability Gap" between genetic prediction and measured value marks the people "most likely to respond"; Price would rank these gaps per person to plan advice that visibly works and keeps them engaged [00:00] (slide 12).
- In the cohort, the gene content of the gut microbiome was the only predictor of weight loss independent of BMI, a correlation of about 0.3; blood metabolites, proteins and a diet questionnaire showed no signal beyond BMI [00:00] (slide 18).
- Gut bacteria in some people convert phosphatidylcholine to trimethylamine, which the liver turns into TMAO, a cardiovascular risk factor; a population trial cannot show who this applies to [00:00] (slide 16).
- Price wants randomised trials that test the personalisation algorithm, so each person's supplement stack differs while one thing is still tested rigorously [00:00].
- The microbiome becomes more unique to each person from around age 50; their "uniqueness" score predicted all-cause mortality in people over about 80 over a four-year follow-up [00:00] (slide 17).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: a science and personalisation talk from a supplement brand's chief scientist, with one point that touches our choline group directly.
- The TMAO point is about phosphatidylcholine [00:00]. My reading: formulators may ask whether any choline source raises TMAO, so we should know what the evidence says for our choline bitartrate before a customer asks.
- Price said butyrate, made when gut microbes ferment carbohydrate, stimulates the cells that release GLP-1 [00:00]. My reading: a line worth checking against the literature for fibre in GLP-1-support products.
- Thorne's direction is algorithm-led personalised stacks [00:00] (slide 21). My reading: platforms like this will favour ingredients with responder data, not just average effects.
summary.Quotes:
- "So genetics are not destiny." Nathan Price [00:00]
- "So you can be aiming to improve your brain health instead be poisoning your heart. That's a personalized insight." Nathan Price [00:00]
- "...the only thing that predicted who would go on to lose weight in this cohort was the gene content of their microbiome" Nathan Price [00:00]
- "It's just that that single thing is not a nutrient on average, it is the personalization strategy embodied by the algorithm." Nathan Price [00:00]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Find the evidence on TMAO for choline sources, choline bitartrate included.
- Find the butyrate and GLP-1 (L cell) evidence Price referred to.
- Related sessions: abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition, pykalisto-nutrigenomics, millbank-nutrition-by-algorithm, personalised-health-panel, cotter-athlete-microbiome.
summary.Detail:
- The deck is marked "Proprietary & Confidential" on its title slide (slide 1). Its title slide reads "AI, Scientific Wellness, and the Future of Personalized Nutrition" (slide 1).
- Price founded Arivale about 10 years ago; it generated much of the data shown and went out of business [00:00].
- Their team has a $52 million US grant, part of which builds a "personalized health span optimizer", using large language models and agentic AI to move from pattern recognition to "deep reason" on one individual [00:00].
- Deloitte (2022): most of the $4 trillion spent on US healthcare goes on treating sickness; Deloitte forecasts a large shift towards wellness and prevention by 2040, which Price called the "$2 trillion pivot" [00:00] (slide 5).
- On Alzheimer's Price contrasted a drug costing $20,000 to $40,000 a year for a couple of months' delay with prevention giving "years, sometimes many years"; Price said 45% of dementia in the US Hispanic population is preventable by lifestyle and nutrition [00:00].
- Pioneer 5000 (PIs Nathan Price and Lee Hood; Price et al, Nature Biotechnology, 2017): whole-genome sequencing; lab tests three times (clinical chemistry 150, metabolites 700, proteins 400, about 1,200 analytes); gut microbiome three times; continual self-tracking; a database of 200 actionable possibilities (slide 6) (slide 7).
- Genetics alone captures about 12% of the variance in LDL cholesterol, enough to move someone across the clinical range (Zubair et al, Scientific Reports, 2019) [00:00] (slide 10). Price said the same holds for raising HDL cholesterol and appears to for a marker of the transition to diabetes [00:00].
- About half the variance in gut microbiome diversity can be predicted from blood metabolites, from as few as 11; the link held across conditions on the slide (abdominal pain, acid reflux, antibiotics, bloating, constipation, diarrhoea, type 2 diabetes) but broke down in extreme obesity, BMI over about 35, which Price thinks is due to inflammation (Wilmanski et al, Nature Biotechnology, 2019) [00:00] (slide 15).
- About 18% of circulating metabolites are made or co-made by the microbiome [00:00]. The slide names indole propionate, TMAO, imidazole propionate, hippurate, secondary bile acids and p-cresol sulfate as nutrients and toxins with effects in the host (slide 16).
- Weight loss: people whose microbiome breaks complex carbohydrate into simple sugars "have a really hard time losing weight"; those whose microbiome turns it more into short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate lost more in a personalised programme (Diener et al, mSystems, 2021) [00:00] (slide 18).
- Biological BMI: traditional BMI "Misclassifies up to 30% of people"; a metric built from metabolites, clinical labs and proteins "May identify metabolically unhealthy individuals who occupy a normal BMI" (Watanabe et al, Nature Medicine, 2023) (slide 19).
- Price ran their own comprehensive blood panel through ChatGPT's deep research function and called the result "probably the most informative health report I've ever gotten" [00:00].
- In questions, asked about Rob Knight's view (heard as "Rob night") that the microbiome may be destiny, Price said "it is an influence", not destiny, and that understanding the genome "gives you a roadmap" to better choices [26:54].
- Price referred to an earlier talk by a speaker heard as "Mary" and "Marion" [00:00]. My reading: probably Mariette Abrahams (abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition), recorded the same day.

Their team has a $52 million US grant, part of which builds a "personalized health span optimizer", using large language models and agentic AI to move from pattern recognition to "deep reason" on one individual [00:00].

Deloitte (2022): most of the $4 trillion spent on US healthcare goes on treating sickness; Deloitte forecasts a large shift towards wellness and prevention by 2040, which Price called the "$2 trillion pivot" [00:00] (slide 5).

On Alzheimer's Price contrasted a drug costing $20,000 to $40,000 a year for a couple of months' delay with prevention giving "years, sometimes many years"; Price said 45% of dementia in the US Hispanic population is preventable by lifestyle and nutrition [00:00].

Pioneer 5000 (PIs Nathan Price and Lee Hood; Price et al, Nature Biotechnology, 2017): whole-genome sequencing; lab tests three times (clinical chemistry 150, metabolites 700, proteins 400, about 1,200 analytes); gut microbiome three times; continual self-tracking; a database of 200 actionable possibilities (slide 6) (slide 7).

Genetics alone captures about 12% of the variance in LDL cholesterol, enough to move someone across the clinical range (Zubair et al, Scientific Reports, 2019) [00:00] (slide 10). Price said the same holds for raising HDL cholesterol and appears to for a marker of the transition to diabetes [00:00].

About half the variance in gut microbiome diversity can be predicted from blood metabolites, from as few as 11; the link held across conditions on the slide (abdominal pain, acid reflux, antibiotics, bloating, constipation, diarrhoea, type 2 diabetes) but broke down in extreme obesity, BMI over about 35, which Price thinks is due to inflammation (Wilmanski et al, Nature Biotechnology, 2019) [00:00] (slide 15).

About 18% of circulating metabolites are made or co-made by the microbiome [00:00]. The slide names indole propionate, TMAO, imidazole propionate, hippurate, secondary bile acids and p-cresol sulfate as nutrients and toxins with effects in the host (slide 16).

Weight loss: people whose microbiome breaks complex carbohydrate into simple sugars "have a really hard time losing weight"; those whose microbiome turns it more into short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate lost more in a personalised programme (Diener et al, mSystems, 2021) [00:00] (slide 18).

Biological BMI: traditional BMI "Misclassifies up to 30% of people"; a metric built from metabolites, clinical labs and proteins "May identify metabolically unhealthy individuals who occupy a normal BMI" (Watanabe et al, Nature Medicine, 2023) (slide 19).
Price ran their own comprehensive blood panel through ChatGPT's deep research function and called the result "probably the most informative health report I've ever gotten" [00:00].

In questions, asked about Rob Knight's view (heard as "Rob night") that the microbiome may be destiny, Price said "it is an influence", not destiny, and that understanding the genome "gives you a roadmap" to better choices [26:54].
Price referred to an earlier talk by a speaker heard as "Mary" and "Marion" [00:00]. My reading: probably Mariette Abrahams (abrahams-glp1-ai-personalised-nutrition), recorded the same day.

takeaways.text: Genetics predicted who lowered LDL cholesterol in a personalised programme: those measured well above their genetic prediction came down "very substantially"; those predicted high showed no significant change [00:00] (slide 11).

The "Modifiability Gap" between genetic prediction and measured value marks the people "most likely to respond"; Price would rank these gaps per person to plan advice that visibly works and keeps them engaged [00:00] (slide 12).

In the cohort, the gene content of the gut microbiome was the only predictor of weight loss independent of BMI, a correlation of about 0.3; blood metabolites, proteins and a diet questionnaire showed no signal beyond BMI [00:00] (slide 18).

Gut bacteria in some people convert phosphatidylcholine to trimethylamine, which the liver turns into TMAO, a cardiovascular risk factor; a population trial cannot show who this applies to [00:00] (slide 16).
Price wants randomised trials that test the personalisation algorithm, so each person's supplement stack differs while one thing is still tested rigorously [00:00].
The microbiome becomes more unique to each person from around age 50; their "uniqueness" score predicted all-cause mortality in people over about 80 over a four-year follow-up [00:00] (slide 17).

quotes.text: "So genetics are not destiny." Nathan Price [00:00]
"So you can be aiming to improve your brain health instead be poisoning your heart. That's a personalized insight." Nathan Price [00:00]
"...the only thing that predicted who would go on to lose weight in this cohort was the gene content of their microbiome" Nathan Price [00:00]
"It's just that that single thing is not a nutrient on average, it is the personalization strategy embodied by the algorithm." Nathan Price [00:00]

followups: Find the evidence on TMAO for choline sources, choline bitartrate included.
Find the butyrate and GLP-1 (L cell) evidence Price referred to.

The programme bills Cotter as Head of Food Biosciences and Head of Microbiology, with Teagasc and SeqBiome logos. The billed title is ours, from the deck's file name; the title slide reads "Harnessing Knowledge Gained from Studies of Athlete Microbiomes". summary.Summary:
Paul Cotter, Head of Food Biosciences at Teagasc and a principal investigator at APC Microbiome Ireland, presented what studies of elite athletes' gut microbiomes have taught their group, and what it means for diet.

Cotter started with the gut microbiome and the many factors that shape it, from antibiotics and birth mode to diet, fibre, fermented foods, probiotics and exercise. Their group's first study compared elite rugby players with men of low and high body mass index. The athletes' microbiomes differed from both control groups, though with exceptions, and later work showed differences in what the microbes can do and the metabolites they make, including short-chain fatty acids.

Cotter then turned to diet. In a 12-week trial in 53 healthy adults, a ketogenic diet lost slightly more fat than a low-sugar diet but raised LDL cholesterol, reduced glucose tolerance and lowered bifidobacteria; cutting sugar changed the microbiome little. Cotter also showed kefirs that differed in their effect on plasma cholesterol, and work separating the effects of diet and exercise on gut microbe and host metabolism.

The deck ends with Sportgenix, a microbiome analysis programme for athletes linked to SeqBiome, the company where Cotter is CTO.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Elite rugby players' microbiomes differed from those of low- and high-BMI controls, "though there are exceptions" (Clarke et al., Gut 2014; 40 athletes, 23 and 23 controls, men aged 18 to 37) (slide 7) (slide 8).
- Athletes' microbiomes also differ in functional potential and in the metabolites they produce; short-chain fatty acids correlate with diet or microbial diversity (Barton et al., Gut 2018) (slide 9).
- Ketogenic diet, 12 weeks in 53 healthy adults: 2.9 kg average fat loss against 2.1 kg on a low-sugar diet, but keto raised LDL cholesterol, reduced glucose tolerance and decreased bifidobacteria; sugar restriction did not significantly change the microbiome (slide 10) (slide 11).
- Fermented foods can differ in effect: kefirs differed in their impact on total plasma cholesterol, under the heading "Fermented foods with anti-obesity impacts" (Bourrie et al., Br J Nutr 2021) (slide 12).
- Diet and exercise each shape microbe and host co-metabolism, scored from urine NMR profiles against WHO healthy-eating guidelines (Penney et al., mSystems 2020) (slide 14) (slide 15).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: gut health in sport is a science story, not yet a product story; the deck names no supplement ingredient or dose. My reading: useful background for fibre and prebiotic pitches to sports brands, within each ingredient's own evidence.
- A low-carbohydrate (keto) diet decreased bifidobacteria in 12 weeks (slide 11). My reading: athletes on low-carbohydrate diets are a possible audience for prebiotic fibres; no study here tested that.
- Other microbiome talks: Minutia on gut microbiome and sport at the same event (minutia-gut-microbiome-sports), and APC colleagues Jens Walter (jens-walter-microbiome-ageing) and Siobhain O'Mahony (omahony-gut-brain-gaps). Sharon Madigan, whose SANS talk is filed (fuel-the-frame-carbohydrate-recovery-and), is among their acknowledged collaborators (slide 13).
summary.Quotes:
- "Dictated by types of microbes, what they do/produce and microbial diversity" (slide 3)
- "The keto diet altered gut microbiome composition, notably decreasing bifidobacteria." (slide 11)
- "Sugar restriction did not significantly impact the gut microbiome composition." (slide 11)
summary.Follow-ups:
- The kefir paper (Bourrie et al., Br J Nutr 2021) for what the samples were and in whom (slide 12).
- The keto trial (Hengist et al., 2024) for the bifidobacteria result in full (slide 10) (slide 11).
- Sportgenix and SeqBiome: whether they recommend supplements to athletes (slide 12).

summary.Summary:
Sergej Ostojic, Professor of Nutrition and Public Health at the University of Agder in Norway, argued that creatine should be treated as a semi-essential nutrient for everyone, not only as a sports supplement.

The body turns over about 2 g of creatine a day and makes about half; the rest has to come from food, almost all of it meat and fish. Older people make less and eat less, and ageing muscle may take it up less well. In US survey data, 65.2% of adults ate less than the 1 g a day Ostojic takes as the requirement.

Ostojic then showed population studies linking low dietary creatine with more depression, heart and liver conditions, poorer cognition, cancer and earlier death, and higher creatine intake with more lean mass and grip strength. These are associations; some weakened once other factors were adjusted for. Ostojic set them beside supplementation trials in older people and the EU-authorised claim for adults over 55 who do resistance training, and called creatine safe on more than 1,000 human studies.

Their advice for older people: 1 g a day for life to prevent a shortfall, 3 to 5 g with exercise for function, and more for the brain. Ostojic wants creatine recognised as a semi-essential nutrient and added to everyday meat-free foods.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Their frame: "Creatine appears to be a semi-essential nutrient for humans". About half of the 2 g daily turnover comes from an omnivorous diet, and older people make less, eat less and may take up less into muscle (slide 8) (slide 10) (slide 23) [00:00].
- Intake is low and falling: 65.2% of NHANES adults ate less than 1.00 g a day, and dietary creatine fell significantly in infants and in children and adolescents, with a tendency in adults, across 89,161 respondents (slide 11).
- Low intake is associated with worse health. Depression prevalence was 42% higher in the lowest intake quartile than the highest; older people under 1 g a day had 2.62 times the risk of angina pectoris and 2.59 times the risk of liver conditions (slide 12) (slide 13). Ostojic presented these as associations from population studies.
- Higher intake is associated with more lean mass and grip strength without exercise, in children, adults and older people; Ostojic said the link weakens and is not always significant once age and sex are adjusted for (slide 16) [00:00].
- The authorised claim: "Daily creatine consumption can enhance the effect of resistance training on muscle strength in adults over the age of 55" (Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/672) (slide 17).
- Doses for older people: 1 g a day for life to prevent a shortfall; 3 to 5 g a day with exercise to raise stores and performance; up to 20 g a day for cognition, for 5 to 7 days and then 3 to 5 g (slide 19).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: a leading creatine researcher makes the public-health case for creatine in healthy ageing, for people who do not train as well as those who do (slide 23) [00:00]. My reading: this supports CreaWin pitches to healthy-ageing and everyday-wellness brands, not only sports.
- The claim we can use is the EU-authorised one, for adults over 55 doing resistance training (slide 17). The population links to depression, cancer and mortality are associations, two of them from papers still in review; they are background for brands, never claims (slide 12) (slide 14) (slide 15) (slide 16).
- Their 1 g a day dose as a "Preventive strategy" and their call for "Market-driven fortification" of convenient foods point to low-dose daily formats: fortified foods, drinks and combinations (slide 19) (slide 21). My reading: a CreaWin food-fortification concept for older and meat-free consumers is worth taking to food and drink brands.
- Ostojic co-founded KRE-ALL, a Norwegian company developing creatine-enriched foods (slide 2). My reading: a possible CreaWin customer; their disclosures also list research support from several creatine suppliers.
- Other speakers agree on the move into healthy ageing: Kreider and Pasco (from-hype-to-healthspan-building-the), Nestlé Research (nutrition-to-improve-mitochondrial-functions) and the premium price of longevity creatine (nick-morgan-longevity). Mark Evans gives the same 3 to 5 g daily dose and 20 g loading (is-the-juice-worth-the-squeeze).
summary.Quotes:
- "Creatine appears to be a semi-essential nutrient for humans" (slide 23)
- "Creatine is a promising food component for public health nutrition for healthy aging" (slide 23)
- "Market-driven fortification = voluntarily enrich convenient foods with creatine" (slide 21)
- "Namely, if you not are able to exercise, just getting some creative might help you to preserve your muscular mass and strength when you're older." Sergej Ostojic [00:00] (Otter's text; "creative" is creatine)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Read the two papers in review once published (mortality, Appl Nutr Physiol Metab; lean mass and grip, J Health Popul Nutr) for the final figures (slide 15) (slide 16).
- KRE-ALL (Norway, creatine-enriched foods): a possible CreaWin conversation (slide 2).
- The Creatine Global Initiative library as a source for CreaWin healthy-ageing material (slide 22).
summary.Detail:
- Disclosures: member of the Scientific Advisory Board on Creatine in Health and Medicine (AlzChem LLC); co-owner of a European patent on liquid creatine supplements (WO2019150323 A1) and a US patent application on creatine for telomere lengthening; research support in the past 36 months from AlzChem GmbH, Kaneka Nutrients, ThermoLife International, Vireo Systems, a science ministry and a provincial secretariat for research; co-founder of KRE-ALL (slide 2).
- 100 years of research: a 1926 paper already suggested "Creatine may be stored as a reserve food material" (slide 4); a PubMed search shows 69,774 results (slide 5).
- Roles beyond energy: neurotransmitter, antioxidant, buffer and appetite regulator; muscle holds 120 mmol/kg of dry mass (slide 6). Ostojic said a just-completed study suggests creatine may affect appetite, submitted the week before [00:00].
- Food sources, in g/kg: herring 6.5 to 10.0, pork 5.0, beef and salmon 4.5, cod 3.0, tuna 4.0, plaice 2.0, milk 0.1; fruit, vegetables and shrimp only trace (slide 8).
- Groups at risk of a shortfall: preterm infants, inherited metabolic disorders, myopathies, multiple sclerosis, sarcopenia, vegetarians, chronic kidney disease and older people (slide 9).
- Why older people run low: less made by the body (lower AGAT and GAMT activity), less eaten, less muscle, and possibly a less effective creatine transporter (SLC6A8), which "is still under investigation" (slide 10).
- Cognition: older people eating more than 0.95 g a day (the top two quartiles) scored higher on cognitive tests (slide 13).
- Cancer: "for every additional milligram of food creatine per kilogram of body mass consumed daily, the cancer rate is reduced by approximately one percent", in US adults aged 20 and over; the slide calls this an association (slide 14).
- Mortality, from a paper in revision: survival was higher in those meeting the recommended intake (P 0.05). Hazard ratios: crude 0.85 (0.62 to 1.00); 1.03 (0.85 to 1.24) after sociodemographic factors; 0.96 (0.77 to 1.19) after lifestyle; 0.79 (0.67 to 0.94, P 0.01) after diet; 0.81 (0.69 to 0.96) after physical examination; 0.92 (0.72 to 1.17) after laboratory measures (slide 15). Ostojic spoke of 20 years of follow-up [00:00].
- Lean mass and grip, from a paper in review: lean mass excluding bone 43.5, 43.9, 46.8 and 50.2, and handgrip 58.9, 57.7, 63.9 and 71.1, from the lowest to the highest intake quartile (up to 0.21 g a day to 1.04 g or more) (slide 16). In people 65 and over the crude coefficients were 2.67 for lean mass and 3.68 for grip, both significant; in the most adjusted model shown for them, lean mass stayed significant (3.12) and grip did not (1.11) (slide 16). Ostojic spoke of 130,000 US adults [00:00].
- Supplementation in older people, as listed: less liver fat, better glycaemic control, slower tumour growth in some cancers, more strength or muscle, less bone loss, better function in knee osteoarthritis, better cognition, an antidepressant effect (slide 17). Ostojic said more than 50 studies in older people in the past 10 years [00:00].
- Safety: no risk in cross-sectional studies; no severe adverse events in long-term trials; over 1,000 human interventional studies at 0.3 to 0.8 g/kg a day for 7 days to 5 years; minor risks from RCTs: weight gain from water (?), kidney problems (?) and passing gut upset (slide 18). Ostojic said stomach upset may occur in the first 10 days [00:00].
- Open questions: no RDA or upper limit for older people; individual needs by sex, illness and microbiota; food composition data; who is at risk; interactions with other foods and medicines (slide 20).
- Fortification: eating less meat for the climate may lower creatine intake; adding creatine to meat-free foods could prevent a large-scale shortfall; first voluntary, market-driven fortification, then possibly mandated fortification (slide 21). Ostojic suggested a company could make a creatine product for older people [00:00].
- Their group in Norway built the Creatine Global Initiative (creatine.global), a library bringing together industry, scientists, regulators and consumers (slide 22) [00:00].
- Q&A: asked whether current production is environmentally friendly, Ostojic said most companies use synthetic processes, which are environmentally friendly compared with the old extraction from meat [23:44].

# Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Recording: "Creatine Nutrition - Sergej Ostojic - ANS25", https://otter.ai/u/IGH9CCTZhH_ecP8MdZJv5yksyG0

## Summary
Sergej Ostojic discussed the importance of creatine for health, particularly in the elderly, highlighting its role in energy production and potential benefits beyond sports. He noted that creatine deficiency can lead to various health issues, including depression, cognitive decline, and increased risk of chronic diseases. Ostojic recommended a daily intake of 1 gram of creatine for general health and 3-5 grams for enhanced performance. He emphasized the need for public health initiatives to address creatine malnutrition, suggesting fortified foods and dietary supplements as solutions. Ostojic also mentioned ongoing research and initiatives to promote creatine's recognition as a semi-essential nutrient.

## Action items
- Company - : Develop a creatine-only product for the elderly to address creatine malnutrition.
- Sergej Ostojic - : Explore environmentally friendly processes for producing creatine.
- Sergej Ostojic - : Promote the recognition of creatine as a semi-essential nutrient with regulatory authorities.
- Sergej Ostojic - : Investigate the feasibility of fortifying food products with creatine.

detail.text: Disclosures: member of the Scientific Advisory Board on Creatine in Health and Medicine (AlzChem LLC); co-owner of a European patent on liquid creatine supplements (WO2019150323 A1) and a US patent application on creatine for telomere lengthening; research support in the past 36 months from AlzChem GmbH, Kaneka Nutrients, ThermoLife International, Vireo Systems, a science ministry and a provincial secretariat for research; co-founder of KRE-ALL (slide 2).
100 years of research: a 1926 paper already suggested "Creatine may be stored as a reserve food material" (slide 4); a PubMed search shows 69,774 results (slide 5).

Roles beyond energy: neurotransmitter, antioxidant, buffer and appetite regulator; muscle holds 120 mmol/kg of dry mass (slide 6). Ostojic said a just-completed study suggests creatine may affect appetite, submitted the week before [00:00].
Food sources, in g/kg: herring 6.5 to 10.0, pork 5.0, beef and salmon 4.5, cod 3.0, tuna 4.0, plaice 2.0, milk 0.1; fruit, vegetables and shrimp only trace (slide 8).
Groups at risk of a shortfall: preterm infants, inherited metabolic disorders, myopathies, multiple sclerosis, sarcopenia, vegetarians, chronic kidney disease and older people (slide 9).

Why older people run low: less made by the body (lower AGAT and GAMT activity), less eaten, less muscle, and possibly a less effective creatine transporter (SLC6A8), which "is still under investigation" (slide 10).
Cognition: older people eating more than 0.95 g a day (the top two quartiles) scored higher on cognitive tests (slide 13).

Cancer: "for every additional milligram of food creatine per kilogram of body mass consumed daily, the cancer rate is reduced by approximately one percent", in US adults aged 20 and over; the slide calls this an association (slide 14).

Mortality, from a paper in revision: survival was higher in those meeting the recommended intake (P 0.05). Hazard ratios: crude 0.85 (0.62 to 1.00); 1.03 (0.85 to 1.24) after sociodemographic factors; 0.96 (0.77 to 1.19) after lifestyle; 0.79 (0.67 to 0.94, P 0.01) after diet; 0.81 (0.69 to 0.96) after physical examination; 0.92 (0.72 to 1.17) after laboratory measures (slide 15). Ostojic spoke of 20 years of follow-up [00:00].

Lean mass and grip, from a paper in review: lean mass excluding bone 43.5, 43.9, 46.8 and 50.2, and handgrip 58.9, 57.7, 63.9 and 71.1, from the lowest to the highest intake quartile (up to 0.21 g a day to 1.04 g or more) (slide 16). In people 65 and over the crude coefficients were 2.67 for lean mass and 3.68 for grip, both significant; in the most adjusted model shown for them, lean mass stayed significant (3.12) and grip did not (1.11) (slide 16). Ostojic spoke of 130,000 US adults [00:00].

Supplementation in older people, as listed: less liver fat, better glycaemic control, slower tumour growth in some cancers, more strength or muscle, less bone loss, better function in knee osteoarthritis, better cognition, an antidepressant effect (slide 17). Ostojic said more than 50 studies in older people in the past 10 years [00:00].

Safety: no risk in cross-sectional studies; no severe adverse events in long-term trials; over 1,000 human interventional studies at 0.3 to 0.8 g/kg a day for 7 days to 5 years; minor risks from RCTs: weight gain from water (?), kidney problems (?) and passing gut upset (slide 18). Ostojic said stomach upset may occur in the first 10 days [00:00].
Open questions: no RDA or upper limit for older people; individual needs by sex, illness and microbiota; food composition data; who is at risk; interactions with other foods and medicines (slide 20).

Fortification: eating less meat for the climate may lower creatine intake; adding creatine to meat-free foods could prevent a large-scale shortfall; first voluntary, market-driven fortification, then possibly mandated fortification (slide 21). Ostojic suggested a company could make a creatine product for older people [00:00].
Their group in Norway built the Creatine Global Initiative (creatine.global), a library bringing together industry, scientists, regulators and consumers (slide 22) [00:00].

Q&A: asked whether current production is environmentally friendly, Ostojic said most companies use synthetic processes, which are environmentally friendly compared with the old extraction from meat [23:44].

takeaways.text: Their frame: "Creatine appears to be a semi-essential nutrient for humans". About half of the 2 g daily turnover comes from an omnivorous diet, and older people make less, eat less and may take up less into muscle (slide 8) (slide 10) (slide 23) [00:00].

Intake is low and falling: 65.2% of NHANES adults ate less than 1.00 g a day, and dietary creatine fell significantly in infants and in children and adolescents, with a tendency in adults, across 89,161 respondents (slide 11).

Low intake is associated with worse health. Depression prevalence was 42% higher in the lowest intake quartile than the highest; older people under 1 g a day had 2.62 times the risk of angina pectoris and 2.59 times the risk of liver conditions (slide 12) (slide 13). Ostojic presented these as associations from population studies.

Higher intake is associated with more lean mass and grip strength without exercise, in children, adults and older people; Ostojic said the link weakens and is not always significant once age and sex are adjusted for (slide 16) [00:00].
The authorised claim: "Daily creatine consumption can enhance the effect of resistance training on muscle strength in adults over the age of 55" (Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/672) (slide 17).

Doses for older people: 1 g a day for life to prevent a shortfall; 3 to 5 g a day with exercise to raise stores and performance; up to 20 g a day for cognition, for 5 to 7 days and then 3 to 5 g (slide 19).

quotes.text: "Creatine appears to be a semi-essential nutrient for humans" (slide 23)
"Creatine is a promising food component for public health nutrition for healthy aging" (slide 23)
"Market-driven fortification = voluntarily enrich convenient foods with creatine" (slide 21)

"Namely, if you not are able to exercise, just getting some creative might help you to preserve your muscular mass and strength when you're older." Sergej Ostojic [00:00] (Otter's text; "creative" is creatine)

followups: Read the two papers in review once published (mortality, Appl Nutr Physiol Metab; lean mass and grip, J Health Popul Nutr) for the final figures (slide 15) (slide 16).
KRE-ALL (Norway, creatine-enriched foods): a possible CreaWin conversation (slide 2).
The Creatine Global Initiative library as a source for CreaWin healthy-ageing material (slide 22).

summary.Summary:
Mariette Abrahams, founder and CEO of Qina, a data and consultancy business for personalised nutrition, described how health, food, pharma and technology are converging, and what that means for brands.

Their first trend was discovery. Consumers now move between Google, ChatGPT and reviews before they buy; "Healthy Living" rose from 75th to 10th among uses of generative AI in a year; and Shopify's link with ChatGPT lets people buy inside the chat. Wearables, AI coaches and gyms are becoming places where health advice happens, and pharma, Bayer in particular, is moving into prevention.

Their second was GLP-1. Prescriptions to adults rose 586.7% over five years, and Abrahams said Europe is two to three years behind the US. One study found GLP-1 users short of vitamin K, magnesium, choline, iron, protein and fibre, though Abrahams stressed it was small and there is much to learn. Consumers will want help while on treatment, coming off it, or instead of it.

Their advice to brands: formulate for nutrient density, smaller appetites and changing body composition; find digital partners; show clinical proof through digital experiences; and lean into AI, because a world without websites and apps may be coming.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The number of adults prescribed a GLP-1 rose 586.7% over five years; Abrahams said about 70% are in the US and that some experts put Europe two to three years behind: "So the wave is forthcoming." [00:07] (slide 19).
- In a study of people on GLP-1 treatment, intake was low in vitamin K, magnesium, choline and iron, and low in protein and fibre; Abrahams called it one study of 60 people and said "we still have an awful lot to learn" [00:07] (slide 20).
- Consumers will look for solutions while on treatment, instead of it, or when coming off it, with concerns over muscle mass, lean mass and nutrient deficiency [00:07].
- AI is changing discovery: on Harvard Business Review's list, healthy living rose from number 75 to number 10 among generative AI uses in a year, and Shopify's ChatGPT link lets consumers buy without visiting a website [00:07] (slide 10) (slide 12).
- On Qina's tracking of features in personalised health solutions, the slide shows food logging (+20%), biomarker testing (+11%), habit tracking, and AI coaches and assistants (54%); Abrahams spoke of a rapid increase in AI coaches [00:07] (slide 14).
- Their four opportunities for brands: formulate better (nutrient density, smaller appetites, body composition, holistic health), partner better, create digital experiences that show clinical proof, and lean into AI (slide 25) (slide 26) (slide 27) (slide 28).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: the GLP-1 nutrient gaps Abrahams cited are categories we sell, and their formulation advice is the brief our customers will write.
- The gaps named were vitamin K, magnesium, choline, iron, protein and fibre (slide 20). My reading: BioK2 MK-7, our magnesium and iron bisglycinates, choline bitartrate and IsoClr: Pea together answer most of that list, for a GLP-1 companion pitch.
- "Create for smaller appetites & changes in body composition" (slide 25). My reading: low-dose, nutrient-dense formats suit us; protein that keeps lean mass on a small serving is the lead.
- The evidence base is thin, by their own words [00:07]. My reading: pitch the nutrient gaps as reported in a small study, not as a proven need.
- Discovery is moving into AI chat and agent shopping [00:07] (slide 12). My reading: our customers' brands, and our ingredient brands, need clear, citable evidence online for AI tools to find.

- Find Johnson et al 2025 and Mozzaffarian et al 2025 (as spelt on the slide) (the GLP-1 nutrient-gap papers on slide 20) and check the nutrients, sample size and wording before we use them.

summary.Detail:
- Qina combines "proprietary data, digital tools and domain expertise to help companies innovate faster and smarter" (slide 2).
- On their hype-cycle slide the technologies are agentic AI, generative AI, computer vision, natural language processing and machine learning; the trends are longevity, food as medicine, active nutrition, women's health, transparency, gut health and GLP-1 (slide 5). Abrahams said agentic AI is at the peak and GLP-1 has dipped as the drugs became widely available [00:07].
- Investment is flowing to DIY biomarker kits (vitamin D levels, for example), access to nutrition experts, smart eating and body-scan devices [00:07]. Notable 2025 investments on the slide include Bioniq, Superpower, Allora, Alba, Welltheory, Hormona, Nourish, Culina, Moom, Biohm, Epicore Biolinq, Aeon, Prenuvo and Habitual (slide 6).
- McKinsey 2025 segments: max optimizers 25% of consumers and 40% of wellness spend; confident enthusiasts 11% and 15%; health traditionalists 20% and 13%; health strugglers 24% and 20% (slide 7).
- Abrahams said younger consumers use ChatGPT as an assistant ("Shall I take my shape before exercise?"), older ones in place of Google; on Qina's data the number of solutions using generative AI had tripled by April 2025 [00:07] (slide 11).
- Partnerships: Dexcom and "aura" (as heard; glucose with sleep data), and a wearable company that pivoted into nutrition [00:07] (slide 15). Gyms are becoming places of health, with doctors, nutritionists and prescriptions inside [00:07].
- Bayer: bought a personalised supplement company for "two 50 million" and later sold it, launched a longevity offer (a genetic test, an app and a non-personalised supplement), bought an inflammatory bowel disease app, and bought top-selling Amazon supplements, which include botanicals [00:07] (slide 17).
- Levels of GLP-1 personalisation on their slide: GLP-1 companion products (food and ingredients), medical food, "phygital" products with generative or agentic AI, and digital plus biological, with digital twin technology (slide 21). Examples Abrahams gave: GLP-1-friendly labelled products, a doctor-prescribed medical food, a high-protein Abbott medical nutrition product, an agentic AI chatbot for GLP-1 users, a UK start-up selling prescription, drug and companion products together, and DNA plus microbiome tests to predict GLP-1 response [00:07].
- Abrahams said a body heard as "the American lifestyle Association" published guidance on behavioural, psychological, exercise and nutrition support for GLP-1 users, and that GLP-1 users adopt wearables and exercise more [00:07].
- Transparency: consumers scan everything, supplements and shakes included, with ingredient apps [00:07] (slide 22). Competition is shifting: consumers want simplicity and transparency, expect personalisation and demand proof of efficacy (slide 23).
- Looking ahead: virtual healthcare marketplaces where consumers upload their own data and ask what to buy, and tech companies' smart glasses pointing to "a world of no websites and no apps" [00:07] (slide 31).

Start and end times are not given; the day, 24 June 2025, is on the title slide, matches the recording's date and the programme (Day 2, "'Ageless' Consumption"). Then, like I said, customers are really educated. You will see, okay, what type of trial? Trial was it? Is it a high impact paper or not? How many times was it cited? What was the design? And it will give you a consensus on the yes or no scientific question. Really good tool. So yeah, to sum it up, longevity supplements are not your accuratizing minerals. They are in group molecules that target the farmers of aging, many of which are already present in our bodies that tend to decline with age, quality, safety, purity and science that dosage are really important to today's customers. summary.Summary:
Sophie Chabloz of AVEA, a Swiss longevity supplement brand, explained what longevity supplements are and how their customers choose them.

Chabloz set the biohackers aside. Bryan Johnson's 105 pills a day and Ray Kurzweil's 200 are not their market: their customers want to feel well for as long as possible, not to live to 150. No supplement has been proven to extend human lifespan, Chabloz said, but evidence for some molecules in healthy ageing grows every week. Several, such as NAD+, CoQ10 and collagen, decline with age and are hard to get from diet alone.

Their customers are mostly 45 to 65, and 70% are women. They are well read and demanding. They ask for third-party purity tests, read trials and check claims on PubMed and AI tools. They do not want tests or ingredient lists; they want their own problems solved. So AVEA tests every batch in a Swiss lab, uses evidence-based doses, runs its own studies and consumer tests, offers a broad range by need, and educates heavily.

Their closing advice was to cover the basics first: vitamin D3 and K2, omega-3, magnesium and methylated B vitamins. Without them, Chabloz said, customers will not feel the full effect of more advanced longevity supplements.

summary.Summary:
Marimiina Pykälistö, a certified nutritionist, presented nutritional genomics as the basis for a new generation of supplements. This summary comes from their deck alone; there is no recording.

Their starting point is that genes do not explain health or illness on their own: humans share 99.9% of their DNA, and lifestyle, environment and nutrition shape how genes are expressed. Pykälistö separates epigenetics, nutrigenomics (how nutrition affects gene expression) and nutrigenetics (how nutrition affects people with different genetic variations).

Food, in their framing, is information, not only calories. Cofactors are the building blocks of epigenetic change, epinutrients modulate epigenetic marks, and transcription factors control how DNA is read. Plant compounds act as epinutrients, with effects Pykälistö describes as balancing and short-lived, and they cannot replace cofactors. Common genetic variations change how much of each a person needs.

Their new generation supplements combine all three: cofactors, epinutrients and transcription-factor modulators. Their examples for metabolic health pair minerals and CoQ10 with botanicals such as berberine and cinnamon, and curcumin, vitamin D and resveratrol. Pykälistö ends on new tools for sequencing, nutrient-gene analysis and phenotyping as the future of healthcare.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Genes alone do not explain health: humans share 99.9% of DNA, and lifestyle, environment and nutrition shape gene expression ("Genes load the gun, lifestyle pulls the trigger") (slide 2).
- Nutrigenomics studies the effect of nutrition on gene expression; nutrigenetics how nutrition affects different genetic variations (slide 3).
- Food as information: cofactors, epinutrients and transcription factors work together, and genetic variations change how the body benefits from nutrients (slide 5) (slide 8).
- Plant compounds as epinutrients are "Multifactorial and polygenetic", "Balancing rather than one-directional" and "More short-lived than long-term", and cannot replace cofactors (slide 7).
- Their metabolic example combines cofactors (chrome, zinc, ALA, CoQ10, L-carnitine), epinutrients (berberine, acacia fiber, cinnamon) and transcription factors (curcumin, vitamin D, resveratrol), sourced to the Institute for Functional Medicine (slide 10).

- My reading: personalisation by genotype is the same direction as Nathan Price's talk (price-ai-scientific-wellness), from a practitioner rather than a cohort.

summary.Summary:
A short panel on the second day, chaired by Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients, with Mariette Abrahams (Qina), Marimiina Pykälistö (nutritionist and consulting advisor), Femke Hoevenaars (TNO) and a fourth panellist Otter does not name.

They agreed the field is moving from personalised nutrition to personalised health: lifestyle, mind and body, with tools that tell people what to do. Digital twins drew caution. Abrahams said fewer than five companies offer them and the term is used loosely; the others called them expensive, promising for research and not yet applicable.

On AI, Abrahams said it is spreading faster than the science and regulators can follow, and that advice built on unrepresentative data may not fit the individual. Weight remains the entry point, with GLP-1 users cycling on and off the drugs, but people link weight loss to energy, sleep and wider health, and a separate group wants longevity.

To build trust they called for transparency and plain explanations of why an ingredient helps. Asked for one change, Abrahams wanted proof of outcomes, Pykälistö statistics that show personalisation works, and the unnamed panellist a personal tool for health data.

- Personalised nutrition is becoming personalised health: "body of mind, soul nutrition" in Otter's words (Abrahams) and the whole lifestyle (Pykälistö) [00:42] [01:22].

summary.Summary:
Jane Durga of Balchem, speaking in the female athlete session, presented Balchem's branded ingredients for active women and its sports partnerships.

Durga opened with partnership: Balchem sponsors the FC Bayern Munich women's football team, paired on their slide with its vitamin K2 brand, K2VITAL, to raise awareness of women's health and create role models. Durga then walked through the range "on the field": K2VITAL for bones, heart and muscle; VitaCholine, choline for the brain-muscle connection; and Creatine MagnaPower, a creatine-magnesium blend that Durga said improves performance where creatine monohydrate plus magnesium did not. "Off the field" came OptiMSM for recovery.

Their nutrient-gap argument ran through iron, choline and folate. Athletes lose more iron than other people and may need up to 70% more; only 7% of US adult women get enough choline from food, and falling oestrogen at menopause limits the body's own choline supply. Chelated iron and methylfolate, Durga showed, are absorbed better than the common forms.

Their conclusion: women are helping shape and expand sports nutrition, and well-absorbed minerals, choline, K2, folate and MSM serve them through every life stage.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Only 7% of adult women in the US get enough choline from food and beverage (USDA, NHANES 2017 to March 2020) (slide 5).
- Choline in one study: targeting 9% closer and 2.6 times fewer misses in a visuomotor task against placebo (Naber et al. 2015) (slide 5).
- Oestrogen helps the body make choline and declines at menopause, so "For Menopausal Athletes, Ensuring Adequate Choline Intake is Important" (slide 6).
- The Institute of Medicine suggests the iron requirement "is up to 70% greater for those who engage in regular exercise" (slide 9).
- Absorption: Ferrochel iron bisglycinate 4.7 times higher than ferrous sulphate; L-5-MTHF 2.25 times higher plasma levels than folic acid (slide 10).
- Creatine MagnaPower, in one study, improved a performance measure that creatine monohydrate plus magnesium oxide did not (Brilla et al. 2003) (slide 7).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: no new science on our own brands, but Balchem competes with much of our range in exactly the women's and active-ageing positioning our customers are chasing.
- My reading, the overlap: K2VITAL against the BioK2 MK-7 we sell; Creatine MagnaPower against CreaWin; VitaCholine against our choline bitartrate; OptiMSM against our MSM; Ferrochel against our iron and magnesium bisglycinates; and L-5-MTHF against Advifolate.
- Their pitch is a nutrient gap plus a life stage plus a better-absorbed form (slide 6) (slide 10) (slide 11). My reading: the same structure works for our bisglycinates, choline and K2 in women's active nutrition, provided the claims are ones our customers can use in the EU; Balchem's own deck warns its claims may not suit marketing (slide 12).
- The team-sponsorship model (slide 3) is beyond our size; my reading, co-marketing with a customer's athlete partner is the realistic version.
- Related: the same female athlete session (women-in-sports-nutrition) and ostojic-creatine-lifelong-nutrition for creatine in women and ageing; Balchem's OptiMSM was also presented at Remedy CDMO 2026 (remedy-cdmo-2026/novosol-optimsm).

- "We need to champion women, listen to their voices with greater intent." (slide 3)
- "Choline transforms potential into performance as the champion of the mind -body connection." (slide 5)
- "Women are helping shape and expand the sport nutrition category." (slide 11)
- "MSM delivers recovery benefits – an overlooked aspect of performance nutrition." (slide 11)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Compare our BioK2, choline, MSM, bisglycinate and Advifolate claims files with Balchem's slides, for women's and menopause positioning in the EU (slide 4) (slide 5) (slide 10).
- Read Brilla et al. 2003 to see what the Creatine MagnaPower chart measures (slide 7).
summary.Detail:
- Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (12). The title slide names Durga and "Women’s Health" (slide 1). The closing slide says the information is for industry professionals, not consumers, that explicit or implied claims in it "may not necessarily be appropriate for marketing purposes", and is copyright 2024 Balchem (slide 12).
- K2VITAL, with the slide's hedges: MK-7 "may help trained athletes maintain maximal cardiac output during aerobic exercise"; K2 "supports ATP production"; K2 MK-7 "supports calcium uptake for strong bones and plays a role in the maintenance of bone mineral density" (slide 4). Slide 2 pairs K2VITAL with FC Bayern Munich Women as "The Perfect Pair" (slide 2).
- Choline is a component of cell membranes and of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, "critical for the connection between your brain and muscles"; it is found mainly in animal foods such as eggs and beef, and the body makes some but not enough (slide 5) (slide 6).
- Creatine MagnaPower: "a unique blend of creatine and magnesium" with "no loading phase required"; claims of improved cellular swelling and anabolic signalling, muscle power and torque, sprinting and bench press work capacity. The chart compares placebo, MgO plus creatine and Creatine MagnaPower before and after, with only Creatine MagnaPower significantly different from baseline; its y-axis is not labelled (slide 7).
- OptiMSM is "a source of sulfur", a component of glutathione; MSM supplementation "has been shown to" reduce oxidative stress after exercise, post-exercise pain and muscle damage, and improve the antioxidant response. The charts show lower pain change at 2 hours and lower exercise-related pain after leg extensions with OptiMSM 3,000 mg a day for 14 weeks (N=24, mean age 25.5) (slide 8).
- Athletes experience greater daily iron loss than the general population, especially in endurance sports such as running, rowing, HIIT, cycling and basketball; younger athletes need iron too (slide 9).
- Their five closing takeaways also include chelated minerals for "a time of lower micronutrient intake", choline for "cognition and active aging", and K2 and folate in "high quality, pure, stable forms"; Balchem names the NY Jets and FC Bayern Munich as team partners (slide 11).

detail.text: Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (12). The title slide names Durga and "Women’s Health" (slide 1). The closing slide says the information is for industry professionals, not consumers, that explicit or implied claims in it "may not necessarily be appropriate for marketing purposes", and is copyright 2024 Balchem (slide 12).

K2VITAL, with the slide's hedges: MK-7 "may help trained athletes maintain maximal cardiac output during aerobic exercise"; K2 "supports ATP production"; K2 MK-7 "supports calcium uptake for strong bones and plays a role in the maintenance of bone mineral density" (slide 4). Slide 2 pairs K2VITAL with FC Bayern Munich Women as "The Perfect Pair" (slide 2).

Choline is a component of cell membranes and of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, "critical for the connection between your brain and muscles"; it is found mainly in animal foods such as eggs and beef, and the body makes some but not enough (slide 5) (slide 6).

Creatine MagnaPower: "a unique blend of creatine and magnesium" with "no loading phase required"; claims of improved cellular swelling and anabolic signalling, muscle power and torque, sprinting and bench press work capacity. The chart compares placebo, MgO plus creatine and Creatine MagnaPower before and after, with only Creatine MagnaPower significantly different from baseline; its y-axis is not labelled (slide 7).

OptiMSM is "a source of sulfur", a component of glutathione; MSM supplementation "has been shown to" reduce oxidative stress after exercise, post-exercise pain and muscle damage, and improve the antioxidant response. The charts show lower pain change at 2 hours and lower exercise-related pain after leg extensions with OptiMSM 3,000 mg a day for 14 weeks (N=24, mean age 25.5) (slide 8).

Athletes experience greater daily iron loss than the general population, especially in endurance sports such as running, rowing, HIIT, cycling and basketball; younger athletes need iron too (slide 9).

Their five closing takeaways also include chelated minerals for "a time of lower micronutrient intake", choline for "cognition and active aging", and K2 and folate in "high quality, pure, stable forms"; Balchem names the NY Jets and FC Bayern Munich as team partners (slide 11).

The Institute of Medicine suggests the iron requirement "is up to 70% greater for those who engage in regular exercise" (slide 9).

sessions.to_check: No recording was found, so the summary is from the deck alone. The day and track are from the advance programme (Day 2, 24 June, "Active Nutrition and Health Weight Management"), not the final programme; start and end times are not given. The billed title is ours, from the deck's file name; the title slide reads "Rapid Weight Loss and Long-Term Outcomes" over "Emerging Research Challenges Established Views". Slides 9 and 21 are images (a table and a chart) read from the slide; slides 25 to 27 are unused template pages. The Copenhagen study's reference is shown only as a title (slide 20). The deck does not mention GLP-1 medicines; the GLP-1 theme is ours (my reading), though the programme's session block is about GLP-1 and weight management. Whether Nathan attended is not known.

summary.Summary:
Mark Gilbert, a nutritionist at The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Plan and former ESSNA vice chair, challenged two established views about rapid weight loss with total diet replacement (TDR): that it costs disproportionately more lean body mass, and that the weight comes back faster.

On lean mass, Gilbert showed that weight loss of any kind removes fat and lean mass in proportion to how much is lost, with or without exercise, and after bariatric surgery too. Exercise adds little to diet for weight or lean mass. Every study Gilbert found comparing rapid TDR with slower dieting seemed, Gilbert said, to show no greater loss of lean mass.

On regain, Gilbert cited the DROPLET trial and Susan Jebb: faster early loss did not lead to faster regain, and those who lost fast were more likely to reach their target. A Copenhagen study kept all of a 10 kg loss over three years of maintenance with meal replacements.

Gilbert closed by asking what lean mass is. Only about 40% is muscle; organs also shrink with weight loss, and that may be healthy. Calorie restriction also triggers autophagy, a cellular clean-up linked to longer lifespan in research from yeast to primates.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Weight loss reduces both fat and lean body mass "in proportion to degree of weight loss", usually even with exercise, and bariatric surgery does the same (slide 6).
- Their conclusion on lean mass: "all of the comparator studies I found seem to disprove the idea that rapid, substantial weight loss (with TDR) causes greater LBM loss" (slide 16).
- In the TEMPO trial (101 postmenopausal women with obesity), severe restriction for 4 months gave twice the weight and fat loss of moderate restriction for 12 months, about 1.5 times as much lean mass loss, and no greater adverse effect on relative lean mass or grip strength (slide 12).
- On regain, Gilbert said experts now believe the idea that fast loss means fast regain "is a myth", citing DROPLET and Susan Jebb: the rapid group "were more likely to achieve their target weight loss and more likely to stick with the programme" (slide 18) (slide 19).
- Only about 40% of lean body mass is muscle; other organs shrink with weight loss, and "it may be healthy for these other organs to shrink" (slide 22).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: TDR and meal replacement products are a protein-led format, and their argument answers the muscle-loss worry that drives much of the weight-management protein story (slide 16). My reading: their data are a counterpoint brands will hear.
- Their view differs from the muscle-protection message heard elsewhere: GLP-1 users' named need is protecting muscle (beyond-the-glp-1-boom-nutrition, from-hype-to-healthspan-building-the). Both are valid; Gilbert argues lean mass loss is proportionate and partly not muscle, and does not discuss GLP-1 medicines (slide 22). My reading: pitch protein and creatine for muscle on its own evidence, not on a claim that rapid weight loss uniquely wastes muscle.
- Cambridge Weight Plan's 1:1 Diet is a TDR brand (slide 2). My reading: a possible customer for proteins and other meal-replacement ingredients.
summary.Quotes:
- "Research “shows clearly that the common claim that more rapid initial weight loss is associated with more rapid regain is false…" Susan Jebb, as quoted on Gilbert's slide (slide 19)
- "Experts now believe this is a myth" (slide 18)
- "Furthermore, it may be healthy for these other organs to shrink…" (slide 22)
summary.Follow-ups:
- The Copenhagen maintenance study's full reference and results (slide 20).
- Cambridge Weight Plan's 1:1 Diet as a contact for meal-replacement ingredients (slide 2), my reading.
summary.Detail:
- Their roles: nutritionist at The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Plan; Science Committee at TDMR Europe; BASc (Nutrition), RNutr, CISSN; sports nutrition consultant on formulas, labels and regulation; pharma and clinical nutrition; former ESSNA vice chair; advisory board and columnist for M&F, Flex and Muscle Insider; co-founder of Fitness Genes and GoMetabolic (slide 2).
- Why lean mass matters: it is associated with healthy ageing, mobility, avoiding falls, survival and a higher metabolic rate, "BUT…Muscle is only one component of LBM" (slide 5).
- Exercise: used for weight loss it usually reduces lean mass; with diet it adds small, often insignificant effects; sustained supervised exercise gives about 2 kg loss (Wing, 1999) (slide 7).
- Weinheimer 2010 review: with diet, 75% of groups lost 5 to 10 kg; diet and exercise both left over 75% of groups losing 0 to 40% of fat-free mass; exercise gave under 5% loss in 94% of studies and 15% gained fat-free mass (slide 8) (slide 9).
- Bariatric surgery: 25 to 33% of loss as lean mass just over a year after surgery (Zalesin, 2010), rising with greater weight loss; up to at least 35% (Haghighat, 2021) (slide 10).
- Coxon 1989: women losing 1.9 kg a week against 1.1 kg a week over 8 weeks lost 0.42 and 0.44 of their weight as fat-free mass (slide 13).
- Coutinho 2018: 35 adults with obesity, 550 kcal TDR for 4 weeks against 1,200 to 1,500 kcal for 8 weeks; both lost about 9% of weight, with similar fat and fat-free mass loss, at 2.2 and 1.2 kg a week; in a one-month maintenance phase the rapid group significantly increased fat-free mass (slide 14).
- Ard 2016: 28 older adults with BMI over 35, 500 kcal deficit against 960 kcal TDR; total lean mass loss did not differ significantly (slide 15).
- DROPLET (University of Oxford, The BMJ): doctor referral of people with overweight to low-energy TDR (slide 18).
- Copenhagen study in people with knee osteoarthritis: intensive 800 kcal weight loss of 10 kg at 1 year, then 3 years of maintenance in 109 people with meal replacements or intermittent use; "Maintained 100% of weight loss – most successful LT weight maintenance study?" (slide 20). The chart shows mean body weight over 156 weeks (slide 21).
- Organ loss: DEXA, MRI and four-compartment research shows several organs beyond muscle shrink with weight loss of 9.5 kg (Bosy-Westphal, 2009) (slide 22).
- Autophagy: calorie restriction triggers it, and research on fasting and calorie restriction shows it "can help incr lifespan of everything from yeast & flies to primates" (Madeo 2015; Balasubramanian 2017) (slide 23).

Rapid Weight Loss, Lean Body Mass &
Weight-Loss Maintenance
• Is rapid weight loss counterproductive?
