Does rapid weight loss (TDR) cause
disproportionately greater loss of LBM &
Weight Regain?
• Studies comparing rapid vs moderate weight loss
• Other data on LBM losses
• Why some LBM loss may be desirable & healthy

--- page 5 ---
Why is LBM Important?
• LBM is associated with healthy aging
• Mobility
• Avoiding falls
• More robust survivability
• LBM is associated with a higher metabolic rate
• BUT…Muscle is only one component of LBM

--- page 6 ---
Rapid Weight Loss, TDR & LBM?
• Broadly, weight loss reduces both body fat (BF) and lean
body mass (LBM)
• It does so in proportion to degree of weight loss
• Even usually when combined with exercise
• Bariatric surgery has a similar effect

--- page 7 ---
Exercise & LBM?
• When used for weight loss, exercise usually reduces LBM
• When combined with diet, Ex has small, often
insignificant additive effects on weight loss or LBM
• Sustained, supervised exercise results in modest weight
loss (~2kg) (Wing, 1999)
Wing RR. Physical activity in the treatment of the adulthood overweight and obesity:
current evidence and research issues. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 1999 Nov;31(11 Suppl):S547-52

--- page 8 ---
Exercise & LBM?
• Systematic review of studies on Ex, Ex + Diet & Diet alone (Weinheimer,
2010)
• Exercise & diet both resulted in >75% of subject groups losing from 0-
40% FFM
• Diet = loss of 5-10kg in 75% of groups
• Exercise resulted in < 5% loss in 94% of studies; 15% gained FFM
Weinheimer EM, et al. A systematic review of the separate and combined effects of energy restriction
and exercise on fat-free mass in middle-aged and older adults: implications for sarcopenic obesity. Nutr
Rev. 2010 Jul;68(7):375-88

--- page 9 ---
Exercise & LBM?
Weinheimer, 2010

--- page 10 ---
Bariatric Surgery & LBM?
• Just over a year after surgery, 25-33% of losses were as LBM (Zalesin,
2010)
• Increasing proportion of LBM loss with > weight loss over one year
• Up to at least 35% LBM loss (Haghighat, 2021)
Zalesin KC, et al. Differential loss of fat and lean mass in the morbidly obese after bariatric surgery.
Metab Syndr Relat Disord. 2010 Feb;8(1):15-20.
Neda Haghighat, et al. Long-term effect of bariatric surgery on body composition in patients with
morbid obesity: A systematic review and meta-analysis,Clinical Nutrition, Volume 40, Issue 4, 2021, Pages
1755-1766.

--- page 11 ---
Does rapid weight loss (TDR) cause
disproportionately greater loss of LBM?
• Several studies have
looked at rapid weight loss
(with TDR) vs gradual
weight loss…

--- page 12 ---
Does rapid weight loss (food vs TDR) cause
disproportionately greater loss of LBM?
• In 101 Obese, PM Women: CR of ~30% x 12 mo. vs ~70% x 4 mo. (TDR)
• 2-fold greater weight and fat loss, approximately 1.5 times as much loss of
whole-body lean mass
• “Severe energy restriction had no greater adverse effect on relative whole-
body lean mass or handgrip strength compared with moderate energy
restriction and was associated with 2-fold greater weight and fat loss over 12
months”
Seimon R.V. Effect of weight loss via severe vs moderate energy restriction on lean mass and body composition among
postmenopausal women with obesity: the TEMPO diet randomized clinical trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2019;2(10)

Does rapid weight loss (TDR) cause
disproportionately greater loss of LBM?
• Female subjects Rapid (1.9 kg/week) vs Moderate (1.1 kg/week) over
8 weeks
• Proportion of weight loss as FFM
• Rapid = FFM/Wt loss of 0.42 vs Moderate = 0.44
Coxon A, et al. Rapid weight loss and lean tissue: evidence for comparable body composition and metabolic rate in differing
rates of weight loss. Int J Obes. 1989;13 Suppl 2:179-81.)

Does rapid weight loss with TDR cause
disproportionately greater loss of LBM?
• 35 Obese Adults; 550 (TDR) x 4 wk vs 1200-1500 kcal x 8 wk
• Both had signiﬁcant & similar weight loss (~9%, P <0.001 for both
groups)
• Fat Mass & FFM losses were also similar
• RWL group lost weight at a rate of 2.2 kg/w Gradual = 1.2 kg/week

<0.001)

1162.

Does rapid weight loss (TDR) cause
disproportionately greater loss of LBM?
• 500kcal deficit diet vs 960kcal TDR; 28 older adults, >35 BMI
• Total lean mass loss was not significantly different between groups
Ard JD, et al. Impact on weight and physical function of intensive medical weight loss in older
adults with stage II and III obesity. Obesity (Silver Spring). 2016;24(9):1861-1866.

--- page 16 ---
Does rapid weight loss with TDR cause
disproportionately greater loss of LBM?
• So all of the comparator studies I found seem to disprove the idea that
rapid, substantial weight loss (with TDR) causes greater LBM loss

--- page 17 ---
What about weight regain?

Rapid weight loss (TDR…) results in
greater weight loss at 1 year
• Often thought that fast, dramatic weight loss increases the risk
of weight re-gain.

Rapid weight loss (TDR…) results in

free mass (FFM)

• The rest is bone, skin, other organs, water & even some essential

damaged organelles and proteins as it improves the metabolic fitness
of cells”

On regain, Gilbert said experts now believe the idea that fast loss means fast regain "is a myth", citing DROPLET and Susan Jebb: the rapid group "were more likely to achieve their target weight loss and more likely to stick with the programme" (slide 18) (slide 19).
Only about 40% of lean body mass is muscle; other organs shrink with weight loss, and "it may be healthy for these other organs to shrink" (slide 22).

"Experts now believe this is a myth" (slide 18)
"Furthermore, it may be healthy for these other organs to shrink…" (slide 22)

followups: The Copenhagen maintenance study's full reference and results (slide 20).
Cambridge Weight Plan's 1:1 Diet as a contact for meal-replacement ingredients (slide 2), my reading.

summary.Summary:
A panel in the second day's Female Athlete session on nutrition for active women. The recording starts after the introductions; matched to the programme, the panel was Steffen Oesser (CRI), on collagen peptide studies; James Morton (SiS); the sports dietitian Renee McGregor; and the doctor Nicky Keay (UCL). The chair is not named.

The panel agreed that the old rigid rules for each day of the menstrual cycle have no evidence behind them. Recent studies, Morton said, largely show no difference in substrate use across the cycle, so the advice is back to fundamentals: fuel consistently, treat each woman as an individual, and coach rather than instruct. McGregor's main message was to stop demonising carbohydrates; Keay called a regular period "a free monthly medical check" and warned that missing ovulation can hide behind normal-looking cycles.

Oesser said research in women is growing and described studies of specific collagen peptides on tendons and ligaments, body composition, endurance in women and bone density in women, with results Oesser called outstanding and very promising.

Asked for one nutrient, Keay chose vitamin D across the lifespan, Morton iron for athletes, and McGregor none: needs come first.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Recent studies largely show no difference in substrate metabolism across the menstrual cycle, Morton said; day-by-day cycle rules have no evidence, so fuel consistently [01:22] [13:50].
- Oesser described studies of specific collagen peptides on ligaments and tendons (with a men-and-women analysis), on body composition alongside training, and on endurance in women only, with an "extra benefit" over placebo when combined with training [09:55].
- Oesser also described a published study on bone density in women: one controlled year, then open-label follow-up to four years, where loss stopped and density rose; a second study with two controlled years is "very promising", final results awaited [22:45].
- Keay: in the luteal phase progesterone slightly raises metabolic rate, so women may need a little more food; in a year-long study of dancers, many with periods were not ovulating or made too little progesterone [14:59] [20:48].
- One nutrient each: vitamin D throughout the lifespan (Keay), iron especially for endurance athletes (Morton), none without a needs analysis (McGregor) [25:05] [26:44] [27:46].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Collagen peptide research in women is cited for tendons, body composition, endurance and bone [09:55] [22:45]. My reading: collagen for active women has a science story, though the product and the studies are not named in the recording (Oesser directs CRI, the Collagen Research Institute, per the programme); find them before using any of it.
- Vitamin D and iron were the two nutrients panellists would recommend [26:44] [27:46]. My reading: pair them with protein or collagen in women's active formats.
- The experts' message is fundamentals and individual needs, not cycle-syncing products [01:22] [25:05]. My reading: avoid pitching menstrual-phase claims to brands; they are the myths this panel set out to bust.
- Relevance is medium: women's sports nutrition is the growth group Euromonitor named the day before (euromonitor-sports-nutrition-trends), but the panel spoke little about ingredients we sell.
summary.Quotes:
- "...we have to stop demonizing carbohydrates." Speaker 2 (Renee McGregor, as matched to the programme) [25:28]
- "...it's a free monthly medical check." Speaker 3 (Nicky Keay, as matched to the programme) [20:48]
- "Actually, the only absolute supplement is vitamin D throughout the lifespan, because not only is it good for your well being, but it's also good for your bone health, also good for muscle recovery..." Speaker 3 (Nicky Keay, as matched to the programme) [26:44]
- "And probably we're not getting enough iron, especially endurance athletes." Speaker 4 (James Morton) [27:46]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Find Oesser's collagen peptide studies (tendons and ligaments, body composition, endurance in women, bone density in women) and the product behind them [09:55] [22:45].
- Identify Morton's earlier talk; find Morton's survey of about 600 female athletes [13:50].
- Find Keay's study of dancers over a year of training (subclinical ovulatory disturbance) [20:48].

# Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

## "Women in Sports Nutrition" (https://otter.ai/u/8wiNhrRgQVxL7wdV_aE6giPhSUo)

The discussion focused on the growing research focus on women in sports, emphasizing the need for individualized approaches rather than rigid protocols. Key points included the importance of psychological factors, the impact of the menstrual cycle on performance, and the need to address myths and misinformation. Studies highlighted the benefits of collagen peptides on ligaments, tendons, and body composition, and the importance of carbohydrates and vitamin D for female athletes. The conversation also stressed the need for better education and communication to improve athlete engagement and performance, and the role of coaches in guiding athletes towards better choices.

Action items:
- Speaker 0 - : Investigate the effects of specific collagen peptides on ligaments, tendons, body composition, and endurance in women.
- Speaker 1 - : Empower women athletes to understand their own bodies and menstrual cycle changes, rather than just providing data.
- Speaker 1 - : Ensure women athletes maintain adequate carbohydrate availability throughout their menstrual cycle to help stabilize energy levels and performance.
- Speaker 2 - : Consider vitamin D as a key supplement for women across the lifespan due to its benefits for bone health, muscle recovery, and immune function.
- Speaker 3 - : Improve education of coaches and nutrition experts on communicating effectively with women athletes and understanding individual needs.

detail.text: Attribution: Speaker 1 is "Stefan" and Speaker 4 is "James", from how the chair and panel address them; Speaker 2 (the sports dietitian) mentions "Nikki" and Speaker 3 (the doctor) mentions "Rene" and "Greg". Matched to the programme's Female Athlete speakers, they are Oesser, Morton, McGregor and Keay; the chair is Speaker 5 (see to_check). Much of Oesser's audio is garbled in Otter, so Oesser's figures are not given here.

Oesser said that in the past most studies were in men because a simple model avoids hormonal changes, and that this "now seems to switch", with more research focused on women in the pipeline [00:00] [09:55].

Oesser's collagen peptide study on ligaments and tendons: "high effect size" and a benefit for professional athletes and "weekend warriors" (Otter's words) [09:55]. On body composition: "it's not enough to take this ingredient and sit on the couch"; training is needed [09:55].

The bone study, as Oesser said it: progressive bone loss "stopped. It goes in the other direction"; not "turning the clock back to zero"; Oesser suggested it may delay the problems of bone loss by years (Otter's figure is garbled) [22:45].

McGregor: women need equity, not only equality, in protocols [00:12]; practitioners need nuance, and social media spreads misinformation [03:13]; understand why an athlete fears carbohydrates or body changes [07:37]; every cycle differs with stress and travel, and knowing your own body is "the biggest gift we can give women" [17:35]; maintain carbohydrate availability, liquid or real food, for steadier performance [19:31]; too much monitoring is "creating more health anxiety" [25:28].

Morton: change the people around an athlete, not only the athlete; "We're coaches" [05:21]. Morton's group surveyed about 600 female athletes; the biggest symptom was cramps (Otter: "crabs"), and low-fibre carbohydrate can keep fuelling on bad days [13:50]. Morton was surprised how little athletes knew about female physiology [19:09].

Keay: hormonal contraception largely flattens the cycle's hormones, which many women do not realise [14:59]; loss of periods (functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea, heard as "FHA function, hyper NRA") is a "big red flag" for low energy availability [20:48].
McGregor said national bodies refer players out to McGregor and a colleague heard as "Nikki" (taken as Keay) when in-house communication fails [07:37].
The Otter recording's own summary is filed as received (files/otter-summary.md).

takeaways.text: Recent studies largely show no difference in substrate metabolism across the menstrual cycle, Morton said; day-by-day cycle rules have no evidence, so fuel consistently [01:22] [13:50].

Oesser described studies of specific collagen peptides on ligaments and tendons (with a men-and-women analysis), on body composition alongside training, and on endurance in women only, with an "extra benefit" over placebo when combined with training [09:55].

Oesser also described a published study on bone density in women: one controlled year, then open-label follow-up to four years, where loss stopped and density rose; a second study with two controlled years is "very promising", final results awaited [22:45].

Keay: in the luteal phase progesterone slightly raises metabolic rate, so women may need a little more food; in a year-long study of dancers, many with periods were not ovulating or made too little progesterone [14:59] [20:48].
One nutrient each: vitamin D throughout the lifespan (Keay), iron especially for endurance athletes (Morton), none without a needs analysis (McGregor) [25:05] [26:44] [27:46].

quotes.text: "...we have to stop demonizing carbohydrates." Speaker 2 (Renee McGregor, as matched to the programme) [25:28]
"...it's a free monthly medical check." Speaker 3 (Nicky Keay, as matched to the programme) [20:48]

"Actually, the only absolute supplement is vitamin D throughout the lifespan, because not only is it good for your well being, but it's also good for your bone health, also good for muscle recovery..." Speaker 3 (Nicky Keay, as matched to the programme) [26:44]
"And probably we're not getting enough iron, especially endurance athletes." Speaker 4 (James Morton) [27:46]

followups: Find Oesser's collagen peptide studies (tendons and ligaments, body composition, endurance in women, bone density in women) and the product behind them [09:55] [22:45].
Identify Morton's earlier talk; find Morton's survey of about 600 female athletes [13:50].
Find Keay's study of dancers over a year of training (subclinical ovulatory disturbance) [20:48].

sessions.title: Branding that moves the right consumer in Active Nutrition
sessions.track: Navigating the Noise: Essential Insights on Marketing, Regulation, and Social Media
sessions.to_check: Day and track are from the advance programme (Day 3, 25 June, "Navigating the Noise"), not the final programme; start and end times, whether Veenstra presented alone or in the session's panel, and who attended for Vita Actives are unknown; no recording was found. The deck's own title slide reads "Built for Trust: Branding that moves the right consumer in Active Nutrition" (slide 4). The creatine on Upfront's creatine tabs pack (brand or grade) cannot be read from the slide.

summary.Summary:
Marit Veenstra, a brand and innovation strategist at HMT, the Healthy Marketing Team, argued that active nutrition brands lose sales to confusion, not to weak science. Shoppers face too many options and unclear benefits, and many walk away without buying. Most launches fail, Veenstra said, because no one understood, trusted or felt anything for them.

Their answer is HMT's FourFactors: a consumer must see who needs the product, accept the ingredient, understand the benefit and trust the brand. The factors sit on an adoption curve that runs from technology and lifestyle buyers to the early mass market and the mass market. Niche trends start with low awareness; embedded trends are familiar to everyone.

Veenstra then split active consumers into four mindsets: professional athletes driven by need and proof, fitness influencers driven by beliefs and novelty, recreational sportspeople who want easy solutions, and "daily strollers" who want what is normal and familiar. Each needs its own message and its own kind of proof. Their examples were Upfront's protein matcha, sold in Dutch-language packs, and Heinz's lycopene drink.

Their conclusion: know where to play and how to win, and translate the message as a product moves from medical to trend to mass market.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Shoppers are confused: 73% feel overwhelmed by too many choices, 72% are confused by how benefits are explained, and 74% have walked away without buying (Consumer Pulse Survey 2024, Waitrose 2024) (slide 6).
- 80% of new launches fail within 12 months, Veenstra said, not for weak science but because no one understood, trusted or felt anything for them (slide 8).
- The FourFactors test for a concept: who needs it, is the ingredient accepted, is the benefit understood, is the brand trusted (slide 11) (slide 34).
- There is not one active consumer but four mindsets, Need, Want, Solution and Normal, each with its own message and trust strategy (slide 19) (slide 35).
- The professional athlete wants scientific proof, health claims and rational branding; the daily stroller wants taste, no change in habit and a mass-price brand (slide 20) (slide 23).
- Crossing from medical to trend to mass market needs different messages, benefits and proof at each step (slide 35).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance medium: a marketing framework, not ingredient science, but it is the lens our customers' brand teams use to judge an ingredient. Factor 2, "accept the ingredient", is where we sit (slide 11). My reading: our pitch decks should say which mindset an ingredient serves, with proof matched to it.
- Their Upfront example pairs 20g protein with matcha for "natural caffeine + L-theanine" energy and clarity, and Upfront also sells creatine tabs (slide 25) (slide 26). My reading: we sell matcha and creatine (CreaWin); Upfront is worth checking as a customer, starting with the creatine in its tabs.
- Their Heinz case puts lycopene in a fruit drink under a trusted food brand (slide 29). My reading: we sell lycopene (LycoLex); their point is that a familiar brand carries an unfamiliar ingredient into the mass market.
- HMT also presented on the probiotics category at Remedy CDMO 2026, the same speaker, as Nathan confirmed (remedy-cdmo-2026/hmt-probiotic-market); the misinformation side of this summit's marketing theme is millbank-nutrition-by-algorithm, and the regulatory side bucchini-essna-regulatory-update.
summary.Quotes:
- "Not because the science was wrong." (slide 8)
- "I don’t care about hype — I need products that are proven, precise, and built to support my performance." (slide 20)
- "I like what I know. I just want something that fits into my day without changing anything" (slide 23)
- "Technology without storytelling stays invisible" (slide 35)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Check Upfront (Dutch-language packs) as a customer for creatine, matcha and protein; the creatine in its tabs is not legible on the slide (slide 25).
- Find the Consumer Pulse Survey 2024 and Waitrose 2024 sources behind the confusion figures (slide 6).
- Their contact is on the closing slide (slide 35); HMT offers a FourFactors analysis.
summary.Detail:
- Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (36). Small print on the framework images reads "Confidential © 2026 All rights reserved to HMT" and credits "Wennström's FourFactors® Brand Acceleration System ©2008", read from the images (slide 14) (slide 16).
- HMT says it has worked with over 500 brands in 60+ markets, and offers insights, strategy and positioning, brand building, and design (slide 2) (slide 3).
- Why confusion stops a purchase: trade-off stress, mental fatigue that leads people to default to the familiar "or nothing at all", and preference uncertainty (slide 7).
- The 80% failure figure is sourced to Richard Howells, Forbes, July 2011 (slide 8).
- The purchase decision is made "in a few seconds" at the shelf (slide 10). Factors 1 and 3 are "factors of motivation", factors 2 and 4 "factors of permission" (slide 11).
- The adoption chart has three lines: consumer awareness and volume (rising, then falling in the mass market), price and margin (falling over time), and a flat line for an innovation consumers do not pick up. Its strategy row reads NC, NSC, WCS, LHNA and FFMO, not spelled out on the slides (slide 14) (slide 16).
- Trends: niche trends enter with low awareness, emerging trends head towards the early mass market, embedded trends are familiar to all in the mass market (slide 16). The sticky notes on their title image read "individual health", "protein shift" and "gut health" (slide 13).
- Fitness influencers want products that fit them, match their values, are trendy, inspire them and make them feel special; recreational sportspeople want familiar, convenient, tasty products that fit their routines (slide 21) (slide 22).
- Upfront's FourFactors: need shown by an active young woman, the ingredient matcha, the benefits "20g protein = supports muscle maintenance" and matcha for "sustained energy + mental clarity", and trust in the Upfront brand. Veenstra placed the product among technology stakeholders on the curve (slide 26) (slide 27).
- Heinz: the Sunshine drink rests on lycopene and the Heinz Tomato Ketchup brand; Veenstra asked where it sits on the curve, then showed what works for ketchup: renovations, convenience, and a no-added-sugar-and-salt version with "NO compromise on taste" (slide 29) (slide 30) (slide 31).
- Their six closing takeouts: confused consumers walk away; most innovations fail due to irrelevance; trends do not matter until they matter to your consumer; four mindsets; technology without storytelling stays invisible; crossing the chasm requires translation (slide 35).

# Cognitive Health: transcript
Source: Otter.ai recording "Kristiina Singer - Biogena - Cognitive Health", https://otter.ai/u/qYyEK3MJwJxKwGyXPipF0GXfkiA, recorded 25 June 2025 (Otter's clock time is not the local time, so none is given), 30m 37s. Speaker labels are Otter's.

[00:00] Olivia Haslam - NutraIngredients: Pill as interest in mind, health remains the key concern for white demographic of consumers. The impact of nutrition on mental health has expanded massively in recent years, and with that, the industry enjoy has enjoyed a bit of an area such as CBD, mushrooms, botanicals, probiotics, Psych biotics, immersing benefits, including sleep quality, stress reduction, good modulation and improve focus. So first up to introduce the topic for cognitive health, the consumer interest on scientific backing, preserving nutrition to support the brain, we have Christina, singer, an expert, a scientific expert in clinical nutrition and supplements, working with Austrian biohacking Plaza and supplements brand biogene group. So please, welcome to stage Christina,
[00:50] Kristiina Singer (BIOGENA): good morning to everyone. I'm happy to start the third and the last day here. It's our first time to attend to Summit. So I'm glad to be here. Thank you very much for finding us and inviting us. Yeah, my name is Christina singer, and I am a clinical nutritionist. I was trained in intermolecular medicine and functional nutrition medicine, and I've been working with Fauci now for over 10 years now, and I'm still totally fascinated by the idea of automolecular medicine, also by by Gina, of course, otherwise I wouldn't be here so long, but especially by automolecular medicine. And as Carl Pfeiffer wants to say, that for every drug, for every medical drug that benefits a person, there is a natural substance, what can achieve the same effect. And today, we are here to unlock our transportation using some natural substances. That's my topic for today. You also probably want to keep your phones close by, because I'm going to use the slido function later on for some questions, also for you. But let's start first. For those who don't know, biochina, we are an Austrian company, and you can also find us in Vienna. So use the possibility that you are here and visit our flagship store by chi Nathan Plaza, right next to State Opera. It's very easy to find great ways to State Opera. Afternoon you have free time go and take a look. Because we of course, have there our store with high quality supplements we offer, but we also have our biogeon diagnostic with doctors working there with laboratory testing possibilities, also infusion packages and also our bio hacking area. We offer cryotherapy, as you can see, also in the picture here, bone density check ups using the ultrasound videos, or offer daily oxygen training, high altitude training, masks, light therapy and so on. So health is for us more than just the supplements. Of course, this is our main business, but it's more than only supplements. But we really are an Austrian family business since 20 years, we produce our supplements ourselves inside. Austria, near Salzburg. You can see the picture of our production site near Salzburg. You can always go there and also visit the production and see how we produce. We have over 300 different products, high quality supplements, and what's important for us is the quality. So we have a biggest scientific team in the industry, 20 different scientists from different areas, working in the scientific team. summary.Summary:
Kristiina Singer, a clinical nutritionist who has worked for Biogena for over ten years, opened the summit's last day with the case for natural cognitive support. Biogena is an Austrian family company that makes its own supplements near Salzburg and runs a flagship store in Vienna.

Their argument started with demand. Cognitive health is no longer only a concern of older people: in US data Singer showed, memory loss is the health problem adults under 40 fear most, and in Germany dementia is feared second only to cancer. Dementia cases are expected to reach 75 million worldwide by 2030 and roughly double by 2050.

Singer then turned to diet. The MIND diet, built on the Mediterranean and DASH diets and rich in berries and leafy greens, was linked in one study to a cognitive age 7.5 years younger. Polyphenols, and anthocyanins in particular, may help through new neurons, synaptic plasticity and protection against oxidative stress. Citicoline, a precursor of acetylcholine that crosses the blood-brain barrier, showed memory and attention effects in old and young people.

Biogena combines both, with activated B vitamins, in one product. Its sales are growing; over 60% of buyers are over 45, and about 16% are aged 25 to 35.

- Cognitive health is a concern for younger adults too: in US data from 2022, memory loss is the health problem people under 40 fear most [00:50].
- A high MIND diet score was associated in one study with a cognitive age 7.5 years younger; Singer framed polyphenols as central to the diet [00:50].
- Polyphenol studies Singer showed: 12 weeks of a blueberry powder standardised to 302 mg anthocyanins in 61 people over 65 improved flow-mediated dilation, systolic blood pressure and immediate recall; a single 600 mg dose of a polyphenol-rich extract in 30 students aged 18 to 25 gave more correct answers and fewer errors than placebo [00:50].
- Citicoline studies Singer showed: brain ATP up 13.6% and membrane turnover up 26% in one study; better attention and psychomotor speed and less impulsivity in 75 healthy males aged 13 to 18; better overall and episodic memory in older adults [00:50].
- Biogena's citicoline, polyphenol and activated-B-vitamin product is its fastest-growing: over 60% of buyers are over 45, and about 16% are 25 to 35 [00:50].

summary.Summary:
Two NutraIngredients hosts, Lauren Nicolle and Olivia Haslam, closed the summit with a six-minute run through what they had heard over three days.

They went through the programme roughly in order. Protein is still big, with hydration supplements rising in the US. There is a gap between how worried people are about sleep and how many buy sleep products. GLP-1 remains a major topic, with brands labelling products as supporting GLP-1 and the question of whether they have the right to make that claim.

From the female athlete session they took the culture of carbohydrate fear and a finding that the menstrual cycle may matter less than thought. Gut health and performance, personalisation, wearables that could mean fewer doctor visits, and a move from "healthy ageing" to "ageless" language followed. Cellular health, beauty from within and recovery were rising. Creatine as a possible semi-essential nutrient, regulation that makes it hard for brands to say what they want, and functional mushrooms rounded it off.

Haslam named active parenting as a space to watch; Nicolle suggested it for next year.

summary.Summary:
Sunna Van Kampen, founder and CEO of Tonic Health, a UK supplement brand, talked with Olivia Haslam of NutraIngredients about building a brand almost entirely on social media.

Van Kampen started the business during COVID after finding that most supermarket supplements were dosed too low to correct deficiencies. Their products use what they called the right doses, without sugar, sweeteners or additives. Science-heavy podcasts and newsletters did not work: focus groups showed customers had no time for them. What did work was short videos, under 60 seconds, telling people to swap one product for another and why. After 10 to 15 TikTok posts, one reached 250,000 views; the brand now gets 50 million views a month.

Their case is that consumers buy supplements on trust and awareness, so click-through rates per post miss the point; they credit the brand's growth entirely to social media. They never make medical claims, but argue the ASA holds back science, and that regulators should focus on safety and fake products, such as a creatine brand found to contain no creatine.

Next come recipe content and a podcast with Channel Four.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The brand's origin: most supermarket supplements were "such low dose" that they did little; Tonic set out to give "the right doses" without sugar, sweeteners and additives [01:11].
- Science content did not reach consumers; under-60-second "swap this for this" videos did, starting on TikTok [02:43] [04:41].
- They do not promote their own products on social media: it is now entertainment media, where the best content wins regardless of followers [05:22].
- Supplements are bought on trust and awareness, so per-post sales tracking is "a big waste of time"; a team of six grew the brand on social media alone [06:42].
- Regulation should target safety and fraud: they cited 75% of mushroom brands on Amazon not containing the mushroom, and a creatine brand with about 10 million in sales and no creatine in it [13:06].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Their pitch rests on proper doses against under-dosed supermarket products [01:11]. My reading: brands like this need ingredients they can dose at study levels and explain simply.
- The creatine fraud example [13:06]. My reading: tested, traceable creatine with a certificate of analysis per batch is a selling point for CreaWin with brands worried about their reputation.
- Social media brands are held to account by their audience on formulation and claims [08:11]. My reading: clean labels and claims we can support protect our customers as well as us.

Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Sunna, founder and CEO of Tonic Health, discussed the company's journey from creating high-quality, functional supplements to building a strong social media presence. Initially, they focused on educating consumers about nutrition through short, digestible videos on TikTok, which led to viral content and significant brand growth. Despite low click-through rates on social media posts, Tonic's strategy of building top-of-funnel awareness has driven their success. Sunna emphasized the importance of consumer trust and engagement, noting that their content aims to help people improve their health through practical advice and transparent communication. They also plan to expand into recipe content and a podcast to further support consumer health.

## Action items
- Sunna - : Launch the Tonic Health podcast in partnership with Channel Four.
- Tonic Health - : Engage with the Tonic Health community by having the in-house nutritionist respond to direct messages.

summary.Summary:
Eric Puro, co-founder and CEO of Nordic Mushrooms, which makes mushroom extracts in Finland, made the case for functional mushrooms in brain health and then warned that much of the market does not contain what its labels say.

Puro opened with growth: their slides put the global functional mushroom market on course for $65B by 2030. Their lead example was lion's mane for the brain: Puro presented nerve growth factor and BDNF as the mechanism, and their company's human trial in healthy adults, which their slide says showed better working memory, complex attention and reaction time, with effects building week on week where caffeine's fade.

Then the problem. In an Italian study, 13 of 19 mushroom supplements did not contain the listed mushroom; in a US study, 74% of reishi supplements did not contain the listed ingredients. Puro named poor-quality material from China as the industry's biggest risk, and argued that the usual quality markers, polysaccharides and beta-glucans, are not what delivers the benefits. Each species should be specified on its own compounds: hericenones and hericenes for lion's mane, cordycepin for cordyceps, ganoderic and lucidenic acids for reishi, inotodiol for chaga.

Puro closed with their NordRelease extraction, which their slide credits with 92% bioavailability, and trials under way on lion's mane and chaga.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Market: from $25B to $65B "in ten years" on one slide, and $31B growing to $65B by 2030 at 11% CAGR on another, both credited to Horizon Grand View Research; growth of 31% in 2023, credited to the American Botanical Council (slide 3) (slide 4) (slide 5).
- Their company's lion's mane trial: healthy adults, four weeks, 50 participants, lion's mane extract against caffeine and placebo (La Monica et al. 2023); their slide says lion's mane "improves cognitive performance, enhancing working memory, complex attention, and reaction time" (slide 11) (slide 12).
- Quality failures: 13 of 19 Italian mushroom supplements did not contain the listed mushroom; 74% of US reishi supplements did not contain the listed ingredients, 58% showed no reishi triterpenes, and a key reishi polysaccharide was found in only 26.3% (slide 16) (slide 18).
- "The biggest industry risk is poor quality material from China." (slide 19)
- Polysaccharides and beta-glucans are, Puro said, not responsible for the benefits people want; quality should be specified on each species' own compounds (slide 21) (slide 22) (slide 23).
- Extraction, as their slide puts it: water 5% bioavailability, dual alcohol-and-water extraction 50% and flagged as "Novel non EU approved extraction technology", NordRelease 92% (slide 25).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: we sell lion's mane, reishi, chaga and cordyceps extracts and a mushroom blend, and our specs lead with polysaccharides and beta-glucans, the markers Puro called the wrong ones (slide 21). My reading: expect customers who heard this to ask for hericenone and hericene, cordycepin, triterpene and inotodiol content; one of our lion's mane extracts already states 1% hericenone.
- Their adulteration evidence and their warning about Chinese material (slide 16) (slide 18) (slide 19). My reading: identity testing and origin for each mushroom SKU should be ready before a customer asks.
- Their slide calls dual extraction a novel technology not approved in the EU (slide 25). My reading: check how each of our mushroom extracts is made and its Novel Food status before selling into the EU; this is their claim and needs checking against the Novel Food catalogue.
- Nordic Mushrooms is a possible supplier or partner for a Finnish, compound-specified range; my reading, not a lead yet.
- Related: the mind-health session's other speakers, e.g. singer-biogena-cognitive-health; caffeine as the comparator ties to the energy positioning in veenstra-hmt-branding.
summary.Quotes:
- "13 out of 19 products tested did not contain the actual listed mushroom." (slide 16)
- "74% of reishi mushroom supplements did not contain the ingredients listed on the product." (slide 18)
- "The biggest industry risk is poor quality material from China." (slide 19)
- "It’s important to align the needs of consumers with the compounds per species." (slide 23)
summary.Follow-ups:
- Read La Monica et al. 2023 to see what it measured (the title says acute effects, with guayusa) and whether it supports the "stacking effect" and caffeine-tolerance points (slide 11) (slide 12).
- Check the production method, origin and Novel Food status of each of our mushroom extracts against their dual-extraction point (slide 25).
- Ask our mushroom suppliers for compound-level specifications (hericenones, hericenes, cordycepin, triterpenes, inotodiol) (slide 23).
- Contact Eric Puro (closing slide) about NordRelease and the three ongoing trials (slide 27) (slide 28).

- Slide numbers are the PDF's pages (28). The title slide reads "Honest and potent mushroom extracts from Finland"; several slides are headed "KÄÄPÄ Mushrooms", and their contact and the NordRelease news link are at Kääpä Biotech (slide 1) (slide 9) (slide 25) (slide 28).
- The market chart is in US$M, 2018 to 2030, with bars from about 20,000 in 2018 to about 65,000 in 2030, read from the chart; its two headline figures differ, $25B as the 2020 start on one slide and $31B as today's market on another (slide 3) (slide 5). Slide 4 carries both a Grand View label and the American Botanical Council Market Report Issue 141 as sources for the 31% figure (slide 4).
- A large market means a large body of research: "1586 results for Reishi alone" (slide 6).
- Lion's mane, as their slides put it: nerve growth factor stimulation, BDNF, "reduction of amyloid beta plaque build-up", neuroprotective and neurocognitive benefits, gastroprotective effects; primary compounds hericenones and hericenes. The problem slide reads "Loss of NGF", and a footnote says depression correlates with significantly lower NGF levels (Chen et al. 2015) (slide 7) (slide 9) (slide 10).
- The paper shown is La Monica et al., "Acute Effects of Naturally Occurring Guayusa Tea and Nordic Lion's Mane Extracts on Cognitive Performance", Nutrients 2023; 15(24): 5018. The slide calls it the "first human clinical research with healthy adults" (slide 11).
- Their slide's further points on the trial: "Results steadily growing weekly", a "stacking effect" of neuroregeneration in which "the impact on mood and cognition effectively gets better every time", and caffeine's effect diminishing over time "because the body builds tolerance" (slide 12).
- Myelin: quoted findings that H. erinaceus extract and its compounds HeA and HeS "display promising functional effects and promote OL maturation", and a regulatory effect on myelin genesis in vitro, under the heading "Potential for myelin regeneration" (slide 13).
- The Italian study is Risoli et al., "Mushroom-Based Supplements in Italy: Let's Open Pandora's Box" (PubMed 36771482): most facilities lacked internationally recognised GMP and some products had contaminants above legal limits (slide 15) (slide 16).
- The US study is Wu et al., "Evaluation on Quality Consistency of Ganoderma Lucidum (Reishi) Dietary Supplements Collected in the United States", Scientific Reports 2017; it concluded quality consistency "was poor" (slide 17) (slide 18).
- Quality markers Puro showed as current: beta-glucans (a Nammex white paper), polysaccharides (Chinese products); their alternative is "bioactive compounds (beyond beta glucans)" (slide 22).
- Compounds and benefits by species: chaga, inotodiol, for longevity and antioxidants; reishi, ganoderic and lucidenic acids, for calmness and sleep; lion's mane, hericenones and hericenes, for brain health and focus; cordyceps, cordycepin and adenosine, for energy and endurance (slide 23).
- History: Ötzi the Iceman (3230 BC) carried two polypores, one probably used medicinally; mushrooms in Han Dynasty medicine (202 to 220 AD); NordRelease introduced in 2019, with a linked news item titled as an EU approval of Kääpä Biotech's NordRelease extract powders (slide 25).
- Trials under way: lion's mane and neurogenesis over 3 months; chaga and stem cell regeneration in healthy ageing; chaga and mitochondrial function and longevity (slide 27).

# Regulatory Updates, Challenges & Opportunities in Active Nutrition: transcript

summary.Summary:
Luca Bucchini, Chair of ESSNA, the European trade association for sports and active nutrition, set out the regulatory issues facing the sector in Europe.

The biggest is maximum amounts of vitamins and minerals. Limits differ between member states today, so a product legal in Belgium may not be legal in Italy. The European Commission has restarted work to harmonise them, and a leaked working document suggested very restrictive limits: sodium might not be allowed in electrolyte drinks without added sugars, and vitamin B6 or potassium might not be allowed in drinks. Bucchini said the real cost is lost functionality and lost health claims, not one-off reformulation. Yet harmonisation matters: if it fails, France and perhaps Germany may set even tighter limits.

Bucchini then covered health claims, where approvals have dried up and botanical claims remain on hold; novel foods, where the scope has grown and approval is slow and costly; the Green Claims Directive; ultra-processed foods, whose definition could catch sports products; and influencers normalising steroids for Gen Z.

Their conclusion: after many years of regulatory certainty, the sector faces a new wave of concern. If the maximum levels are set right, they could open markets.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The European Commission plans EU-wide maximum amounts for vitamins and minerals in supplements and fortified foods; details "may change", but "very restrictive" limits may come, for example no sodium in electrolyte drinks without added sugars [00:00] (slide 7).
- Bucchini said the real loss would be functionality and the ability to make authorised health claims, not one-off reformulation costs [00:00] (slide 8).
- Harmonisation still matters: if it fails, "France (and potentially Germany)" appear poised to propose even more restrictive maximum amounts [00:00] (slide 8).
- Health claims: valid claims have been rejected, "on hold" botanical claims fragment the market, approvals have stopped and applications have fallen to zero; new sports probiotics cannot communicate their benefits [00:00] (slide 9).
- Novel foods: the regulation's scope has expanded and approval is "expensive, lengthy and complex"; the EFSA performance review may be a chance to streamline it [00:00] (slide 10).
- Influencers are making steroid use look normal to Gen Z; ESSNA is working with authorities, Europol included, and calls on the industry to explain what safe sports nutrition is [00:00] [14:58] (slide 13).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance high: EU maximum amounts, health claims and novel food rules decide what our customers can formulate and say with our ingredients.
- Our vitamin and mineral ingredients (the iron and magnesium bisglycinates, BioK2 MK-7, Advifolate) sit inside the maximum-amounts work (slide 7). My reading: follow ESSNA's position and the Commission's draft so we can tell customers early if a dose they use is at risk.
- Botanical claims stay on hold (slide 9). My reading: for botanicals we sell, such as KSM-66 ashwagandha, pitches rest on the science, not on an EU claim, and that will not change soon.
- Novel food approval is slow and costly (slide 10). My reading: any new ingredient we bring to the EU should have its novel food status settled before launch plans.

- "So it's a difficult balancing act, we still hope." Luca Bucchini [00:00]
- "So it's very difficult to do innovation." Luca Bucchini [00:00]
- "Ultra-Processed Foods should not be our concern," (slide 14)

summary.Summary:
Ewa Hudson of Lumina Intelligence presented consumer survey data on biotics and health tech. The deck is the short version released for distribution. Their question: how changing health goals, medicines such as GLP-1 drugs and technology shape what consumers buy for their microbiome.

The data come from Lumina's Global Nutrition Research for NutraIngredients, November 2024, with 6,000 respondents. In the five European countries shown, ageing in good health and better sleep are the top two health goals. Sleep, stress and mental health lead for younger adults; longevity enters the top three at 45 to 54 and leads from 55.

Europeans who take biotics do so mainly for the gut microbiome, general wellbeing and immunity. Few take them for sleep or mood, or alongside antibiotics. Hudson set this against two numbers: 84% think they lead a healthy life, yet 70% took antibiotics, GLP-1 drugs, laxatives, metformin or proton-pump inhibitors in the past two years.

Their close was technology. Over half use health or fitness apps, and almost all of those buy a product an app recommends at least once a year. Their message: tech is changing behaviour, so build new habits on it.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Ageing in good health and longevity ranks first or second as a health goal in all five countries; better sleep ranks first in France and the UK; mood and mental health ranks first in Spain (slide 5).
- By age, sleep, stress and mental health are the top three goals from 18 to 44; longevity joins at 45 to 54 and leads at 55 to 64 and 65 plus, with sleep and weight, read from the chart (slide 6).
- Why Europeans take biotic supplements, food and beverages: to improve the gut microbiome 15%, general wellbeing 14%, immunity 14%, digestive issues 10%, energy 8%, sleep 6%; alongside antibiotics only 4% (slide 7).
- 84% believe they lead a very or fairly healthy life, but 70% took antibiotics, GLP-1 drugs, laxatives, metformin or proton-pump inhibitors in the past two years; regular users: antibiotics 7%, GLP-1 receptor agonists 5%, laxatives 8% (slide 8).

summary.Summary:
Nora Cavani, co-founder of Alba Health, pitched as one of NutraIngredients' Probiota Pioneers for 2025. Alba Health, based in Sweden, sells a gut microbiome test for children aged nought to two, with a diet plan and probiotic recommendations.

Cavani started the company after their own eczema. Their argument is that how microbes settle in a baby's gut in the first years is linked to later asthma, obesity, eczema and allergies, and to everyday symptoms such as colic and constipation that have no good answer today. Testing early could spot imbalances and correct them with diet, lifestyle and possibly probiotics.

Their edge is data: a partnership with a University of Helsinki study that followed 1,000 children for over six years, and its own Swedish cohort of 300 children. Customers report their children's eczema or constipation easing, though no trial was presented.

In the panel Cavani said their biggest hurdle is consumer education. Alba Health sells no probiotics of its own and recommends other companies' products with clinical evidence; Cavani said most customers buy the one recommended. Given money for one thing, Cavani would spend it on marketing.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The product: "a gut microbiome test specifically developed for children, zero to two years old", used to detect imbalances early, restore them with diet and possibly probiotics, and track development [14:42].
- Evidence claimed is the partner cohort: 1,000 children followed for over six years, over 10,000 samples, over 50,000 data points on diet and health; Cavani said a 2024 paper showed an early-life test predicts later allergies, coughs, colds and crying [14:42].
- Results so far are customer reports: "a lot of our users and customers tell us that their children's eczema or constipation significantly reduced" [14:42].
- Alba Health recommends existing probiotics from other companies and takes no profit on them; "most of our customers buy the probiotic we recommend" [49:19].
- Trust comes from a scientific advisory board with doctors from each market, and simple messages through social media and podcasts [47:04].
- 90% of customers opt into research [14:42] [51:58].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance low: a test for infants, outside our sports and healthy-ageing markets and our range.
- My reading: an independent recommender that sells nothing itself can drive which branded probiotic a parent buys. That is a channel worth knowing for any partner with a clinically backed strain.
- My reading: the panel's shared lesson, that education is the hurdle and that a neutral expert voice beats ads, applies to how we pitch evidence-based ingredients to brands.
summary.Quotes:
- "the gut microbiome in early life is both linked to here and now, symptoms that have no solution today, but also to health later life" [14:42]
- "when people see ads, they're so used to just filtering them out as ads" [49:19]
- "we every time we deliver our results, we do that with a certified nutrition and health coach" [55:45]
summary.Follow-ups:
- Confirm the start time, the co-founder's name and the currency of the funding figure.
- The 2024 University of Helsinki paper on early-life microbiome tests and later health, if infant or family nutrition ever comes up.
summary.Detail:
- Figures Cavani gave: one in three people in the US has an allergic disease and almost two in three a chronic disease; the UN puts chronic diseases' cost at $47 trillion by 2030; 40% of US children have at least one chronic disease; over 50% of babies have unresolved symptoms such as colic and constipation [14:42].
- Cavani tied this to diet: a Swedish public health warning, two days earlier, that children eat more processed food and little fibre [14:42].
- Own cohort: 300 children, over 1,000 samples, over 300,000 health data points, with universities in Sweden, Denmark and Belgium [14:42].
- Company: started three years earlier with a professor co-founder; 2.6 million raised in pre-seed in the past year; "well over 1000 tests since the fall"; a market opportunity Cavani put at 80 billion; publications in microbiome science rose to 20,000 a year in 2024 [14:42].
- Each sample carries answers to over 300 questions on diet, probiotic and formula use; Alba Health complies with GDPR and uses a consent form [51:58].
- On whether testing makes parents of healthy children anxious: Cavani said they have not seen it; results are delivered on a call with a nutrition and health coach, with doctors for children with symptoms [55:45].
- Their differentiator: scientific credibility with universities and doctors plus very simple explanations, both in-house [51:58].
- The moderator described Alba Health as a Danish-Swedish company using machine learning and metagenomics [13:38]. Figures date from February 2025.

summary.Summary:
Arno Bouwens, R&D Director at Perseus Biomics, one of NutraIngredients' Probiota Pioneers for 2025, presented DynaMAP, the company's way of profiling a microbiome without sequencing. Their problem: benefits are strain-specific and labels must name the strain, but today's methods have low resolution and sensitivity.

DynaMAP labels long strands of native DNA with fluorescent dye at a short sequence motif, stretches and images them, and matches each pattern of dots to a reference database. Because it reads genome structure, Bouwens said it can tell apart strains almost identical in sequence, without PCR amplification.

Their evidence is the company's own preprint. In a standard mock community all strains were found, spikes down to 0.1% were detected, and strains up to 99.9% identical were told apart. On a stool sample, results matched shotgun sequencing closely.

Bouwens closed with the roadmap: a profiling service from the company's lab in Belgium with under five days' turnaround, available now, and a benchtop device from the second quarter of 2025.

In the panel Bouwens said customers had failed to find their own probiotic in samples with amplification-based methods. Their customers are experts, so the hurdle is conservatism, not education; new money would go on marketing.
summary.Key takeaways:
- The pitch: strain specificity drives benefit, and labels must declare genus, species and strain, yet current methods face low resolution, sensitivity issues and noise (slide 2).
- The method reads 100,000+ long native DNA molecules per sample in under 20 minutes; the label pattern on each is a taxonomic barcode "down to strain level" (slide 4). Strains with average nucleotide identity (ANI) above 99.5% were told apart, and up to 99.9% in the mock community (slide 7) (slide 8).
- In the Zymo D6300 mock community it had a 100% recall rate, no significant Gram-positive against Gram-negative bias, a limit of detection better than 0.1%, and no false positives above 0.05% (slide 6).
- On one healthy adult's stool sample, profiles correlated 70 to 80% (log-log) with shotgun metagenomic sequencing, with equivalent reproducibility (slide 9).
- In the panel: customers came to Perseus after failing to detect their probiotic in samples, "most likely because of amplification bias"; shotgun sequencing and DynaMAP found it [54:50].
- Roadmap: a service from an EU-based central lab, under 5 business days, available now; a fully automated benchtop device with a 6-hour turnaround, from Q2 2025 (slide 10).
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance low: a microbiome testing technology for probiotic makers and researchers; it touches none of our ingredients or our sports and healthy-ageing markets.
- My reading: strain-level identity checks matter to probiotic brands and their quality control, the same proof-of-identity question buyers ask of any branded ingredient. Background only.

- "Strains specificity maximizes therapeutic benefits…" (slide 2)
- "DynaMAP measures strain-level resolved microbiome profiles" (slide 5)
- "Strains with ANI higher than 99.5% can be differentiated with DynaMAP!" (slide 7)
- "amplification bias can be so strong that it altogether misses some species" [54:50]

summary.Detail:
- Slide 2 reproduces a figure from Spacova et al., Frontiers in Microbiology 2023: probiotic foods and probiotic supplements, the claims generally possible (structure-function, nutrient, general or strain-specific health claims and disease risk reduction, requiring pre-approval), and the labelling of genus, species, subspecies and strain (slide 2).
- Five steps and times: high-molecular-weight DNA extraction; fluorescent labelling (about 60 minutes); molecular combing (about 10 minutes); optical mapping (about 20 minutes); matching to a reference database (about 30 minutes) (slide 3).
- Strains can share over 99% ANI yet differ in genome structure; DynaMAP labels a site such as "TCGA" on fragments over 30 kbp and reads native DNA without amplification (slide 5).
- Mock community: eight bacteria at 12.5% each, three easy-to-lyse Gram-negative and five tough-to-lyse Gram-positive; spike-ins at 1%, 0.1% and 0.01%; the 1% and 0.1% spikes were reliably detected by both DynaMAP and sequencing (slide 6).
- Strain test: the reference database held all complete NCBI genomes over 200 kb; for Enterococcus faecalis the true strain was identified and the nearest false positives had ANI over 99.9% (slide 7). The slide's own definition puts the strain threshold at ANI 99.5% to 99.9% (slide 8).
- Stool test: five aliquots of one sample, compared with Kraken classification of sequencing on the same reference database, GTDB taxonomy (slide 9).
- Spoken: the central lab is "based in Belgium", turnaround "less than five days", and the device for use in a customer's own lab is being introduced "this year" [31:35].
- The shotgun comparison used about 10 gigabases of sequencing [43:01].
- Cost: "we were able to reach the same level as 60 this" (Otter; the method compared is unclear), including sample preparation and bioinformatics; a relative abundance profile is delivered [43:21].
- Customers hold their data and can reprocess it, under the FAIR principles [50:35]. What makes a microbiome start-up stand out, Bouwens said, is data quality, comparable across technologies [53:58].
- All performance data are the company's own, from its preprint (bioRxiv, December 2024) (slide 6). Figures and the roadmap date from February 2025; whether the benchtop device launched is not known. No slide is marked Confidential.

summary.Summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired the Day 1 gut-brain panel after the break. Siobhain O'Mahony of APC Microbiome Ireland and Julia Rode of Örebro University had spoken before it; Katie Guzzetta of ETH Zurich and Emily Prpa, head of science at Yakult UK and Ireland, joined them. Daniells's question: how far does the science on gut microbes and the brain really go?

The panel agreed it is early. Most human evidence comes from clinical groups, such as people with depression, where probiotics helped as an add-on to treatment rather than on their own. Data on cognition in humans are sparse, and trials in healthy people are few, short and measure small shifts on subjective scales. Prpa said nutritional psychiatry is only about 50 years old and that probiotics are food, not medicine.

On products, nobody could say whether single strains or blends work better, and O'Mahony said formulators are limited to the few strains that are stable and safe. Prebiotics may need the right bacteria present first, which points to synbiotics.

Guzzetta brought mouse work: faecal transplants from young to old mice improved memory, and gut-made acetate reached the brain. Guzzetta warned that gut-made serotonin or GABA probably does not reach the brain. The recording ends as the panel turned to athletes' microbiomes.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Most of the evidence is in clinical populations, with only a handful of studies in healthy people, and what counts as a good enough outcome in a healthy person is still unclear (Emily Prpa) [1:03:46].
- In bipolar and major depressive disorder, probiotics "can be well effective when used as an adjunct, not when administered on their own"; Prpa said translating that to the everyday person is not there yet, and randomised trials run about 12 weeks at most [1:08:40].
- Cognition in humans has little data; probiotics are the best studied, "But also there, it's quite sparse", and repeat testing makes change hard to capture (Julia Rode) [1:06:34] [1:07:09]. The panel asked whether prevention, before disease, is the window to act [1:07:33] [1:08:00].
- Single strain or multi-strain cannot be called: the studies differ in products, doses and durations (Rode) [1:11:44]; O'Mahony finds the single-strain evidence compelling but says formulators can only use the few strains that are stable and safe [1:12:47].

# Otter.ai's automatic summary, as received. Not ours.

Recording "Probiotic brain - morinaga & debate" (https://otter.ai/u/N8RsEzPJAJ1NAWHYtprSTk53jUE). It covers the whole recording: the Morinaga talk (morinaga-b-breve-cognitive) and the gut-brain panel (gut-brain-debate-psychobiotics).

The discussion focused on the role of probiotics, particularly MCC 1274, in cognitive health and dementia prevention. Key points included the increasing global dementia rates, with 46 million cases in 2015 and projected to double by 2050. MCC 1274, a human residential strain, showed promising results in clinical trials, improving cognitive function and reducing brain atrophy. The conversation also highlighted the need for more research on sex differences in microbiome studies, the potential of prebiotics, and the challenges of translating research to healthy populations. The panel emphasized the importance of personalized approaches and the role of in silico methods in advancing psychobiotic research.

detail.text: Sex differences are under-studied, even in animals; Guzzetta called this "really, really critical", and O'Mahony said it would help male-based therapies too [1:02:53] [1:03:32].
In rodents there is a decent amount of data linking microbes to memory; in humans, O'Mahony said longitudinal studies going back to the years before symptoms are needed [1:05:06].

Prpa: nutritional psychiatry, food or supplements as an adjunct or alternative to treatments such as antidepressants, is "like 50 years young"; a one-point drop on a subjective stress scale may be statistically significant but not felt [1:08:40].

O'Mahony said they are developing a women's health supplement; half the strains first chosen were not stable or possible to put into a capsule, so fibres are used to support the bacteria wanted [1:14:15].
Prpa: probiotics show strength in depression; for cognition there is "some interesting data out there" on relational memory; prebiotics show their strength in cognition and memory [1:15:27].
Guzzetta: preclinical work in mice found that phages isolated from faeces and given back after stress reverted the stress response, so the virome may also be a target [1:16:54].

Guzzetta: about 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut but probably does not change systemic levels; whether tryptophan- or serotonin-producing bacteria act through those metabolites is unclear [1:19:11].
Guzzetta: a 2021 mouse study traced carbon-13 labelled acetate from the gut to the brain, where it entered microglia [1:21:23].

Guzzetta's own study: faecal transplants from young to aged mice improved long-term memory and changed 35 metabolites in the hippocampus; Guzzetta pointed to Sean Gibbons's talk the next day on ageing trajectories (sean-gibbons-ageing-gut-microbiome) [1:22:59].

Two case studies in Alzheimer's patients reported improved scores after faecal transplants, with follow-up to 12 weeks in one; Guzzetta noted the risks, and that many transplant trials were halted [1:24:41] [1:25:40].
Rode and Guzzetta: short-chain fatty acids may affect blood-brain barrier permeability in cell culture, and act through immune cells that reach the brain [1:26:21] [1:27:00].
Daniells asked whether, as with elite athletes and centenarians, special strains could be mined for psychobiotics [1:27:13].

takeaways.text: Most of the evidence is in clinical populations, with only a handful of studies in healthy people, and what counts as a good enough outcome in a healthy person is still unclear (Emily Prpa) [1:03:46].

In bipolar and major depressive disorder, probiotics "can be well effective when used as an adjunct, not when administered on their own"; Prpa said translating that to the everyday person is not there yet, and randomised trials run about 12 weeks at most [1:08:40].

Cognition in humans has little data; probiotics are the best studied, "But also there, it's quite sparse", and repeat testing makes change hard to capture (Julia Rode) [1:06:34] [1:07:09]. The panel asked whether prevention, before disease, is the window to act [1:07:33] [1:08:00].

Single strain or multi-strain cannot be called: the studies differ in products, doses and durations (Rode) [1:11:44]; O'Mahony finds the single-strain evidence compelling but says formulators can only use the few strains that are stable and safe [1:12:47].

A single prebiotic such as inulin may fail in depressed people whose gut lacks the bacteria to make short-chain fatty acids; Prpa suggested the gut may need conditioning first [1:15:27]. Guzzetta said a synbiotic may be needed [1:14:52].
Mechanisms remain open: gut-made neurotransmitters probably do not reach the brain (Guzzetta) [1:19:11], and the effect is "definitely not only inflammation" (Rode) [1:26:21].

"I think it's definitely not only inflammation." (Julia Rode) [1:26:21]

summary.Summary:
Stephen Daniells of NutraIngredients chaired the panel that closed the opening postbiotics session. Maria Rescigno and Simone Guglielmetti, the two speakers, were joined by Richard Day of ADM, Hongwei Wang of Biogrowing and Marco Pane.

Asked why postbiotics opened a probiotics event, Rescigno called them a possible next generation that acts without depending on the host. Guglielmetti said every probiotic product already holds postbiotics. On safety, Guglielmetti said yes, they are safer, from a 2023 review of trials. Wang and Pane said it must be measured, not assumed.

On efficacy, Day said ADM's heat-treated ES1 strain matched its live form in one trial in adults with diarrhoea-predominant IBS. With its BPL1 strain the two forms differed in metabolic effects. Guglielmetti stressed that the way cells are killed changes the product. Pane favoured flow cytometry for counting cells.

On regulation, George of the IPA said no government is yet ready to regulate postbiotics; some call them marketing. Wang described China's stepwise route. Pane warned against a health-benefit definition, citing the EU's claims experience, and saw new formats such as shelf-stable juices and cosmetics. Audience questions covered mechanism and the microbiome; Rescigno and Day reported clinical effects with little change in microbiome composition.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Guglielmetti: "it's not possible to have a probiotic product without postbiotic inside", and postbiotics are sometimes the real reason probiotics work [04:48].
- Safety is split: Guglielmetti cites a 2023 review of about 52 trial papers, including preterm infants, with extremely low side effects; Wang says it cannot be generally claimed, and Pane says postbiotics "may be safer" but it must be measured [06:22] [07:48] [08:55].
- ADM (Day): ES1 as heat-treated whole cells and as a live probiotic gave "pretty much identical" results in a published trial in adults with diarrhoea-predominant IBS; for BPL1, the postbiotic had a more pronounced effect on glucose control and the probiotic on BMI [11:29].
- How cells are inactivated matters: gamma-irradiated biomass kept membrane integrity and enzyme activity over 18 months of storage, and differed from the same biomass heat-treated; Guglielmetti was unsure gamma irradiation is allowed in EU food [14:49].
- Regulation: George of the IPA says some governments call postbiotics marketing and none is ready to put forward a regulation yet [28:56]; Biogrowing is helping lead a postbiotics standard with the Chinese Nutrition Society [25:18].
- Pane sees formats beyond capsules: no live-cell stability problem, so juices that keep longer and cosmetics become possible [31:55].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance low: postbiotics are outside our range, and none of creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm comes up.
- My reading: Pane's format point is the one that touches us. Shelf-stable postbiotics could appear in drinks and powders next to our ingredients, as co-actives rather than competitors.
- My reading: Pane's warning about defining a category by health benefit, after the EU's claims experience, matches what our own ingredients face under EU health-claim rules.
- ADM's ES1 and BPL1 figures are ADM's own, from its published trials as Day described them; we have not checked them.

- "postbiotics are sometimes the real reason why probiotics work" [04:48]
- "So in principle, os biotics mean, may be safer, but it's something that has to be measured" [08:55]
- "So some governments tell me it's marketing." [28:56]
- "you don't have to care about stability in the classic thermal viability of the cells" [31:55]

- Find ADM's published ES1 trial in IBS and its BPL1 metabolic trials before quoting any figure.
- Confirm Marco Pane's and Simone Guglielmetti's organisations, and George's surname, from the programme.
- Check whether the Chinese Nutrition Society postbiotics standard has been published.

- Rescigno says the production set-up took almost 10 years and makes metabolites without culture medium, under patent [02:24].

summary.Summary:
Professor Maria Rescigno of Humanitas University spoke second, on why their group works with postbiotics. The gut keeps its microbes behind a two-layer mucus wall, the epithelium and a gut vascular barrier that their group described. Postbiotics, Rescigno argues, are small enough to cross all three, so they are "the mediators" of a probiotic's benefit.

Their postbiotics are metabolites made by fermenting a fibre with a Lactobacillus paracasei strain, in a patented process that also removes the gas. In their lab work the postbiotic, not the live bacteria, damped inflammatory signals in immune cells and in gut tissue from patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Live probiotics made that tissue worse.

Rescigno then linked a leaky gut to liver disease and, through a second barrier in the brain, to anxiety and depression. In mice, pre-treatment with the postbiotic protected the gut barrier against Salmonella. In a trial at Humanitas in women with breast cancer on a CDK4/6 inhibitor, no patient taking the postbiotic had grade 3 diarrhoea or had to cut or stop treatment in the first cycle. In mice it also made immunotherapy work better. Rescigno closed on personalised use.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Postbiotics can cross the inner mucus layer, the epithelium and the gut vascular barrier, so Rescigno calls them the mediators of a probiotic's benefit [01:59].
- Their postbiotics are metabolites of Lactobacillus paracasei fermenting a fibre, separated from the bacteria; the patented process removes the gas that fibre can cause [01:59].
- In tissue from patients with inflammatory bowel disease, the probiotics tested worsened inflammation while the postbiotic reduced it [01:59].
- In mice, one week of a high-fat diet opened the gut vascular barrier and let bacteria reach the liver; pre-treatment with the postbiotic protected the barrier against Salmonella [01:59].
- In a Humanitas trial in women with breast cancer on a CDK4/6 inhibitor, grade 3 diarrhoea was avoided and no dose was cut or stopped while patients took the postbiotic; it returned when they stopped [01:59].

- Relevance low: postbiotics are outside our range, and none of creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm comes up.
- My reading: the claims are clinical and mechanistic (inflammatory bowel disease, cancer therapy), far from the healthy-consumer supplement claims our customers can make.
- My reading: their process, a probiotic fermenting a fibre, ties the prebiotic and postbiotic stories together; fibre suppliers may pitch this.

summary.Summary:
Simone Guglielmetti opened the first day with the postbiotics roadmap that the International Probiotics Association (IPA) has coordinated. Their starting point is confusion. Academic definitions disagree, and products sold as postbiotics range from heat-killed cells to metabolites and even sodium butyrate. For the talk Guglielmetti used a broad working definition: any non-viable agent of microbial origin that confers a physiological benefit.

The roadmap is meant for commercial and regulatory use, which academic definitions do not address. It was reworked after about 400 stakeholder comments received in July. Its decision tree asks, in order: is it alive, was it inactivated on purpose, is it meant for food and supplements rather than disease, and is the parent microbe safe or approved? Purified molecules are now left out. What remains falls into four groups: microbial metabolites, intact cells, fragmented cells and complex mixtures. Guglielmetti placed real products in each, with pasteurised Akkermansia as the intact-cell case.

Their aim is to stop postbiotics being seen as a marketing gimmick. The paper was in draft. In questions Guglielmetti said the IPA kept the word "postbiotic" because the market uses it, that yeast extract would count, and that the evidence needed for a benefit depends on each regulator.
summary.Key takeaways:
- Definitions clash: the academic one Guglielmetti cites covers inactivated cells and fragments but excludes metabolites, while products sold online use the word for metabolites, sodium butyrate and heat-killed cells [00:00].
- The IPA-coordinated roadmap was revised after "around 400 different specific comments from stakeholders", mostly companies, received in July [00:00].
- The decision tree's gates: not alive (probiotics and phages are out), intentional and reproducible inactivation, food or supplement use rather than treating disease, and a safe or approved parent microbe [00:00].
- Purified molecules (a metabolite, an enzyme, butyrate, beta-glucans) are now outside the category, one of the biggest changes made [00:00].
- Four groups remain: microbial metabolites (MM), intact cells (IC), fragmented cells (FC) and complex (CX), with combinations counted as complex [00:00].
- In questions Guglielmetti said the word "postbiotic" was reinstated because companies use it widely, and that excluding metabolites would mostly create confusion [17:15].
summary.For Vita Actives:
- Relevance low: postbiotics are outside our range, and none of creatine, clear pea protein or Oxystorm comes up.
- My reading: the decision tree is a useful model for how an industry body tidies a loose ingredient term before regulators do it; the same pressure could reach other loosely used category names.
- My reading: the gate on a safe or approved parent microbe mirrors the novel-food and QPS logic in the UCAM postbiotics-regulation talk at the same event (ucam-postbiotics-new-frontier).
summary.Quotes:
- "the word postbiotics is used to indicate any non viable agents of microbial origin that is conferring beneficial physiological effects" [00:00]
- "The inactivation must be intentional." [00:00]
- "trying to avoid that the whole category of post bionics can be perceived as a commercial marketing gimmick" [00:00]

- Confirm Guglielmetti's organisation and the session's billed title and time from the Probiota 2025 programme.
summary.Detail:
- Their examples from an e-commerce search: metabolites produced by probiotics, sodium butyrate, heat-killed cells, and metabolites made by probiotics grown on prebiotics [00:00].
- The work began two to three years earlier (Guglielmetti gives both), was first shown in June at what Otter renders as the "IPC" probiotic conference, and drew on IPA members, regulators and governments' views [00:00].
- A parent microbe without a long history of safe use (not on the EU QPS list) can still be used once the final ingredient is approved by a competent authority [00:00].
- Akkermansia example: a product with pasteurised Akkermansia at 30 million units counted by flow cytometry; Guglielmetti says the live microbe had a negative QPS opinion in 2020 and a positive EFSA novel-food opinion a year later. Intact-cell group [00:00].
- Other examples: a lysate of lactic acid bacteria and bifidobacteria (fragmented cells); a fermented skim milk ingredient, heat-treated, with no separation from the medium (complex); hyaluronic acid purified from a non-food microbe (not a postbiotic); a cell-free product fermented by a paracasei strain (microbial metabolites) [00:00].
- All the groups still need notification or approval for efficacy; Guglielmetti did not cover efficacy [00:00].
- The roadmap paper was being finalised for publication [00:00].
- Yeast extract made in a standardised, reproducible way with a shown health benefit would, in their opinion, be a fragmented-cell postbiotic [18:50].
- On the burden of evidence Guglielmetti said they could not answer; it depends on regulators, and Europe's health-claim rules make it complex [19:32].
- Unfiltered beer with dead yeast could, in their opinion, be a food containing a postbiotic if standardised and a benefit shown, though it contains alcohol [20:12].
